modules.title: Complexity Analysis
modules.summary: Welcome to Complexity Analysis — the first module of the DSA & System Design Core, the shared spine of IL-13. I'm your instructor, and in this module we build the vocabulary of every technical interview: reading a solution's cost at a glance and saying it out loud without hand-waving. We cover Big-O, Big-Theta, and Big-Omega; time versus space as the two axes; amortized analysis through dynamic arrays; best, average, and worst-case reasoning; and where log n and n log n come from. By the end, you will state a complexity bound, the case it describes, and the dominant operation driving it — while pointing at your own code.
objectives: Understand and apply: big-O, Big-Theta, Big-Omega
Understand and apply: time vs space: the two axes
Understand and apply: amortized analysis: dynamic arrays
Understand and apply: best, average, and worst-case reasoning
Understand and apply: log n from halving; n log n from divide-and-conquer

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Big-O** — An upper bound on growth: f(n) is O(g(n)) if f grows no faster than a constant multiple of g for large n — the worst-case language interviews expect by default.
- **Big-Theta** — A tight bound: f(n) is Theta(g(n)) when it is both O(g(n)) and Omega(g(n)) — the growth rate pinned from both sides.
- **Big-Omega** — A lower bound on growth: f(n) is Omega(g(n)) if f grows at least as fast as a constant multiple of g — how you describe best cases and optimality.
- **Time complexity** — How the number of primitive operations scales with input size n — the axis interviewers ask about first.
- **Space complexity** — How auxiliary memory scales with n — the second axis; the tradeoff partner of time in nearly every optimization discussion.
- **Amortized analysis** — Averaging a costly operation's price over a whole sequence: a dynamic array's occasional O(n) resize spreads to O(1) per append across n appends.
- **Best / average / worst case** — Three lenses on one algorithm: quicksort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst case on sorted input with a naive pivot — the input distribution decides which you pay.
- **Log n from halving** — Each step discards a constant fraction of the problem — binary search halves n times, so the step count is log₂ n.
- **n log n from divide-and-conquer** — Divide into halves, do linear work per level: log n levels × n work per level — mergesort's shape, and the price of comparison-based sorting.
- **Dominant operation** — The operation whose count drives the bound — saying it out loud ('the nested scan of the inner loop') is what makes a complexity answer gradable.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Pick any two solutions you have written recently and, for each, state the time and space bound aloud in one sentence — bound, case, dominant operation.
2. Re-derive log n and n log n from scratch on paper: halving for binary search, levels-times-work for mergesort, until the derivation takes under sixty seconds.
3. Take one O(n²) solution you know (e.g. a nested-loop pair search) and write the hash-map version beside it; state both complexities and the space cost of the improvement.
4. Write the dynamic-array amortized argument in your own words: total cost of n appends with doubling, divided by n — then say it aloud as you would to an interviewer.
5. Run a timed drill: read an unseen problem statement and within two minutes name the pattern, the expected complexity, and the case (best/average/worst) you are quoting.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Complexity teardown of your own code. Pick three programs or solutions you have written — one you are proud of, one you suspect is slow, and one from a practice set. For each, write a one-page brief: the algorithm in two sentences, the time bound with the dominant operation named, the space bound, and the best/average/worst-case split where it applies. Then propose one concrete optimization for the slowest of the three and re-state its new bounds. Deliverable: three briefs plus the optimization — the exact artifacts you will narrate in a coding round.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: complexity fluency gets you past coding rounds, but it confers no credential — this course awards no certificate and no employer recognizes it as one. Interview rubrics differ by company and even by interviewer; the numbers here are practice for a human conversation, not a guarantee of an offer.

cards.front: An interviewer asks: ‘What’s the time complexity of your solution?’ What does a strong answer include?
cards.back: The Big-O bound, which case it describes (best/average/worst), the dominant operation driving it, and the space complexity — said out loud while pointing at the code, e.g. ‘O(n log n) time worst case from the sort, O(n) space for the output.’

cards.front: Time vs space: how do you discuss the tradeoff?
cards.back: As the two axes every solution is measured on: faster often costs memory (hash maps, memoization, caches), leaner often costs time (recompute vs store). The interview line: ‘I’ll name both complexities for every solution I propose.’

cards.front: How do you explain amortized analysis of a dynamic array in an interview?
cards.back: ‘Appending is O(1) amortized: most appends are constant time, and the occasional doubling resize costs O(n) but happens rarely enough that the cost spreads to O(1) per append across a sequence of n appends.’

cards.front: Why do interviewers ask for best, average, AND worst case?
cards.back: Because the bound alone hides behavior: quicksort is O(n log n) average but O(n²) worst case on sorted input — and the input distribution in the real system decides which one you actually pay.

cards.front: How do you derive log n and n log n on the spot?
cards.back: ‘Halving the problem each step gives log n levels — binary search. Divide-and-conquer that does linear work per level, like mergesort, gives n work × log n levels = n log n.’ Say the recurrence, then the level count.

quiz.q: Stating complexity aloud during coding:
choices: Makes your reasoning gradable and forces self-checks
quiz.explain: Verbalized reasoning is scorable reasoning — and it catches your own mistakes mid-stream.

quiz.q: Binary search on n sorted elements is O(log n) because:
choices: Each comparison halves the remaining search space
quiz.explain: Halving n times reaches 1 element: the number of halvings is log₂ n.

quiz.q: Quicksort with a naive first-element pivot on an already-sorted array degrades to:
quiz.explain: Bad pivots make partitions maximally unbalanced: n levels of n work each.

quiz.q: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. The amortized cost per append is:
quiz.explain: The O(n) copy cost of a resize is spread over the ~n/2 appends since the last resize: O(1) each.

modules.title: Arrays, Strings, and Hashing Patterns
modules.summary: Welcome to Arrays, Strings, and Hashing Patterns — module 2 of the DSA & System Design Core. I'm your instructor, and this is the highest-yield module in the path: the handful of patterns behind the majority of array and string questions, trained until recognition is instant. We cover two pointers (same-direction and opposite-ends), fixed and variable sliding windows, hash maps for O(1) lookups, prefix sums and difference arrays, and monotonic stacks and queues. By the end, you will map a novel problem to a known pattern and name its complexity within two minutes.
objectives: Understand and apply: two pointers: same and opposite ends
Understand and apply: sliding windows: fixed and variable
Understand and apply: hash maps for O(1) lookups
Understand and apply: prefix sums and difference arrays
Understand and apply: monotonic stacks and queues

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Two pointers (opposite ends)** — Pointers starting at both ends of ordered data and converging — sorted two-sum, container-with-most-water — O(n) time, O(1) space.
- **Two pointers (same direction)** — Fast/slow pointers moving through one pass — cycle detection, in-place dedup — O(n) time, O(1) space.
- **Sliding window** — A window over contiguous subarrays/substrings that expands on the right and shrinks on the left while a constraint is violated — each element enters and leaves once, hence O(n).
- **Hash map unlock** — Trading space for time: O(1) average lookups turn O(n²) pair-searches into O(n) single passes — two-sum, frequency counts, seen-sets.
- **Prefix sums** — pre[i] = sum of arr[0..i] after O(n) preprocessing, giving O(1) range sums: sum(i..j) = pre[j] − pre[i−1].
- **Difference arrays** — Range-update companion to prefix sums: mark +v at l and −v at r+1, then one prefix pass applies all range updates in O(n + q).
- **Monotonic stack** — A stack kept in increasing (or decreasing) order; each element is pushed and popped at most once — O(n) for next-greater-element and histogram problems that look O(n²).
- **Monotonic queue** — A deque maintaining candidates in order for sliding-window maximum/minimum — O(n) windowed extremes without rescanning.
- **Pattern recognition** — The interview skill this module trains: mapping an unseen problem to a known pattern under time pressure, then executing the template cleanly.
- **Fixed vs variable windows** — Fixed: the window size is given (max sum of k). Variable: the size adapts to a constraint (longest substring without repeats) — shrink the left edge while violated.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. For each of the five core patterns, write the 10-line template from memory (window loop, two-pointer loop, prefix build, hash-map single pass, monotonic stack) until it is mechanical.
2. Take one unseen array problem and run the recognition drill: read the prompt, name the pattern aloud in under two minutes, state the expected complexity, then code it.
3. Solve two-sum three ways — brute force O(n²), sorted two-pointer O(n log n), hash map O(n) — and narrate the space-for-time tradeoff for each, as if an interviewer asked 'can you do better?'
4. Build a prefix-sum array by hand on a 6-element array, then answer three range-sum queries from it without rescanning — verify each against a brute-force sum.
5. Do a timed set: five problems, 20 minutes each, pattern-first. Log every miss as 'pattern seen late' or 'template fumbled' — that log is your next drill list.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Pattern atlas. Build a one-page reference you will actually use: for each pattern (two pointers, sliding window, hash map, prefix sums, monotonic stack/queue), write the recognition trigger ('sorted + pairs' → opposite-ends two pointers), the template in your language, the complexity, and one canonical problem it solves. Then validate the atlas: solve one unseen problem per pattern using only your atlas, timed at 20 minutes each. Deliverable: the atlas plus five solved write-ups naming where the atlas helped and where it didn't.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: patterns are recognition tools, not a guarantee — interviewers write problems designed to resist template-matching, and this course confers no certificate. Fluency here buys composure for the novel problems; it does not replace the thinking the novel problems require.

cards.front: When do you reach for two pointers?
cards.back: Ordered data and pair-finding: opposite ends for sorted two-sum or container-with-most-water; same-direction fast/slow pointers for cycle detection or in-place dedup — O(n) time, O(1) space. Name which variant and why.

cards.front: Sliding window vs two pointers: what’s the distinction you’d state in an interview?
cards.back: Sliding window is for contiguous subarrays/substrings under a constraint (max sum of k, longest substring without repeats): expand the right edge, shrink the left while the constraint is violated — O(n) because each element enters and leaves once.

cards.front: Why is ‘use a hash map’ the most common interview unlock?
cards.back: It trades space for time: O(1) average lookups turn O(n²) pair-searches into O(n) single passes — two-sum, frequency counts, memoization keys, and seen-sets all run on this trade.

cards.front: What do prefix sums buy you in an interview?
cards.back: O(1) range-sum queries after O(n) preprocessing: subarray sums become prefix[j] − prefix[i−1], and ‘subarray summing to k’ becomes a hash map over prefix values — the standard follow-up when brute force is O(n²).

cards.front: When does a monotonic stack appear in interviews?
cards.back: ‘Next greater element’ and histogram-rectangle problems: the stack keeps candidates in increasing order, and each element is pushed and popped once — O(n) for problems that look O(n²).

quiz.q: Pattern-recognition drilling works because interviews test:
choices: Mapping novel problems to known patterns under time pressure
quiz.explain: You’ll never see the exact problem again — but you’ll see the pattern.

quiz.q: A monotonic stack solves ‘next greater element’ in O(n) because:
choices: Each element is pushed and popped at most once
quiz.explain: Amortized O(1) work per element: once popped, an element never re-enters the stack.

quiz.q: With prefix[k] = sum of arr[0..k], the sum of arr[i..j] is:
quiz.explain: Subtract the sum before i from the sum through j; what remains is exactly arr[i..j].

quiz.q: A hash map reduces two-sum from O(n²) to O(n) because:
choices: Each complement lookup becomes O(1) average
quiz.explain: For each x, checking whether target−x was seen is one hash lookup instead of a full rescan.

modules.title: Trees, Graphs, and Recursion
modules.summary: Welcome to Trees, Graphs, and Recursion — module 3 of the DSA & System Design Core. I'm your instructor, and here we take the mystique out of non-linear structures: recursion with explicit base cases and call-stack costs, tree traversals, the BST invariant, heaps and priority queues, and graph representations with the BFS/DFS decision reflex every interview expects. By the end, you will write clean recursive solutions, choose adjacency lists by default, and justify heap versus sort in one sentence.
objectives: Understand and apply: recursion: base cases and the call stack
Understand and apply: binary trees: in-order, pre-order, post-order
Understand and apply: bSTs: invariants and operations
Understand and apply: heaps and priority queues
Understand and apply: graph representations: adjacency lists

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Recursion contract** — Base case first, then the recursive step's promise: 'assume it works for n−1, here is how I build n' — plus the call-stack cost: depth × frame size.
- **Pre-order traversal** — Visit node, then children — natural for copying trees and prefix expressions.
- **In-order traversal** — Left, node, right — yields sorted order on a BST; the traversal that proves the invariant.
- **Post-order traversal** — Children before the node — natural for deletion and bottom-up computations like subtree heights.
- **BST invariant** — Left subtree < node < right subtree at every node — buys O(log n) search/insert/delete when balanced; degenerate insertion order gives O(n) without balancing.
- **Heap** — A complete binary tree with the heap property: min or max at the root, push/pop in O(log n), peek in O(1) — for repeated access to the extreme, not full order.
- **Adjacency list** — The default interview graph representation: O(V+E) memory with fast neighbor iteration — the right choice for sparse graphs, which interview graphs are.
- **BFS** — Level-order exploration with a queue — shortest path in unweighted graphs, because the first visit to a node is via the fewest edges.
- **DFS** — Depth-first exploration with a stack or recursion — cycle detection, topological sort, connected components; watch the recursion depth.
- **Priority queue** — The abstract interface heaps implement: repeated min/max extraction — top-k, merge-k-sorted, streaming medians.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write in-order, pre-order, and post-order traversals from memory on a 7-node tree drawn on paper, then verify each against a hand simulation.
2. Implement a BST insert and search; then insert the sorted keys 1..n and observe the degeneration to O(n) — state aloud why balancing matters.
3. Solve one BFS problem (shortest path) and one DFS problem (cycle or component count) back to back, stating the representation choice ('adjacency list, sparse graph') before coding.
4. Implement top-k with a min-heap of size k and narrate the justification: 'I need repeated access to the extreme, not a full sort.'
5. Run the recursion drill: for any recursive solution, write the base case, the contract sentence, and the stack-depth bound before writing a single line of code.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Traversal and graph toolkit. Build a small library in your language: iterative and recursive traversals, BST insert/search with an invariant checker, a binary heap with push/pop, and BFS/DFS over adjacency lists. For each, include a one-paragraph docstring stating when to use it and its complexity. Then apply it: solve two tree problems and two graph problems using only your toolkit, and write a debrief on where the toolkit's shape helped or hindered. Deliverable: the toolkit plus four solved write-ups.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: traversal fluency and the BFS/DFS reflex are table stakes, not a differentiator — interviewers score the reasoning around the code, and this course confers no certificate. The toolkit is practice equipment; the graded artifact is how you think aloud while using it.

cards.front: How do you reason about recursion out loud in an interview?
cards.back: State the base case first, then the recursive step’s contract: ‘assume it works for n−1, here’s how I build n.’ Then name the call-stack cost — depth × frame size — because interviewers probe stack depth and overflow.

cards.front: In-order, pre-order, post-order — how do you keep them straight under pressure?
cards.back: It’s about when you visit the node relative to its children: pre = before, in = between (gives sorted order on a BST), post = after (children before parent — natural for deletion and bottom-up computations).

cards.front: What’s the BST invariant, and why do interviewers care?
cards.back: ‘Left subtree < node < right subtree’ at every node. It buys O(log n) search/insert/delete when balanced — and the follow-up is always about what breaks it: degenerate insertion order gives O(n) without balancing.

cards.front: Heap vs sorted array: how do you justify a heap in an interview?
cards.back: When you need the min/max repeatedly but not full order: push/pop in O(log n), peek in O(1). Top-k, merge-k-sorted, and streaming medians are heap problems — say ‘I need repeated access to the extreme, not a full sort.’

cards.front: How do you represent graphs in interviews?
cards.back: Adjacency lists by default: O(V+E) memory, fast neighbor iteration — the right choice for sparse graphs (which interview graphs are). Adjacency matrix only for dense graphs or O(1) edge queries. The interview line: ‘list unless I can say why matrix.’

quiz.q: Shortest path in an unweighted graph is a BFS problem because:
choices: BFS explores in increasing distance from the source
quiz.explain: BFS’s level order guarantees the first time you reach a node is via the fewest edges.

quiz.q: Adjacency lists beat matrices for typical interview graphs because:
choices: O(V+E) memory and fast neighbor iteration on sparse graphs
quiz.explain: Interview graphs are sparse; matrices would waste O(V²) on empty edges.

quiz.q: Finding the k largest elements in a stream is a heap problem because:
choices: A min-heap of size k keeps the k largest with O(log k) updates
quiz.explain: Keep a min-heap of the k best seen; each new element is compared against the heap top in O(log k).

quiz.q: A BST built by inserting the sorted keys 1..n degenerates to:
choices: A linked list with O(n) operations
quiz.explain: Each insertion goes right every time; height becomes n and the log-n guarantee evaporates.

modules.title: Dynamic Programming
modules.summary: Welcome to Dynamic Programming — module 4 of the DSA & System Design Core. I'm your instructor, and this is the module most candidates skip and most offers require. We demystify DP into a repeatable method: recurrence first, then memoization versus tabulation, the 1D ladder (climbing stairs, house robber), knapsack and subset patterns, and DP on strings (LCS, edit distance). By the end, you will define the state, write the recurrence, and name the overlapping subproblems before you write code — because interviewers score the recurrence, and the code is transcription.
objectives: Understand and apply: recurrence first: overlapping subproblems
Understand and apply: memoization vs tabulation
Understand and apply: the 1D ladder: climbing stairs, house robber
Understand and apply: knapsack and subset patterns
Understand and apply: DP on strings: LCS and edit distance

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Overlapping subproblems** — The property that makes DP valid: the same subproblems recur, so caching their results beats recomputation — the precondition you must name before memoizing.
- **Optimal substructure** — The optimal solution is built from optimal solutions to subproblems — the property that makes a recurrence correct.
- **Recurrence** — The decision equation — dp[i] = max(skip, take) — written in words before code; the single most-scored line of a DP answer.
- **Memoization** — Top-down DP: recursion plus a cache — natural to write, pays recursion overhead and risks stack depth.
- **Tabulation** — Bottom-up DP: iterate the table directly — no stack risk, often better constants; the same complexity as memoization, different direction.
- **State design** — Choosing what the state captures: exactly the information future decisions need — too little and the recurrence can't decide, too much and the table explodes.
- **1D DP ladder** — The progression: climbing stairs (dp[i] = dp[i−1] + dp[i−2]) → house robber (add skip-or-take) → harder 1D problems — every 1D DP is a variation on the ladder.
- **0/1 knapsack** — 'Choose a subset under a capacity to maximize value': dp[i][w] = max(skip, take) — the skeleton behind partition, coin change, and target-sum.
- **LCS / edit distance** — The 2D prefixes-table skeleton: dp[i][j] from dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1], dp[i−1][j−1]; match extends the diagonal, mismatch takes the best neighbor.
- **State compression** — Keeping only the rows or values the recurrence actually reads — the follow-up optimization after the table version works.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. For any DP problem, write the recurrence in English first ('dp[i] = best value considering the first i items'), then the state definition, then code — never code first.
2. Climb the 1D ladder in order: climbing stairs, then house robber, then one harder 1D variant — stating each recurrence aloud before coding.
3. Solve one knapsack-family problem by naming the disguise aloud: 'this is 0/1 knapsack on capacity W' — then write dp[i][w] = max(skip, take).
4. Solve one string DP with the prefixes table: define dp[i][j] on the two prefixes, fill a small table by hand for 3×3 inputs, then code it.
5. Redo one problem both ways — memoized top-down and tabulated bottom-up — and state the tradeoff: recursion overhead versus iteration, same asymptotic cost.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: DP playbook. Write a five-page playbook: the recurrence-first method, the 1D ladder with worked recurrences, the knapsack recognition checklist, the prefixes-table skeleton for string DP, and the state-design questions you ask yourself ('what must the state remember?'). Validate it: solve six unseen DP problems using only the playbook, logging where the recurrence came easily and where state design stalled you. Deliverable: the playbook plus six solved write-ups with the stall log.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: DP is the most grind-gated topic in the core — recognition comes from reps, and no module confers a certificate. The playbook compresses the method, not the practice; interviewers will still hand you problems you have never seen, which is the point of the method.

cards.front: What’s the first thing you write for a DP problem?
cards.back: The recurrence in words, before any code: ‘dp[i] = …’ stated as a decision — e.g. ‘rob or skip house i.’ Interviewers score the recurrence; the code is transcription. Then name the overlapping subproblems that make memoization valid.

cards.front: Memoization vs tabulation: how do you compare them in an interview?
cards.back: Same complexity, different direction: memoization is top-down recursion + cache (natural to write, pays recursion overhead); tabulation is bottom-up iteration (no stack risk, often better constants). State both, pick one, justify.

cards.front: What’s the 1D DP ladder?
cards.back: The progression: climbing stairs (dp[i] = dp[i-1] + dp[i-2]) → house robber (add the skip-or-take decision) → harder 1D problems. Master the ladder and every 1D DP is a variation — the interview line: ‘I climb the ladder before I attempt the roof.’

cards.front: How do you recognize a knapsack problem in disguise?
cards.back: ‘Choose a subset under a capacity to maximize value’ — partition-equal-subset, coin change, and target-sum are all knapsack variants. Name the pattern out loud: ‘this is 0/1 knapsack on capacity W,’ then write the recurrence.

cards.front: LCS and edit distance: what’s the shared DP skeleton?
cards.back: A 2D table over the two strings’ prefixes: dp[i][j] from dp[i−1][j], dp[i][j−1], dp[i−1][j−1]. Match → extend the diagonal; mismatch → take the best neighbor. Say ‘prefixes table’ and the interviewer knows you see it.

quiz.q: Good DP state design means the state:
choices: Captures exactly the information needed to make future decisions — no more, no less
quiz.explain: Too little state and the recurrence can’t decide; too much and you blow up the table for nothing.

quiz.q: In edit distance, dp[i][j] represents:
choices: The min edits to convert the first i chars of A to the first j chars of B
quiz.explain: The prefixes-table framing: every cell solves the subproblem on the two prefixes.

quiz.q: The 0/1 knapsack decision at each item is:
choices: Take it or skip it, respecting remaining capacity
quiz.explain: The 0/1 constraint forces a binary choice per item: dp[i][w] = max(skip, take).

quiz.q: House robber’s recurrence dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]) encodes:
choices: The skip-or-take decision at each house
quiz.explain: Each house: skip it (dp[i-1]) or rob it plus the best up to i-2.

modules.title: System Design Fundamentals
modules.summary: Welcome to System Design Fundamentals — module 5 of the DSA & System Design Core. I'm your instructor, and this module treats the system-design interview as a skill, not a memorization exercise: scoping with functional and non-functional requirements, back-of-envelope estimation, load balancers, caches, and CDNs, the honest SQL-versus-NoSQL choice, and CAP theorem discussed as a real tradeoff rather than a recited textbook. By the end, you will walk the standard interview walkthrough — requirements, estimation, API, data, scaling, failure modes, tradeoffs — with estimation math you can defend.
objectives: Understand and apply: functional vs non-functional requirements
Understand and apply: back-of-envelope estimation
Understand and apply: load balancers, caches, CDNs
Understand and apply: SQL vs NoSQL: choosing honestly
Understand and apply: CAP theorem and consistency models

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Functional requirements** — What the system does — the features and behaviors; stated first, before any box is drawn.
- **Non-functional requirements** — How the system behaves — scale, latency, availability, consistency; the constraints that shape the architecture.
- **Back-of-envelope estimation** — Order-of-magnitude math with stated assumptions: users → QPS → storage → bandwidth, rounded aggressively to drive design decisions.
- **Load balancer** — Spreads traffic across healthy servers — placed first along the request path; health checks decide 'healthy'.
- **Cache** — Serves hot data without hitting the origin — Redis/Memcached; the invalidation story is the real design work.
- **CDN** — Pushes static content to edge locations near users — latency for cacheable bytes, offload for the origin.
- **CAP theorem** — Under a network partition, choose consistency or availability — partitions are a fact; CP or AP is the decision, argued from the product's needs.
- **Consistency models** — The spectrum from strong to eventual: who sees what, when — 'the feed can be eventually consistent, but payments cannot.'
- **Access patterns** — How data is read and written — the honest deciding factor in SQL versus NoSQL, not hype or habit.
- **Bottleneck-first design** — Designing toward the constraint the estimation reveals: shard the hot key, cache the hot read, CDN the static bytes.

notes.title: Worked estimation
notes.body:
Estimation is order-of-magnitude judgment with stated assumptions, narrated aloud. Work each estimation below on paper, stating every assumption before the arithmetic.

1. Work the canonical estimation: 100M daily users × 10 requests each = 10⁹ requests/day ÷ 86,400 ≈ 12k average QPS — write every step, state the rounding, name the peak multiplier assumption.
2. Estimate storage for a photo-sharing sketch: 10M uploads/day × 2 MB average = 20 TB/day; × 365 × retention years — then decide what the number forces (object storage, CDN, thumbnails).
3. Estimate bandwidth for a video feed: concurrent viewers × bitrate — convert to Gbps and state what breaks first (origin egress, cache hit ratio).
4. Take any estimation above and change one assumption (DAU doubles, retention triples); recompute and name which design decision flips.
5. Practice the estimation monologue: 5 minutes, assumptions stated aloud, driving toward one decision ('so we shard by user id') — the interview shape of this skill.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Design-brief portfolio piece. Pick one familiar product (a URL shortener, a pastebin, a notification feed) and write a two-page design brief: functional and non-functional requirements, back-of-envelope estimation with every assumption stated, the architecture sketch (LB → app → cache → DB, CDN at the edge), the SQL-versus-NoSQL decision argued from access patterns, the CAP choice argued from the product, and three failure modes with mitigations. Deliverable: the brief — the artifact you will adapt live in the design round.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: system-design rounds are the most subjective interviews in the loop — there is no single correct architecture, and this course confers no certificate. Estimation is order-of-magnitude judgment, not precision; interviewers score the reasoning chain and the tradeoffs, not the arithmetic.

cards.front: How do you open a system design round?
cards.back: Requirements before architecture: restate functional requirements (what the system does), then non-functional (scale, latency, availability, consistency). Scoping first proves you design the right system — candidates who draw boxes before asking get failed.

cards.front: What are interviewers actually testing with back-of-envelope estimation?
cards.back: Order-of-magnitude judgment, not arithmetic: powers of 10 for users, QPS, storage, and bandwidth, with stated assumptions. Round aggressively, narrate the assumptions, and drive toward a design decision (shard? cache? CDN?).

cards.front: Load balancer, cache, CDN — the one-line job of each?
cards.back: Load balancer: spread traffic across healthy servers. Cache: serve hot data without hitting the origin (Redis/Memcached). CDN: push static content to the edge near users. In a design, place them in that order along the request path.

cards.front: SQL vs NoSQL: how do you ‘choose honestly’ in an interview?
cards.back: Name the workload, not the hype: need joins, transactions, and flexible queries → relational; massive write scale, simple key access, flexible schema → NoSQL family by access pattern (document, key-value, wide-column). The honest answer always starts from the access patterns.

cards.front: How do you discuss CAP without reciting the textbook?
cards.back: ‘During a network partition, I choose between consistency and availability — and here’s which my system needs and why.’ Then name the real tradeoff in your design: e.g. ‘the feed can be eventually consistent, but payments cannot.’

quiz.q: CAP says a distributed system under partition must sacrifice:
quiz.explain: Partitions are a fact of networks; the choice is CP (consistent, unavailable) or AP (available, inconsistent).

quiz.q: The deciding factor in SQL vs NoSQL should be:
choices: The data’s access patterns and consistency needs
quiz.explain: Storage choice follows how data is read and written and what consistency the product needs.

quiz.q: A CDN primarily reduces:
choices: Latency for static content by serving from edge locations
quiz.explain: Edge caches put bytes near users; origin round-trips disappear for cacheable content.

quiz.q: 100M daily active users making 10 requests each ≈ what average QPS?
quiz.explain: 100M × 10 = 10⁹ requests/day ÷ 86,400 s/day ≈ 11,574 — roughly 12k QPS.

modules.title: Guided System Design Build
modules.summary: Welcome to the Guided System Design Build — module 6 of the DSA & System Design Core. I'm your instructor, and here we convert design knowledge into interview performance: three full design reps — a URL shortener, a rate limiter, and a notification service — each with docs and a timer, plus the one-page design doc and the 45-minute presentation cadence. By the end, you will have presented a design on camera with timeboxes you actually kept, and a doc an interviewer could build from.
objectives: Build and demonstrate: designing a URL shortener end to end
Build and demonstrate: designing a rate limiter
Build and demonstrate: designing a notification service
Build and demonstrate: writing the one-page design doc
Build and demonstrate: presenting the design in 45 minutes

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **URL shortener design** — The canonical rep: requirements, API (POST /shorten, GET /{id} → 301), ID generation (counter vs hash, base62), key-value storage, cache hot URLs, shard by hash.
- **Rate limiter design** — Token bucket for bursts versus leaky bucket for smoothing; distributed state in Redis with Lua for atomicity; 429 + RateLimit-* headers communicating limits.
- **Notification service design** — Channels (push/email/SMS), fan-out estimation, queue-based workers per channel with retries and dead-letter queues, templates, provider rate limits, idempotency.
- **One-page design doc** — Requirements, architecture sketch, API and data model, scaling math, failure modes, open tradeoffs — one page forces decisions.
- **45-minute cadence** — 5 requirements, 5 estimation, 10 API/data, 15 deep-dive on the hard part, 10 tradeoffs and failures — the timebox that proves you can drive.
- **Review rubric** — Fixed axes for judging designs — comparable, complete feedback that prevents reviews from fixating on one pet concern.
- **ID generation tradeoffs** — Counter (needs coordination, e.g. ZooKeeper-style ranges) versus hash (collision handling) — the classic 'hard part' deep-dive of the shortener.
- **Fan-out math** — Followers × messages: the estimation that decides push versus pull and queue depth for the notification service.

notes.title: Worked estimation
notes.body:
Estimation is order-of-magnitude judgment with stated assumptions, narrated aloud. Work each estimation below on paper, stating every assumption before the arithmetic.

1. Design the URL shortener on paper: requirements, 100M URLs/month estimation (writes/sec, storage for 5 years at ~500 bytes/record), then the full walkthrough — time it at 45 minutes.
2. Work the shortener's ID math: 7 base62 characters = 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion IDs — state how long that lasts at your write rate and what happens at exhaustion.
3. Design the rate limiter: 10k requests/sec per API key, burst allowance 2× — size the Redis state, choose token bucket, and write the Lua atomicity argument.
4. Design the notification service: 1M notifications/day across three channels — fan-out math, worker count from per-worker throughput, queue depth for a 10× spike.
5. Record yourself presenting one design in 45 minutes; watch it back with the rubric and log every timebox you broke and every tradeoff you failed to name.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Three documented designs. Produce the full artifacts: one-page design docs for the URL shortener, the rate limiter, and the notification service — each with requirements, estimation, architecture, API/data model, scaling math, failure modes, and open tradeoffs — plus a 45-minute recorded walkthrough of one of them. Peer-review (or self-review with the rubric) all three. Deliverable: three design docs and one recording with the rubric scores — your design-round portfolio.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: three guided designs do not make you a distributed-systems engineer — they make you practiced at the interview's design genre, which is a different and narrower skill, and this course confers no certificate. Real systems have constraints (org, cost, legacy) the interview hand-waves; name that gap when you feel it.

cards.front: Walk the URL-shortener design in 60 seconds.
cards.back: Requirements (shorten + redirect, scale), estimation, API (POST /shorten, GET /{id} → 301), ID generation (counter vs hash, base62), storage (key-value, cache hot URLs), scaling (shard by hash, CDN for redirects).

cards.front: How do you structure the rate-limiter design answer?
cards.back: Requirements (limit per user/IP, burst policy), algorithm choice (token bucket for bursts, leaky bucket for smoothing — say which and why), distributed state (Redis with Lua for atomicity), and headers communicating limits to clients.

cards.front: How do you design a notification service in an interview?
cards.back: Requirements (channels: push/email/SMS, ordering, dedup), estimation (fan-out math), queue-based workers per channel with retries and DLQs, templates service, rate limits per provider, and idempotency so retries don’t double-notify.

cards.front: What goes in the one-page design doc?
cards.back: Requirements and constraints, the architecture sketch, API and data model, scaling math, failure modes, and open tradeoffs — one page forces decisions. Interviewers score whether the doc could actually guide a build.

cards.front: How do you present a design in 45 minutes?
cards.back: Timebox: 5 min requirements, 5 estimation, 10 API/data, 15 deep-dive on the hard part, 10 tradeoffs/failures/Q&A. End with ‘here are the three tradeoffs I’d revisit with more time’ — it shows judgment and invites the discussion interviewers want.

quiz.q: A review rubric’s value is:
choices: Comparable, complete feedback — every design judged on the same axes
quiz.explain: Fixed axes prevent reviews from fixating on one pet concern.

quiz.q: Ending a design round with open tradeoffs is strong because:
choices: It shows judgment about what matters and invites collaborative discussion
quiz.explain: Naming what you’d revisit proves you see the design’s limits — a senior signal.

quiz.q: A design doc’s failure-modes section exists to:
choices: Show you’ve thought about what breaks and how the system degrades — the senior signal
quiz.explain: Anyone can draw the happy path; naming failure modes and mitigations proves operational thinking.

quiz.q: Notification workers are typically queue-based because:
choices: Bursty send volume decouples from provider rate limits — workers drain at a sustainable pace with retries
quiz.explain: Queues absorb spikes and give retry/DLQ semantics per channel; direct calls would collapse under bursts.

modules.title: Mock Interview Circuit
modules.summary: Welcome to the Mock Interview Circuit — the final module of the DSA & System Design Core. I'm your instructor, and this module treats the interview as a performance discipline: timed coding rounds with a stranger, system-design rounds on camera, the STAR behavioral ledger, the debrief template that names what leaked and what held, weak-spot triage after every mock, and the final two-week taper plan. By the end, the real loop will be the second time you have done it — not the first.
objectives: Apply in professional practice: timed coding rounds with a stranger
Apply in professional practice: system-design rounds on camera
Apply in professional practice: behavioral: the STAR ledger
Apply in professional practice: the debrief template: what leaked, what held
Apply in professional practice: weak-spot triage after each mock

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Timed coding bar** — The 30-minute shape: 5 clarify + plan, 20 code, 5 test — brute force stated first buys time and shows honesty; a working brute force beats a half-written optimal.
- **Design round walkthrough** — Requirements → estimation → API → data model → happy path → scaling → failure modes → tradeoffs — with the interviewer as collaborator, not examiner.
- **STAR** — Situation (2 sentences), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — the bulk), Result (measurable outcome + lesson) — a complete evidence unit per story.
- **Behavioral ledger** — Your running record: story bank, which stories you told where, feedback received, questions that stumped you — no repeated stories, every round becomes training data.
- **Debrief template** — Within an hour of a mock: what leaked, what held, the single biggest leak, and the 48-hour redrill plan — mocks without debriefs are stage-fright practice.
- **Weak-spot triage** — Rank leaks by frequency × interview weight — fix what costs the most points most often; expected-value studying.
- **Taper plan** — Final two weeks: no new material, redrill weak patterns from the debrief log, full timed mocks, sleep fixed, story bank rehearsed aloud.
- **Thinking aloud** — Verbalized reasoning is scorable reasoning — narrating complexity, tradeoffs, and the plan as you code turns silent work into graded evidence.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Book or simulate one timed coding mock (30 minutes, stranger or recording): run the 5/20/5 budget aloud, state complexity before optimizing, test at the end.
2. Run one system-design mock on camera (45 minutes): drive the walkthrough, treat the interviewer as collaborator, end with three tradeoffs you would revisit.
3. Write your STAR ledger: five stories in full STAR form, each with the measurable result and the lesson — rehearse two aloud until they fit in two minutes.
4. Within one hour of each mock, fill the debrief template: what leaked, what held, the single biggest leak ranked by frequency × weight, the 48-hour redrill.
5. Execute the taper in miniature: one week of no-new-material redrills from your debrief log, then a full timed mock — measure the leak count before and after.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Mock circuit portfolio. Run a four-mock circuit over two weeks: two coding rounds, one system-design round, one behavioral round — each with a partner or on camera. For each, produce the debrief (leaks, holds, biggest leak, redrill plan) and the updated STAR ledger. Close the circuit with the taper plan written for your real loop dates. Deliverable: four debriefs, the ledger, and the taper schedule — the paper trail that proves the loop is your second time, not your first.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: mocks are the closest simulation available, not the real thing — real interviewers, nerves, and stakes differ, and this course confers no certificate. A taper improves performance; it does not guarantee an offer. What the circuit honestly buys is the removal of surprise — which is most of what sinks first attempts.

cards.front: How do you handle the 30-minute coding bar?
cards.back: Budget aloud: 5 min clarify + plan, 20 min code, 5 min test. Start with brute force stated and its complexity (it buys time and shows honesty), then optimize the bottleneck. A working brute force beats a half-written optimal.

cards.front: What’s the standard system-design walkthrough?
cards.back: Requirements → estimation → API → data model → happy-path design → scaling/bottlenecks → failure modes → tradeoffs summary. Drive with questions, think aloud, and treat the interviewer as a collaborator, not an examiner.

cards.front: What’s the STAR structure, and why does it work for behavioral rounds?
cards.back: Situation (2 sentences of context), Task (your responsibility), Action (what YOU did — the bulk), Result (measurable outcome + lesson). It works because interviewers score evidence of behavior, and STAR forces a complete evidence unit.

cards.front: What makes a mock interview actually improve you?
cards.back: The debrief loop: within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), pick the single biggest leak, and redrill it within 48 hours. Mocks without debriefs are just stage fright practice.

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: The highest-value activity right after a mock is:
choices: A written debrief naming what leaked, plus a redrill plan
quiz.explain: Improvement comes from the feedback loop: name the leak, target the redrill, verify next time.

quiz.q: In a STAR answer, the ‘A’ should emphasize:
quiz.explain: ‘We’ stories hide your contribution — interviewers evaluate you, so make your decisions explicit.

quiz.q: In a design round, the interviewer is best treated as:
choices: A collaborator — ask questions, incorporate feedback, design together
quiz.explain: Design rounds simulate real design work: collaborative, iterative, tradeoff-driven.

modules.title: API Design Patterns
modules.summary: Welcome to API Design Patterns — the opening module of the Backend Engineering Interview Prep path. I'm your instructor, and we treat APIs as the product here: resource modeling, idempotent mutations, and error contracts — the design judgment backend interviews probe first. We cover REST (resources, verbs, status codes), idempotency and safe retries, pagination, filtering and versioning, GraphQL's honest tradeoffs, and gRPC contract-first design. By the end, you will design a contract a client team could program against — and defend every choice in it.
objectives: Understand and apply: REST: resources, verbs, status codes
Understand and apply: idempotency and safe retries
Understand and apply: pagination, filtering, versioning
Understand and apply: graphQL: when queries beat endpoints
Understand and apply: gRPC and contract-first design

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **REST** — Resources as nouns in URLs, HTTP verbs as actions, status codes as the contract (200/201/400/401/403/404/429/500), stateless requests — plus the judgment calls: pagination, filtering, idempotency.
- **Idempotency** — 'Safe to retry': repeating the request doesn't change the outcome beyond the first application — designed with idempotency keys on writes, paired with exponential backoff + jitter.
- **Cursor pagination** — Keyset paging relative to a stable key: immune to the shifting-row problem of offset, stable under inserts — the choice for feeds; offset remains fine for admin UIs.
- **GraphQL tradeoffs** — Client-shaped queries that fix over/under-fetching — at the cost of harder caching, query-complexity limits, and N+1 resolvers needing batching (dataloaders).
- **gRPC** — Service-to-service inside the trust boundary: binary protobufs, strict .proto contracts, streaming RPCs — poor browser support keeps it off public APIs.
- **Error contracts** — Errors clients can program against: stable codes, messages, and request IDs for correlation — the contract's unhappy-path half.
- **Versioning** — How the contract evolves without breaking clients: URL, header, or additive-only evolution — a decision, not an afterthought.
- **Safe retries** — Retries that can't corrupt: idempotent endpoints plus backoff with jitter — the client-side half of reliability.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Model a small API's resources as nouns: list the resources, assign verbs, and write the status code each endpoint returns for success and for the three most likely failures.
2. Add idempotency to one mutating endpoint: design the idempotency-key header, the server-side key store, and the replay response — then write the retry policy (backoff + jitter) a client would use.
3. Compare offset vs cursor pagination for a feed endpoint: write both, insert rows mid-page in a test, and observe which one skips or duplicates.
4. Write the GraphQL-vs-REST decision for one product surface: name the over/under-fetching cost, the caching cost, and the verdict with the condition that would flip it.
5. Sketch a .proto contract for one internal service: messages, RPCs, and one streaming RPC — then list what breaks if a field is renamed (the contract-evolution lesson).

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Public API contract. Design the full contract for a rate-limited public API (the companion build in this path's design module): resources and verbs, status codes, the error model with request IDs, idempotency keys on writes, cursor pagination on list endpoints, versioning strategy, and the rate-limit headers (429, RateLimit-*, Retry-After). Write it as an OpenAPI-style sketch a client team could build against. Deliverable: the contract document — the interface before the implementation.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: API design taste is argued, not certified — conventions differ across companies, and this course confers no certificate. The contract you write here is practice for defending judgment calls aloud; real APIs also answer to existing clients, legacy, and org politics.

cards.front: What makes an API ‘RESTful’ in an interview answer?
cards.back: Resources as nouns in URLs, HTTP verbs as actions, status codes as the contract (200/201/400/401/403/404/429/500), stateless requests, and versioning — then the judgment calls: pagination, filtering, and idempotency.

cards.front: How do you explain idempotency to an interviewer?
cards.back: ‘Safe to retry’: repeating the request doesn’t change the outcome beyond the first application. Design it with idempotency keys on writes, and pair it with safe retries (exponential backoff + jitter) for distributed calls.

cards.front: Offset vs cursor pagination: the interview-ready comparison?
cards.back: Offset is simple but skips/duplicates rows when data changes and gets slower deep into the list; cursor (keyset) pagination is stable and O(1)-ish per page using an indexed column. Choose cursor for feeds, offset for admin UIs.

cards.front: When do queries beat endpoints — your GraphQL judgment call?
cards.back: When clients need varied, nested data and over/under-fetching hurts (mobile, aggregations): one query, exact fields, typed schema. The costs you must name: caching is harder, query complexity needs limits, and N+1 resolvers need batching (dataloaders).

cards.front: When is gRPC the right answer?
cards.back: Service-to-service inside the trust boundary: binary protobufs (fast, small), strict contracts via .proto, and streaming RPCs. The tradeoff: poor browser support and harder debugging than JSON — so internal microservices yes, public APIs usually no.

quiz.q: A good API error response includes a request ID so that:
choices: Support can correlate the client’s error with server-side logs
quiz.explain: Correlation IDs connect the client’s report to the exact server-side trace.

quiz.q: gRPC’s contract-first design means:
choices: Services share .proto definitions so clients and servers stay in sync
quiz.explain: The .proto file is the single source of truth generating typed clients and servers.

quiz.q: GraphQL’s main cost vs REST that you must name in an interview is:
choices: Caching and rate-limiting are harder without per-endpoint semantics
quiz.explain: A single endpoint with arbitrary query shapes defeats HTTP caching and simple per-route limits — you need query-cost analysis.

quiz.q: Cursor pagination avoids the ‘missing rows’ problem of offset because:
choices: It pages relative to a stable key instead of a shifting row number
quiz.explain: New inserts shift offsets; a keyset cursor anchors to the last seen key, immune to shifts.

modules.title: Databases and the Data Layer
modules.summary: Welcome to Databases and the Data Layer — module 2 of the Backend path. I'm your instructor, and this is the data layer interviews actually test: index design, isolation levels, and the honest SQL-versus-NoSQL decision — not trivia, judgment. We cover schema design and normalization, B-tree/covering/composite indexes, transactions and isolation levels, the NoSQL families, and connection pooling with the N+1 trap. By the end, you will argue storage choices from access patterns.
objectives: Understand and apply: schema design and normalization
Understand and apply: indexes: B-trees, covering, composite
Understand and apply: transactions and isolation levels
Understand and apply: noSQL families: document, key-value, wide-column
Understand and apply: connection pooling and N+1 queries

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Normalization** — 1NF→2NF→3NF: atomic values, no partial or transitive dependencies — normalize by default, denormalize deliberately by measurement, documenting why.
- **B-tree index** — Turns O(n) scans into O(log n) lookups on indexed columns — at the cost of write overhead and storage; the workhorse of relational access.
- **Composite index** — Multi-column index serving filters left-to-right — column order follows the query patterns, not the table definition.
- **Covering index** — An index that answers the query without touching the table — the read-path optimization that removes the heap fetch.
- **Isolation levels** — The ladder: read uncommitted → read committed → repeatable read → serializable — trading anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms) for concurrency.
- **NoSQL families** — Document (flexible JSON), key-value (single-key lookups), wide-column (massive write scale), graph (relationship traversals) — fit follows access pattern.
- **Connection pooling** — Reusing a bounded set of DB connections — because connection setup is expensive and unbounded connections collapse the database.
- **N+1 queries** — Loading N parents then one query per parent's children: N+1 round trips — fixed by eager loading (JOIN or batched query).
- **Expand-contract migrations** — Backward-compatible schema steps where old and new code coexist; the old shape is removed only after readers move — migrations without downtime.
- **Access-pattern-first choice** — The honest SQL-versus-NoSQL method: name the reads, writes, and consistency needs first — the storage follows.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Take a small schema you know and normalize it to 3NF on paper; then pick one read-heavy query and denormalize deliberately — write the measurement that would justify it.
2. Design indexes for three query patterns against one table: single-column filter, two-column filter, and an aggregation — state which are composite, which covering, and the write cost.
3. Walk the isolation ladder for a money-transfer workload: name the anomaly each level permits, pick the level, and justify why the workload can't tolerate the cheaper one.
4. Choose storage for three workloads (shopping-cart sessions, product catalog, time-series metrics): name the access pattern, pick the family, state the rejected alternatives.
5. Write the expand-contract steps for adding a non-nullable column to a live table: expand, migrate, contract — with the rollback story at each step.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Data-layer design brief. For the order pipeline in this path's guided build, write the data-layer section: schema with normalization notes, the index list with the queries each serves, the isolation level chosen for order placement with the anomaly analysis, the session/cache store choice, and the zero-downtime migration plan for the first schema change. Deliverable: the data-layer brief — the section interviewers read to judge judgment.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: storage advice is workload-specific — the 'right' database changes with scale, team, and budget, and this course confers no certificate. Interview answers are argued from access patterns; production answers also involve cost, hiring, and the systems you already run.

cards.front: How do you discuss schema design and normalization?
cards.back: Normalize to remove redundancy (1NF→2NF→3NF: atomic values, no partial or transitive dependencies), then denormalize deliberately where read performance demands it — documenting why. The interview line: ‘normalize by default, denormalize by measurement.’

cards.front: How do you explain indexes in a backend interview?
cards.back: B-tree indexes turn O(n) scans into O(log n) lookups on the indexed columns — at the cost of write overhead and storage. Composite indexes serve multi-column filters left-to-right; covering indexes answer the query without touching the table.

cards.front: How do you talk about transaction isolation levels?
cards.back: The ladder: read uncommitted → read committed → repeatable read → serializable, trading anomalies (dirty reads, non-repeatable reads, phantoms) for concurrency. Name the anomaly your workload can’t tolerate, then pick the level.

cards.front: Name the NoSQL families and their fit in one breath.
cards.back: Document (flexible JSON, e.g. product catalogs), key-value (blazing simple lookups, sessions/caches), wide-column (massive write scale, time series), graph (relationship-heavy traversals). Fit follows access pattern.

cards.front: What’s the N+1 query problem and its fix?
cards.back: Loading N parents then one query per parent’s children: N+1 round trips. The fix is eager loading — a JOIN or batched second query (and ORMs have explicit eager-loading APIs). Name it when you see loops over queries.

quiz.q: The expand-contract migration pattern’s core idea is:
choices: Backward-compatible steps where old and new code coexist
quiz.explain: Every intermediate state must work with both old and new code; the old shape is removed only after readers move.

quiz.q: Eager loading fixes N+1 by:
choices: Fetching related rows in bulk (JOIN or batched query) instead of one query per parent
quiz.explain: One bulk fetch replaces N per-row queries; round trips collapse from N+1 to ~2.

quiz.q: A shopping-cart session store is a natural key-value fit because:
choices: Access is by a single session key with simple read/write
quiz.explain: Single-key access with no relations is exactly the key-value sweet spot.

quiz.q: Repeatable read prevents ___ but still allows ___:
quiz.explain: Repeatable read holds read locks so re-reads are stable, but new rows matching the predicate (phantoms) can still appear.

modules.title: Caching and Message Queues
modules.summary: Welcome to Caching and Message Queues — module 3 of the Backend path. I'm your instructor, and this is scale's two workhorses: caches that absorb reads and queues that absorb bursts — with the failure modes (stampedes, poison messages) interviewers love to ask about. We cover cache-aside/read-through/write-through, TTL and invalidation, Redis data structures in practice, delivery semantics, Kafka topics/partitions/consumer groups, and backpressure with dead-letter queues. By the end, you will pair every speedup with its invalidation story.
objectives: Understand and apply: cache-aside, read-through, write-through
Understand and apply: TTL, invalidation, and the thundering herd
Understand and apply: redis data structures in practice
Understand and apply: queues: at-least-once vs exactly-once
Understand and apply: kafka topics, partitions, consumer groups

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Cache-aside** — App checks cache, falls back to DB, populates cache — flexible, with the stale-read risk you must name.
- **Read-through / write-through** — Read-through: the cache loads from the DB itself. Write-through: writes go to cache and DB together — consistent, slower writes.
- **TTL and invalidation** — Time-to-live bounds staleness; the invalidation strategy is caching's permanent tax — every caching decision must name it.
- **Thundering herd** — A hot key expires and every request stampedes the DB — stopped by request coalescing (single-flight), probabilistic early refresh, or staggered TTLs with jitter.
- **Redis data structures** — Strings (counters, rate limits), hashes (objects), lists (queues), sets (membership), sorted sets (leaderboards, time-ordered feeds) — five tools, one store.
- **At-least-once delivery** — The practical default: retries can duplicate — made safe by idempotent consumers, which is effectively exactly-once processing.
- **Exactly-once semantics** — Needs idempotent consumers or transactions (Kafka EOS) — the honest answer names the machinery, not the wish.
- **Kafka** — Distributed commit log: topics split into partitions (the parallelism unit), consumer groups split partitions across consumers, offsets track progress — ordering guaranteed per partition only.
- **Backpressure** — Bounded queues that block or shed so the producer feels the consumer's slowness — an unbounded queue is a deferred outage.
- **Dead-letter queue** — Where poison messages go after retries exhaust: quarantine for inspection instead of blocking the stream or looping forever.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Implement cache-aside for one read path in a toy app: read, miss, load, populate — then write the invalidation rule for the corresponding write path.
2. Simulate a thundering herd: expire a hot key under synthetic load, observe the DB spike, then add single-flight coalescing and re-run — compare the curves.
3. Model three features in Redis data structures (a leaderboard, a rate limiter, a job queue): pick the structure per feature and state why the others don't fit.
4. Design a consumer for at-least-once delivery: write the idempotency check (processed-IDs set), the retry policy, and the dead-letter routing for poison messages.
5. Sketch a Kafka topic for an order pipeline: choose the partition key, state the ordering guarantee it gives, and assign consumer groups for two independent consumers.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Cache-and-queue architecture brief. For the order pipeline: the caching layer (what is cached, the strategy per path, TTLs, the invalidation plan, the herd defense), and the queue topology (topics/queues, partition keys, consumer groups, retry and dead-letter policy, the backpressure story). Include the failure modes: cache outage, consumer lag, poison message. Deliverable: the brief — the section that proves you design for the unhappy path.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: caching and queue topologies are capacity-shaped — the right answers change with traffic, budget, and the managed services you actually run, and this course confers no certificate. The interview rewards naming failure modes honestly; production rewards measuring them.

cards.front: Cache-aside vs read-through vs write-through?
cards.back: Cache-aside: app checks cache, falls back to DB, populates cache (flexible, stale-risk). Read-through: cache loads from DB itself. Write-through: writes go to cache and DB together (consistent, slower writes). Name the invalidation story for whichever you pick.

cards.front: What’s the thundering herd, and how do you stop it?
cards.back: A hot cache key expires and every request stampedes the DB at once. Fixes: request coalescing (single-flight — one request loads, others wait), probabilistic early refresh, or staggered TTLs with jitter.

cards.front: Why does Redis show up in backend interviews constantly?
cards.back: Because it’s five tools in one: strings (counters, rate limits), hashes (objects), lists (queues), sets (unique membership), sorted sets (leaderboards, time-ordered feeds) — all in-memory with persistence options. Name the structure that fits the access pattern.

cards.front: At-least-once vs exactly-once: the honest interview answer?
cards.back: At-least-once is the practical default (retries can duplicate); exactly-once needs idempotent consumers or transactions (Kafka EOS). The strong answer: ‘I design consumers idempotent, so duplicates are harmless — then at-least-once delivery is effectively exactly-once processing.’

cards.front: Kafka in 60 seconds for an interview.
cards.back: Distributed commit log: topics split into partitions (the parallelism unit), producers append, consumer groups split partitions across consumers, offsets track progress. Choose it for durable event streaming with replay — and name the ordering guarantee: per-partition only.

quiz.q: A bounded queue with a drop-or-block policy implements:
choices: Backpressure — the producer feels the consumer’s slowness
quiz.explain: Bounded buffers propagate slowness upstream instead of growing memory until collapse.

quiz.q: In Kafka, ordering is guaranteed:
quiz.explain: A partition is an append-only log — total order holds inside it, not across partitions.

quiz.q: The most robust way to handle duplicate deliveries is:
choices: Preventing all duplicates in the broker
Idempotent consumers, so reprocessing is safe
quiz.explain: Duplicates are inevitable in distributed systems; idempotency makes them harmless.

quiz.q: A leaderboard is a natural Redis sorted-set fit because:
choices: Members are ordered by score with O(log n) updates and range queries
quiz.explain: Sorted sets keep members ordered by score: rank lookups and top-N ranges are native operations.

modules.title: Concurrency and Rate Limiting
modules.summary: Welcome to Concurrency and Rate Limiting — module 4 of the Backend path. I'm your instructor, and this is concurrency the way interviews test it: the primitives, the classic bugs (races, deadlocks), and rate limiting as a designed system rather than a library call. We cover threads, processes, and event loops; locks, semaphores, and deadlock; async I/O and backpressure; token-bucket and leaky-bucket limiters; and distributed locking with Redis. By the end, you will answer hazards with mechanisms, not buzzwords.
objectives: Understand and apply: threads, processes, and event loops
Understand and apply: locks, semaphores, and deadlock
Understand and apply: async I/O and backpressure
Understand and apply: token bucket and leaky bucket limiters
Understand and apply: distributed locking with Redis

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Threads vs processes vs event loops** — Processes: isolated, expensive. Threads: shared memory, need locks. Event loops: single-threaded async I/O — great for I/O-bound, terrible for CPU-bound.
- **Deadlock's four conditions** — Mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait — break any one; lock ordering (global acquisition order) is the classic fix.
- **Backpressure** — When consumers lag producers, pressure must go somewhere: bounded queues, demand signaling, consumer-lag alerting — never an unbounded queue.
- **Token bucket** — Tokens accumulate to capacity: sustained rate plus short bursts allowed — the limiter for APIs that should tolerate spikes.
- **Leaky bucket** — Requests queue and drain at a constant rate: smooth output, no bursts — the limiter for steady downstream capacity.
- **Distributed lock (Redis)** — SET with NX + PX expiry, fencing tokens for ordering, short critical sections — because a crashed holder without a TTL deadlocks every waiter.
- **Idempotent consumers** — Reprocessing the same input yields the same output — the concurrency-safe way to survive duplicate deliveries and retries.
- **Race condition** — Outcome depends on uncontrolled scheduling interleaving — fixed by making the critical section atomic or the operation idempotent.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write a tiny multithreaded counter with and without a lock; run it under contention and observe the lost updates — then fix it and state which hazard you removed.
2. Draw a deadlock from two locks acquired in opposite orders; then impose a global lock ordering and show the cycle can't form — state the broken condition aloud.
3. Implement a token bucket and a leaky bucket for the same API: configure burst tolerance on one and smooth output on the other, and state which product need each serves.
4. Build the Redis distributed-lock pattern (SET NX PX + fencing token + short critical section); then kill the holder mid-section and verify the TTL bounds the damage.
5. Design the backpressure story for one pipeline: bounded queue depth, the drop-or-block policy, the alert on consumer lag — and the load-shedding rule when it fills.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Rate limiter design brief. Design the rate-limited public API from this path's build: limits per key and per IP, burst policy with the token-vs-leaky-bucket decision argued, distributed state in Redis with the Lua atomicity argument, 429 + RateLimit-* + Retry-After headers, and per-endpoint tiers. Include the concurrency hazards (thundering increments, clock skew across instances) and their mitigations. Deliverable: the brief — rate limiting as a designed system.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: distributed-locking and limiter tuning are environment-shaped — clock behavior, Redis topology, and traffic shape change the answers, and this course confers no certificate. The interview tests whether you name the hazards; production tests whether you measured them.

cards.front: Threads vs processes vs event loops?
cards.back: Processes: isolated memory, expensive. Threads: shared memory, cheap-ish, need locks. Event loop: single-threaded async I/O (Node, asyncio) — great for I/O-bound, terrible for CPU-bound. Match the model to the bottleneck.

cards.front: How do you explain deadlock prevention?
cards.back: Deadlock needs four conditions (mutual exclusion, hold-and-wait, no preemption, circular wait) — break any one: lock ordering (always acquire in the same global order) is the classic fix. In an interview, draw the wait cycle, then name the broken condition.

cards.front: What is backpressure, and where do you put it?
cards.back: When consumers are slower than producers, pressure must go somewhere: bounded queues that block/shed, reactive streams with demand signaling, or Kafka consumer-lag alerting. The interview point: an unbounded queue is a deferred outage.

cards.front: Token bucket vs leaky bucket — which allows bursts?
cards.back: Token bucket: tokens accumulate up to capacity, so short bursts above the sustained rate are allowed. Leaky bucket: requests queue and drain at a constant rate — smooth output, no bursts. State which behavior the product needs.

cards.front: Why is distributed locking hard, and what’s the Redis answer?
cards.back: Locks must survive holder crashes (TTL/lease) and clock issues; naive SETNX without expiry deadlocks on crash. The pattern: SET with NX + PX expiry, fencing tokens for ordering, and always keep the critical section short.

quiz.q: An idempotent pipeline stage guarantees:
choices: Reprocessing the same input produces the same output — no duplicates
quiz.explain: Reruns are inevitable; idempotency makes them safe.

quiz.q: A distributed lock MUST have an expiry because:
choices: A crashed holder would otherwise hold the lock forever
quiz.explain: Without TTL, a holder that dies mid-section deadlocks every waiter — the lease bounds the damage.

quiz.q: An API that should allow brief traffic spikes should use:
quiz.explain: Accumulated tokens absorb bursts up to bucket capacity; a leaky bucket would queue or drop them.

quiz.q: A bounded queue with a drop-or-block policy implements:
choices: Backpressure — the producer feels the consumer’s slowness
quiz.explain: Bounded buffers propagate slowness upstream instead of growing memory until collapse.

modules.title: Microservices Architecture
modules.summary: Welcome to Microservices Architecture — module 5 of the Backend path. I'm your instructor, and this is microservices without the hype: decomposition judgment, the distributed-systems costs (sagas, observability), and the honest counterargument for when a monolith wins — the senior answer. We cover bounded-context decomposition, sync versus async communication, service discovery and API gateways, sagas for distributed transactions, and observability (traces, metrics, logs). By the end, you will argue distribution as a cost you pay deliberately.
objectives: Understand and apply: decomposition: bounded contexts
Understand and apply: synchronous vs asynchronous communication
Understand and apply: service discovery and API gateways
Understand and apply: distributed transactions and sagas
Understand and apply: observability: traces, metrics, logs

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Bounded contexts** — DDD decomposition along business capabilities with clean ownership — split by capability, not by technical layer; each service owns its data.
- **Sync vs async** — Sync (REST/gRPC): simple, couples availability and latency. Async (queues/events): decoupled and resilient, but eventually consistent and harder to debug.
- **Service discovery** — How services find each other's current addresses as instances churn — registry or DNS-based; the answer to 'what's the URL?' in a dynamic fleet.
- **API gateway** — Single entry point: routing, auth, rate limiting, aggregation for clients — cross-cutting edge concerns in one policy point.
- **Saga** — Distributed transactions without 2PC: a sequence of local transactions, each with a compensating action — choreography (events) for simple flows, orchestration (coordinator) for complex ones.
- **Observability trio** — Metrics: 'is something wrong' (alerts). Logs: 'what happened' (events with context). Traces: 'where did the request go' (latency across services).
- **Modular monolith** — Bounded-context discipline inside one deployable — the honest starting point until a proven seam demands distribution.
- **Distributed-systems tax** — The permanent costs of distribution: network failures, eventual consistency, observability burden, deployment complexity — paid only for proven seams.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Decompose a familiar monolith (an e-commerce app) into bounded contexts on paper: name the contexts, draw the ownership lines, and state what data each service owns.
2. For each cross-service call in your decomposition, choose sync or async and write the one-sentence justification ('sync: the user waits for this answer; async: this work can wait').
3. Design the saga for an order flow (payment → inventory → notification): list the steps, write each compensating action, and choose choreography vs orchestration with reasons.
4. Write the observability plan: which metrics alert, what the logs carry per request (correlation IDs), and where traces would have found the last incident you remember.
5. Argue the counter-case: write the modular-monolith version of your decomposition and name the exact conditions (scale seam, team seam) that would flip you to services.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Decomposition brief. Take the order pipeline and write the microservices decision document: bounded contexts with ownership, the sync/async map, the saga with compensating actions, service discovery and gateway placement, and the observability plan (metrics, logs, traces with correlation). Close with the honest counterargument: the modular-monolith alternative and the conditions that would change the call. Deliverable: the brief — distribution argued, not assumed.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: microservices advice is org-shaped — team size, deployment maturity, and domain complexity change the answer, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers reward the tradeoff argument; the industry's hype cycles are not engineering evidence.

cards.front: How do you decompose a monolith in a design interview?
cards.back: By bounded contexts (DDD): split along business capabilities with clean ownership, not technical layers. Each service owns its data; cross-service needs go through APIs or events. And name the honest counterargument: start modular-monolith until the seams are proven.

cards.front: Sync vs async service communication?
cards.back: Sync (REST/gRPC): simple, but couples availability and latency — a slow downstream slows you. Async (queues/events): decoupled, resilient, but eventual consistency and harder debugging. The interview line: ‘sync for queries needing answers now, async for work that can wait.’

cards.front: What do service discovery and API gateways do?
cards.back: Service discovery: services find each other’s current addresses as instances churn (registry or DNS-based). API gateway: single entry point handling routing, auth, rate limiting, and aggregation for clients.

cards.front: Distributed transactions: what’s the saga answer?
cards.back: No 2PC across services — use sagas: a sequence of local transactions where each step has a compensating action (refund, cancel) for rollback. Choreography (events) for simple flows, orchestration (a saga coordinator) when the flow needs central control.

cards.front: Logs, metrics, traces — when do you reach for each?
