cards.back: Metrics: ‘is something wrong’ (alerts, dashboards). Logs: ‘what happened’ (discrete events with context). Traces: ‘where did the request go’ (latency across services). The interview line: ‘metrics alert me, traces show me where, logs tell me why.’

quiz.q: A modular monolith is often the right starting point because:
choices: It keeps bounded-context discipline without paying the distributed-systems tax prematurely
quiz.explain: Distribution is a cost; pay it when a proven seam demands independent scaling or ownership.

quiz.q: A distributed trace’s primary value is:
choices: Following one request across services to find where latency/errors originate
quiz.explain: Trace spans stitch the request path across service boundaries — the only view that crosses them.

quiz.q: A saga handles failure of step 3 in a 5-step flow by:
quiz.explain: Each completed step’s compensating transaction semantically undoes it — the distributed answer to rollback.

quiz.q: An API gateway centralizes:
choices: Cross-cutting edge concerns: routing, auth, rate limiting for inbound traffic
quiz.explain: One policy-enforcement point at the edge beats reimplementing auth and limits in every service.

modules.title: Guided Backend Design
modules.summary: Welcome to the Guided Backend Design — module 6 of the Backend path. I'm your instructor, and here we do two backend design reps from contract to failure modes, documented and presented: a rate-limited public API and an order pipeline with queues — plus the API contract sketch, a k6 load-test plan, and the failure-mode writeup. By the end, you will have portfolio evidence that survives the onsite: designs with contracts, load plans, and unhappy paths written down.
objectives: Build and demonstrate: designing a rate-limited public API
Build and demonstrate: designing an order pipeline with queues
Build and demonstrate: writing the API contract and OpenAPI sketch
Build and demonstrate: load-test plan with k6
Build and demonstrate: failure-mode writeup

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Rate-limited API design** — Limits per key/IP, burst policy, token bucket in Redis with atomic Lua, 429 + RateLimit-* headers — the limiter as part of the contract.
- **Order pipeline with queues** — API accepts and validates → order events to a queue → workers for payment/inventory/notification with retries + DLQ → saga compensation — the queue as the reliability seam.
- **OpenAPI contract sketch** — Endpoints, methods, schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits, versioning — enough for a client team to build against.
- **k6 load-test plan** — JS-scripted load tests with thresholds as gates: the script, the stages, the assertions — code-reviewed load tests in the pipeline.
- **k6 vs JMeter** — k6: scripted, CI-friendly, thresholds as gates. JMeter: GUI-driven, mature, broad protocol support — pick by team context, not fashion.
- **Failure-mode writeup** — Per component: how it fails, blast radius, detection (which alert), mitigation (the responder's move), graceful degradation — the unhappy path designed like the happy one.
- **45-minute presentation** — The design-round cadence: requirements, estimation, API/data, deep-dive, tradeoffs — ending with the tradeoffs you'd revisit.
- **Contract-first** — Interface decisions made early when they're cheap — and client/server work parallelized; the habit interviewers want to see generalized.

notes.title: Worked estimation
notes.body:
Estimation is order-of-magnitude judgment with stated assumptions, narrated aloud. Work each estimation below on paper, stating every assumption before the arithmetic.

1. Estimate the rate-limited API: 10k req/s sustained, 2× burst — size the Redis token-bucket state, compute per-key memory, and state the Lua atomicity requirement.
2. Estimate the order pipeline: 50k orders/day, peak 10× — queue depth for the peak hour, worker count from per-worker throughput, DLQ sizing for a 1% poison rate.
3. Write the k6 script plan for the API: stages (ramp, sustain, spike), thresholds (p95, error rate), and the gate assertion that fails the run.
4. Recompute the pipeline estimate with one changed assumption (orders 5×, or a new channel added) and name which design decision flips.
5. Present one design in 45 minutes on camera: timebox visibly, end with three tradeoffs you'd revisit — then score yourself against the rubric.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Two documented backend designs. Produce the full artifacts: the rate-limited public API (contract, limiter design, estimation, failure modes) and the order pipeline (queue topology, workers, saga, load-test plan, failure-mode writeup) — each as a one-page design doc plus a 45-minute recorded walkthrough of one. Deliverable: two design docs and one recording — the portfolio evidence that survives the onsite.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: two guided designs are interview practice, not production systems — real APIs answer to existing clients, cost constraints, and on-call burden, and this course confers no certificate. The value here is the documented reasoning habit; the numbers are estimates, stated as such.

cards.front: How do you design a rate-limited public API?
cards.back: Requirements (limits per key/IP, burst policy) → token-bucket in Redis with atomic Lua → 429 + RateLimit-* headers + Retry-After → per-endpoint tiers. The interview line: ‘the limiter is part of the API contract, not an afterthought.’

cards.front: How do you design an order pipeline with queues?
cards.back: API accepts and validates → order events to a queue → workers for payment, inventory, notification (each with retries + DLQ) → saga/compensation for failures. The interview line: ‘the queue is the seam where reliability lives.’

cards.front: What goes in an API contract / OpenAPI sketch?
cards.back: Endpoints, methods, request/response schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits, and versioning — enough that a client team could build against it. The interview line: ‘the contract is the interface; code is the implementation.’

cards.front: k6 vs JMeter — how do you compare them?
cards.back: k6: JS-scripted, developer-friendly, great for CI-integrated load tests with thresholds as gates. JMeter: GUI-driven, mature, huge protocol support, heavier. The interview line: ‘k6 for code-reviewed load tests in the pipeline; JMeter where the team already lives in it.’

cards.front: What goes in a failure-mode writeup?
cards.back: For each component: how it fails, blast radius, detection (which alert fires), mitigation (what the responder does), and whether degradation is graceful. The interview line: ‘I design the unhappy path with the same care as the happy one.’

quiz.q: Ending a design round with open tradeoffs is strong because:
choices: It shows judgment about what matters and invites collaborative discussion
quiz.explain: Naming what you’d revisit proves you see the design’s limits — a senior signal.

quiz.q: A failure-mode writeup’s audience is:
choices: The future on-call responder — it’s a pre-written triage guide
quiz.explain: Written calmly now, it guides panicked decisions at 3am.

quiz.q: k6’s thresholds turn a load test into:
choices: A gate: breaching p95/error-rate assertions fails the run
quiz.explain: Thresholds are pass/fail assertions on metrics — the test proves the SLO or it fails.

quiz.q: Writing the contract before the implementation is strong because:
choices: It forces interface decisions early, when they’re cheap — and enables parallel client/server work
quiz.explain: Contract-first surfaces disagreements before code cements them.

modules.title: Backend Mock Circuit
modules.summary: Welcome to the Backend Mock Circuit — the final module of the Backend path. I'm your instructor, and these are backend-flavored mocks: API design under time, concurrency and data-layer deep dives, system design on camera, and the behavioral ledger for backend roles — each debriefed into the next week's study plan. By the end, your debrief log will have converted every mock into targeted reps.
objectives: Apply in professional practice: timed API-design rounds
Apply in professional practice: concurrency and data-layer deep dives
Apply in professional practice: system design on camera
Apply in professional practice: behavioral ledger for backend roles
Apply in professional practice: debrief template and triage

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Timed API-design round** — The budget: 5 requirements, 10 resources + verbs + status codes, 10 edge cases (pagination, idempotency, versioning), 5 tradeoffs — thinking in resources and contracts.
- **Concurrency deep dive** — Hazards named with mechanisms: races, deadlocks, N+1, isolation anomalies — each tied to a concrete scenario, never a buzzword list.
- **Data-layer deep dive** — Index choices, isolation levels, storage decisions — argued from access patterns under follow-up pressure.
- **Behavioral ledger** — Story bank, stories-told-where, feedback, stumping questions — the running record that stops repeated stories.
- **Debrief and triage** — Within the hour: what leaked, what held, biggest leak by frequency × weight, the 48-hour redrill — the mock is the test, the debrief is the studying.
- **Taper plan** — Final two weeks: no new material, redrill from the debrief log, timed mocks, rest — consolidation over cramming.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Run a timed API-design mock (30 min): budget aloud, design the contract a client could program against, close with tradeoffs.
2. Run a concurrency deep-dive mock: a partner probes races, deadlocks, and limiter design — answer every hazard with a mechanism and a scenario.
3. Run a data-layer deep-dive mock: defend an index list and an isolation choice against 'why not cheaper?' follow-ups.
4. Run one system-design round on camera (45 min): the walkthrough with estimation, ending in named tradeoffs.
5. Debrief all four within the hour each: fill the template, rank the leaks, schedule the 48-hour redrills, update the ledger.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Backend mock portfolio. Run the four-mock circuit over two weeks — API design, concurrency deep dive, data-layer deep dive, system design on camera — each with a partner or recorded. Produce the debrief per mock (leaks, holds, biggest leak, redrill plan) and the updated behavioral ledger, then write the taper plan for your real loop. Deliverable: four debriefs, the ledger, the taper — the paper trail from mocks to study plan.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: mocks simulate the format, not the stakes — real loops add nerves, unfamiliar interviewers, and company-specific bars, and this course confers no certificate. What the circuit honestly delivers is leak discovery while it's still cheap to fix.

cards.front: How do you handle timed API-design rounds?
cards.back: Budget: 5 min requirements, 10 min resources + verbs + status codes, 10 min edge cases (pagination, idempotency, versioning), 5 min tradeoffs. Think in resources and contracts — the interview line: ‘I design the contract a client could program against.’

cards.front: How do you survive concurrency + data-layer deep dives?
cards.back: Name the hazards (races, deadlocks, N+1, isolation anomalies), then the tools (locks with ordering, idempotent consumers, eager loading, right isolation level) — each tied to a concrete scenario. The interview line: ‘I answer hazards with mechanisms, not buzzwords.’

cards.front: What’s a behavioral ledger?
cards.back: Your running record: story bank entries, which stories you’ve told where, feedback received, and follow-up questions that stumped you. It stops you from repeating the same story and turns each behavioral round into training data.

cards.front: What makes a mock interview actually improve you?
cards.back: The debrief loop: within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), pick the single biggest leak, and redrill it within 48 hours. Mocks without debriefs are just stage fright practice.

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: The highest-value activity right after a mock is:
choices: A written debrief naming what leaked, plus a redrill plan
quiz.explain: Improvement comes from the feedback loop: name the leak, target the redrill, verify next time.

quiz.q: A behavioral ledger prevents:
choices: Repeating the same story across rounds and losing track of feedback
quiz.explain: Loops have multiple behavioral touchpoints; the ledger keeps each one fresh and improving.

quiz.q: Deep-dive answers score when they:
choices: Connect each hazard to a concrete mechanism and scenario
quiz.explain: Mechanism + scenario proves understanding; tool lists prove vocabulary.

modules.title: JavaScript and TypeScript Depth
modules.summary: Welcome to JavaScript and TypeScript Depth — the opening module of the Frontend Engineering Interview Prep path. I'm your instructor, and this is the language half of every frontend loop: closures, the event loop, and async — plus the TypeScript depth that signals seniority. We cover closures, scope, and the module pattern; prototypes, classes, and this; microtasks versus macrotasks; promises, async/await, and their error paths; and TypeScript narrowing, generics, and utility types. By the end, the ten interview questions that never die will be guaranteed points.
objectives: Understand and apply: closures, scope, and the module pattern
Understand and apply: prototypes, classes, and this
Understand and apply: event loop: microtasks vs macrotasks
Understand and apply: promises, async/await, and error paths
Understand and apply: typeScript: narrowing, generics, utility types

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Closure** — A function capturing its enclosing scope's variables — the variables live as long as the closure does; the module pattern, private state, and the classic captured-loop-variable bug.
- **Scope** — Where bindings are visible: function, block (let/const), and module scope — the map you read before reasoning about any variable.
- **this** — Set by the call site — method call, plain call, new, or arrow functions inheriting lexically; prototypes are the delegation chain classes sit on top of.
- **Event loop** — The runtime's scheduling loop: run a macrotask, drain the microtask queue fully, render — the model behind every async interview question.
- **Microtasks vs macrotasks** — Microtasks (promises, queueMicrotask) drain completely after each macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, rendering) — so promise callbacks run before setTimeout(0), and a microtask loop can starve rendering.
- **Promise error paths** — Unhandled rejections, try/catch around await, Promise.all failing fast versus allSettled for independent work — the senior signal is 'here's how this fails and how the caller learns about it.'
- **Narrowing** — typeof/instanceof checks and discriminated unions that shrink a type — with exhaustiveness checking via never proving every variant is handled.
- **Generics with constraints** — Type parameters bounded by constraints — reusable functions and components that stay type-safe across shapes.
- **Utility types** — Partial, Pick, Omit, Record — the standard transformations for deriving types instead of rewriting them.
- **Module pattern** — Closures used to expose a public API over private state — the pre-class encapsulation idiom that still explains how privacy works.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write the closure bug and its fix from memory: the loop-variable capture, then the let-scoped version — explain both aloud in under a minute.
2. Trace an event-loop ordering exercise by hand: interleaved promises, setTimeout(0), and queueMicrotask — predict the order, then run it to verify.
3. Convert a callback-based function to async/await with proper error paths: try/catch, an allSettled for independent calls, and no unhandled rejections.
4. Write a discriminated union with exhaustive narrowing: switch on the discriminant, put never in the default, and let the compiler prove completeness.
5. Drill the ten perennial questions aloud — two minutes each, layered: the 30-second answer, the mechanism, the classic bug — until none of them cost you composure.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Language-depth portfolio. Write a ten-question self-interview: for each perennial question (closures, this, event loop, promises, narrowing, generics, and four more from the module), record a two-minute spoken answer following the layered shape — answer, mechanism, classic bug. Transcribe the two weakest and rewrite them until they're clean. Deliverable: ten recordings plus two rewritten transcripts — guaranteed points, banked.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: language trivia is the floor of frontend interviews, not the ceiling — fluency here buys composure for the novel problems, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers use these questions to calibrate; the offer comes from what you build with the language.

cards.front: Explain closures like the interviewer is testing depth.
cards.back: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope — the variables live as long as the closure does. That’s the module pattern, private state, and also the classic bug: loop variables captured by reference (fixed with let in modern JS).

cards.front: How do you explain ‘this’ and prototypes without rambling?
cards.back: ‘this’ is set by the call site (method call, plain call, new, arrow functions inherit lexically). Prototypes are the delegation chain: property lookup walks up the chain. Classes are syntax over the same prototype mechanism.

cards.front: Microtasks vs macrotasks — the interview-ready version?
cards.back: The event loop drains the microtask queue (promises, queueMicrotask) completely after each macrotask (setTimeout, I/O, rendering steps). So promise callbacks run before setTimeout(0) — and a microtask loop can starve rendering.

cards.front: What do interviewers probe in promises/async-await?
cards.back: Error paths: unhandled rejections, try/catch around await, Promise.all failing fast vs allSettled for independent work, and never mixing raw callbacks with await. The senior signal: ‘here’s how this fails and how the caller learns about it.’

cards.front: What TypeScript features do interviewers actually ask about?
cards.back: Narrowing (typeof/instanceof/discriminated unions — exhaustiveness checking with never), generics with constraints, and utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record). The pitch: ‘types as executable documentation that the compiler checks.’

quiz.q: Rehearsing the perennial questions pays off because:
choices: They’re guaranteed points — fluency here buys composure for the novel problems
quiz.explain: Banking the predictable questions preserves mental budget for the unpredictable ones.

quiz.q: A discriminated union’s power in TypeScript is:
choices: Exhaustive narrowing: the compiler proves you handled every variant
quiz.explain: Switching on the discriminant literal lets TS narrow each branch — and ‘never’ in default proves exhaustiveness.

quiz.q: Promise.all vs Promise.allSettled: the difference is:
choices: all rejects on the first rejection; allSettled waits for every outcome
quiz.explain: all short-circuits on first failure; allSettled reports each promise’s fulfilled/rejected status.

quiz.q: Promise.then callbacks run before setTimeout(0) callbacks because:
quiz.explain: The spec processes the entire microtask queue after each macrotask — promises always win the race.

modules.title: Component Models and React Internals
modules.summary: Welcome to Component Models and React Internals — module 2 of the Frontend path. I'm your instructor, and we study React as a runtime, not an API list: reconciliation, hook closures, and render discipline — the internals senior loops actually probe. We cover components as functions of state, hooks (rules, closures, stale state), reconciliation and keys, memoization (memo, useMemo, useCallback), state management tradeoffs, and the server-components mental model. By the end, you will answer 'why did this re-render?' with a mechanism, not a guess.
objectives: Understand and apply: components as functions of state
Understand and apply: hooks: rules, closures, stale state
Understand and apply: reconciliation and keys
Understand and apply: memoization: memo, useMemo, useCallback
Understand and apply: state management: lifting, context, stores

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **UI = f(state)** — Components as pure rendering functions of state: same state, same output — why unidirectional data flow works and why components are easy to test.
- **Hook closures** — Effects and callbacks capture the render's values — stale state is a closure problem; the fix is reading the capture, not fighting the linter.
- **Reconciliation** — React's diff of old and new trees, matched by key — stable keys let it move and reuse DOM nodes; index keys on reorderable lists cause wrong state reuse.
- **Keys as identity** — Keys are identity, not decoration: identity must follow the item, not its position.
- **memo** — Skips re-rendering a component when props are shallow-equal — for expensive subtrees, measured first, not everywhere.
- **useMemo / useCallback** — useMemo caches an expensive computation; useCallback stabilizes a function identity so memoized children don't re-render — memoize by measurement.
- **State management ladder** — Lift state to the lowest common parent → context for truly global low-churn data → external stores for complex shared state with selective subscriptions.
- **Context's re-render cost** — No selectors: one context value change re-renders all consumers — why context is a poor state manager for high-churn state.
- **Server components** — Components that render on the server and never hydrate — non-interactive UI ships less client JavaScript.
- **Render discipline** — The habit of asking 'what re-rendered and why' before optimizing — profile, then memoize the measured hotspot.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Build a tiny app with a stale-closure bug in an effect; diagnose it by naming the captured render's values, then fix it — explain the mechanism aloud.
2. Render a reorderable list with index keys, observe the wrong-state-reuse bug, switch to stable keys, and state the reconciliation rule that changed the behavior.
3. Profile a slow subtree, add memo/useMemo/useCallback at the measured hotspot only, and re-profile — write the before/after numbers.
4. Move shared state through the ladder for one feature: lifted state, then context, then an external store — state at each step what broke or got awkward.
5. Answer 'why did this re-render?' for three scenarios (parent re-render, context change, new function identity) — mechanism first, fix second.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Internals deep-dive write-up. Pick one real performance bug (or plant one): a list that re-renders wrongly, a context that re-renders everything, a stale effect. Document the symptom, the mechanism (reconciliation, keys, closures), the fix, and the measured before/after. Write it as the answer you'd give a senior interviewer probing internals. Deliverable: the write-up — proof you reason about the runtime, not the API list.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: React internals change across versions — the mental models here are durable, but API details drift, and this course confers no certificate. Verify against the current docs before an interview; interviewers reward current knowledge over memorized snapshots.

cards.front: What does ‘components as functions of state’ mean?
cards.back: UI = f(state): given the same state, the component renders the same output — no hidden dependencies. It’s why unidirectional data flow works and why testing components is easy: set state, assert output. The interview line: ‘pure rendering functions; side effects at the edges.’

cards.front: Explain closures like the interviewer is testing depth.
cards.back: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope — the variables live as long as the closure does. That’s the module pattern, private state, and also the classic bug: loop variables captured by reference (fixed with let in modern JS).

cards.front: Why do keys matter in React lists?
cards.back: Reconciliation matches old and new elements by key: stable keys let React move/reuse DOM nodes; index keys on reorderable lists cause wrong state reuse and wasted re-renders. Keys are identity, not decoration.

cards.front: memo, useMemo, useCallback — when is each the right call?
cards.back: memo: skip re-rendering a component when props are shallow-equal (for expensive subtrees). useMemo: cache an expensive computation. useCallback: stabilize a function identity passed to memoized children. And the caveat: don’t memoize everything — measure first.

cards.front: How do you discuss state management tradeoffs?
cards.back: Lift state to the lowest common parent first; context for truly global low-churn data (theme, auth) — not as a state manager, since context re-renders all consumers; external stores (Zustand/Redux) for complex shared state with selective subscriptions.

quiz.q: React Server Components primarily reduce:
choices: Client-side JavaScript shipped for non-interactive UI
quiz.explain: Server-rendered components never hydrate: their code stays off the client bundle.

quiz.q: React context is a poor state manager for high-churn state because:
choices: Every consumer re-renders on any context value change
quiz.explain: Context has no selectors: one value change re-renders all consumers regardless of what they use.

quiz.q: useCallback’s purpose is:
choices: Preserving function identity across renders so memoized children don’t re-render
quiz.explain: A new function identity each render defeats memo on children; useCallback stabilizes it.

quiz.q: Using array index as key breaks when:
choices: Items reorder or are inserted — React reuses the wrong component state
quiz.explain: Identity must follow the item, not its position; index keys lie about identity on reorder.

modules.title: Browser Rendering and Performance
modules.summary: Welcome to Browser Rendering and Performance — module 3 of the Frontend path. I'm your instructor, and here performance is interview currency: the rendering pipeline, the vitals that measure it, and the optimizations that move them — all demonstrable in DevTools. We cover the critical rendering path, reflow versus repaint versus compositing, Core Web Vitals (LCP, INP, CLS), profiling with the DevTools Performance panel, code splitting, and caching/CDN/resource hints. By the end, your first move in any perf question will be 'profile first' — and you'll mean it.
objectives: Understand and apply: critical rendering path
Understand and apply: reflow, repaint, compositing
Understand and apply: core Web Vitals: LCP, INP, CLS
Understand and apply: profiling with DevTools Performance
Understand and apply: code splitting and lazy loading

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Critical rendering path** — Parse HTML → DOM, parse CSS → CSSOM, render tree, layout, paint, composite — sync scripts and render-blocking CSS delay first paint.
- **Reflow** — Layout: geometry changes — expensive, cascades to descendants; the cost to avoid in animations.
- **Repaint** — Visual changes without geometry — cheaper than reflow, still per-frame budget to watch.
- **Compositing** — GPU layer moves (transform/opacity) — the cheapest visual change; the animation discipline is 'transform and opacity only.'
- **LCP** — Largest Contentful Paint: loading — when the main content appears; lower is better.
- **INP** — Interaction to Next Paint: responsiveness — worst-case input latency; lower is better.
- **CLS** — Cumulative Layout Shift: visual stability — unexpected movement; lower is better.
- **Flame-chart reading** — Record an interaction, read the long tasks, layout/paint blocks, and JS stacks — the bottleneck decides the fix, not intuition.
- **Code splitting** — Ship only what the route needs: route-level splits plus lazy loading cut initial JS — and parse/compile time is the real mobile bottleneck.
- **Resource hints** — preload (high-priority, current page) vs prefetch (low-priority, likely next navigation) — intent and priority, declared up front.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Open DevTools Performance on a slow page you know: record an interaction, identify the longest task, and name the category (scripting, rendering, network) before proposing any fix.
2. Fix one layout-thrash pattern: batch DOM reads and writes, or move an animation to transform/opacity — re-measure and write the before/after.
3. Audit a page's vitals: find LCP, INP, CLS, name the likely cause of the worst one, and propose the single highest-leverage fix.
4. Add route-level code splitting to a toy app: measure initial JS before and after with the coverage panel — state the parse/compile saving.
5. Write the perf-investigation script you'd narrate in an interview: profile → bottleneck → fix → re-measure — and rehearse it on one real page.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Performance case study. Take a slow page (a demo app or a public page you can analyze): profile it, identify the bottleneck with flame-chart evidence, apply one fix (code split, animation discipline, resource hints, or caching), and re-measure. Write it as a case study: baseline vitals, diagnosis, fix, after-numbers. Deliverable: the case study — the artifact that turns 'I know performance' into 'here's the proof.'

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: performance numbers are device- and network-specific — a fix that wins on a flagship phone may not move a budget device, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers score the method (profile, fix, re-measure); absolute numbers are context, not truth.

cards.front: Walk the critical rendering path.
cards.back: Parse HTML → build DOM, parse CSS → CSSOM, combine → render tree, layout (positions/sizes), paint, composite. Anything blocking (sync scripts, render-blocking CSS) delays first paint — that’s why script placement and resource hints matter.

cards.front: Reflow vs repaint vs compositing?
cards.back: Reflow (layout): geometry changes — expensive, cascades. Repaint: visual changes without geometry. Compositing: GPU layer moves (transform/opacity) — cheapest. The perf rule: animate transform and opacity only; batch DOM reads/writes to avoid layout thrash.

cards.front: LCP, INP, CLS — what does each measure?
cards.back: LCP (Largest Contentful Paint): loading — when the main content appears. INP (Interaction to Next Paint): responsiveness — worst-case input latency. CLS (Cumulative Layout Shift): visual stability — unexpected movement. For all three, lower is better.

cards.front: How do you profile with DevTools Performance?
cards.back: Record an interaction, read the flame chart: long tasks, layout/paint blocks, and JS call stacks. Find the bottleneck first (scripting? rendering? network?), fix that, re-measure. The interview line: ‘profile before optimizing — otherwise you’re guessing.’

cards.front: How do you justify code splitting in a perf interview?
cards.back: Ship only what the route needs: route-level splits plus lazy-loading below-the-fold/heavy components cut initial JS, which cuts parse/compile time — the real mobile bottleneck. Measure with coverage/devtools before and after.

quiz.q: prefetch differs from preload in that:
choices: prefetch is low-priority for likely-future navigations; preload is high-priority for the current page
quiz.explain: Priority and intent differ: current-page critical vs next-navigation likely.

quiz.q: Code splitting improves load performance mainly by:
choices: Reducing initial JavaScript parsed and executed
quiz.explain: Initial bundle size drives parse/compile cost; splitting defers non-critical code.

quiz.q: The first step of any performance investigation is:
choices: Profiling to find the actual bottleneck
quiz.explain: Optimizing without measurement optimizes the wrong thing; the flame chart decides.

quiz.q: A high CLS score means:
choices: The page visibly jumps around as content loads — poor visual stability
quiz.explain: CLS sums unexpected layout shifts; late-loading content pushing text around is the classic cause.

modules.title: CSS Layout Systems
modules.summary: Welcome to CSS Layout Systems — module 4 of the Frontend path. I'm your instructor, and this is CSS as engineering: layout systems, architecture at scale, and accessibility — the craft half that separates frontend engineers from JS generalists. We cover the box model, specificity, and the cascade; flexbox and grid; responsive design and container queries; CSS architecture (BEM, modules, utilities); animation discipline; and accessibility. By the end, you will choose layout systems with reasons and keep specificity flat by process.
objectives: Understand and apply: box model, specificity, cascade
Understand and apply: flexbox and Grid: choosing well
Understand and apply: responsive design and container queries
Understand and apply: CSS architecture: BEM, modules, utilities
Understand and apply: animations: transform and opacity discipline

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Box model** — Content + padding + border + margin — with box-sizing: border-box making widths sane; the first thing to verify when layout looks wrong.
- **Specificity** — Inline > ID > class > element, ties broken by source order — kept flat (BEM/utilities) so overrides stay predictable.
- **Flexbox** — One-dimensional layout: a row or column of items with content-driven sizing — the tool for components.
- **Grid** — Two-dimensional layout: rows AND columns with explicit placement — the tool for page-level structure; most real UIs compose both.
- **Container queries** — Components responding to their container's size — reusable in any layout; viewport queries adapt pages, container queries adapt components.
- **BEM** — block__element--modifier: one class of specificity per selector — specificity wars prevented by naming discipline.
- **Transform/opacity discipline** — Animate only transform and opacity (GPU-composited); animating width/left/top triggers reflow — jank.
- **Semantic HTML** — Buttons as <button>, real inputs with labels — keyboard support, focus, and screen-reader semantics for free; divs need all of it rebuilt.
- **Focus and contrast** — Visible focus states and sufficient color contrast — the accessibility checks interviewers actually run.
- **Architecture at scale** — One system (BEM, modules, or utilities), enforced — 'specificity wars are a process failure, not a CSS failure.'

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Build the same card layout three ways (flexbox, grid, floats-free) and state the choosing rule for each — then pick the right one and justify it aloud.
2. Convert a media-query page section to container queries: place the same card in a sidebar and a full-width region and verify it adapts to its container.
3. Refactor a specificity-war stylesheet to flat BEM: cap every selector at one class, remove the !important overrides, and verify the visuals are unchanged.
4. Fix one janky animation by moving it to transform/opacity; record the frame rate before and after — state the reflow you eliminated.
5. Audit a form for accessibility: keyboard-only completion, visible focus, labels on every input, contrast check — fix what fails and log the checklist.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Layout-system showcase. Build a small responsive page (a dashboard or gallery) demonstrating: grid for page structure, flexbox for components, container queries for a reusable card, flat-specificity architecture throughout, transform/opacity animations, and a passing accessibility self-audit. Document the choosing rule at each decision. Deliverable: the page plus the decision log — craft you can point at.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: CSS 'best practices' are team- and codebase-shaped — BEM versus modules versus utilities is a process decision, and this course confers no certificate. The interview tests reasoning about systems; production tests whether the team actually enforces the one it picked.

cards.front: Box model and specificity in 30 seconds?
cards.back: Content + padding + border + margin; box-sizing: border-box makes widths sane. Specificity: inline > ID > class > element; the cascade resolves ties by source order. Keep specificity flat (BEM/utilities) so overrides stay predictable.

cards.front: Flexbox vs Grid: the choosing rule?
cards.back: Flexbox for one-dimensional layout (a row or column of items, content-driven sizing). Grid for two-dimensional layout (rows AND columns, explicit placement). Most real UIs compose both.

cards.front: How do you discuss responsive design modernly?
cards.back: Fluid layouts + breakpoints for viewport adaptation, container queries for component-level responsiveness (the component adapts to its container, not the viewport). The interview line: ‘viewport queries adapt pages; container queries adapt components.’

cards.front: How do you keep CSS maintainable at scale?
cards.back: Architecture with flat specificity: BEM naming (block__element--modifier), CSS modules for scoping, or utility classes — pick one and enforce it. The interview line: ‘specificity wars are a process failure, not a CSS failure.’

cards.front: What’s the transform-and-opacity discipline?
cards.back: Animate only transform and opacity: they composite on the GPU without layout or paint. Animating width/left/top triggers reflow — jank. The interview line: ‘if it moves pixels through layout, it’s not an animation, it’s a slideshow.’

quiz.q: Using a <div> with onClick instead of <button> harms accessibility because:
choices: It loses built-in keyboard support, focus, and screen-reader semantics
quiz.explain: Native controls carry keyboard handling and ARIA roles for free; divs need all of it rebuilt.

quiz.q: A janky animation’s usual cause is:
choices: Animating layout-triggering properties instead of transform/opacity
quiz.explain: Layout per frame blows the 16ms budget; composited properties don’t.

quiz.q: BEM’s naming discipline prevents:
choices: Specificity wars — flat, predictable selectors instead of deep nesting
quiz.explain: block__element--modifier keeps every selector at one class of specificity: overrides stay sane.

quiz.q: Container queries improve on media queries by:
choices: Letting components respond to their container’s size — reusable in any layout
quiz.explain: Component-level responsiveness: the same card works in a sidebar and a full page.

modules.title: Frontend System Design
modules.summary: Welcome to Frontend System Design — module 5 of the Frontend path. I'm your instructor, and this is system design through the browser's lens: the classic frontend design questions, practiced with component trees, data flow, and tradeoff narration. We cover designing a news feed, typeahead/autocomplete, and a photo gallery at scale; client-side caching and state sync; real-time options (polling, SSE, WebSockets); and the frontend design-round walkthrough. By the end, you will design the client as a system, not a page.
objectives: Understand and apply: designing a news feed
Understand and apply: designing typeahead and autocomplete
Understand and apply: designing a photo gallery at scale
Understand and apply: client-side caching and state sync
Understand and apply: real-time: polling, SSE, WebSockets

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **News-feed fan-out** — Push for normal users, pull for celebrities — the famous hybrid; ranking separated from delivery, hot feeds cached, paginated.
- **Typeahead design** — Debounced input (~200–300ms), prefix index (trie or indexed prefix column), popularity/recency ranking, aggressive caching of hot prefixes — plus canceling stale in-flight requests client-side.
- **Photo pipeline** — Upload → object storage → async thumbnails (multiple sizes) → CDN → lazy loading + responsive images (srcset): 'bytes are the budget.'
- **Client cache (SWR-style)** — Normalized server data with stale-while-revalidate: instant render from cache, fresh data moments later — invalidation tied to mutations.
- **Optimistic updates** — Apply the mutation to UI immediately, roll back on server rejection — the UX bet with the hedge built in.
- **Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets** — Polling: simple, wasteful. SSE: server→client stream with auto-reconnect — feeds and notifications. WebSockets: full duplex — chat, games, collaboration. Weakest tool that satisfies direction and frequency.
- **State sync** — Server as truth, client cache as a performance layer allowed to be briefly wrong, never permanently wrong.
- **Frontend walkthrough** — Requirements → component tree and data flow → API → caching/sync → rendering perf → real-time — the client-side shape of the standard walkthrough.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Whiteboard the news feed in 45 minutes: requirements, API, data model, fan-out decision with the celebrity math, caching, pagination — narrate tradeoffs throughout.
2. Design typeahead end to end: debounce timing, prefix index choice, ranking inputs, cache layers, and the stale-request cancellation on the client.
3. Design the photo gallery: upload flow, thumbnail sizes, CDN placement, lazy loading and srcset strategy — with the byte budget stated.
4. Choose the real-time mechanism for three features (notifications, chat, live dashboard): name direction and frequency, pick the weakest sufficient tool, state the rejected options.
5. Draw one client architecture (state, cache/sync, rendering, real-time) and present it in 10 minutes — the frontend design-round compressed rep.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Frontend design portfolio. Write two one-page design docs — the news feed and one more (typeahead or photo gallery) — each with requirements, component tree and data flow, API, caching/sync strategy, rendering-perf plan, and real-time choice. Record a 20-minute walkthrough of one. Deliverable: two docs plus the recording — the client-side design evidence.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: frontend design rounds are the least standardized interviews in the loop — expectations swing widely by company, and this course confers no certificate. The walkthrough is a communication skill; the 'right' architecture always depends on the product's actual constraints.

cards.front: How do you structure the ‘design a news feed’ answer?
cards.back: Requirements (post, follow, ranked feed), API, data model (posts, edges), fan-out: push for normal users, pull for celebrities (the famous hybrid), ranking separate from delivery, cache hot feeds, pagination.

cards.front: Design typeahead/autocomplete: the key decisions?
cards.back: Debounce input (~200–300ms), prefix index (trie or indexed prefix column), rank by popularity/recency, cache hot prefixes aggressively. Client: cancel stale in-flight requests so slow responses don’t overwrite fresh ones.

cards.front: How do you design a photo gallery at scale?
cards.back: Upload → object storage → async thumbnails (multiple sizes) → CDN in front → lazy loading + responsive images (srcset) on the client. The interview line: ‘bytes are the budget — every decision serves fewer, smaller, closer bytes.’

cards.front: How do you handle client-side caching and state sync?
cards.back: Normalize server data in a client cache (React Query/SWR style): stale-while-revalidate for freshness, cache keys as query keys, optimistic updates with rollback on error, and invalidation tied to mutations. The interview line: ‘the server is the truth; the client cache is a performance layer with an eviction policy.’

cards.front: Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets?
cards.back: Polling: simple, wasteful (empty responses). SSE: server→client stream over HTTP, auto-reconnect — perfect for notifications/feeds. WebSockets: full duplex — chat, games, collaboration. Choose the weakest tool that satisfies the direction and frequency.

quiz.q: A frontend design round emphasizes:
choices: Client architecture: state, caching/sync, rendering perf, real-time
quiz.explain: The graded system is the client: how it manages state, data, and performance at scale.

quiz.q: Server-Sent Events fit a live notification feed because:
choices: They’re a simple server-to-client stream with auto-reconnect — exactly the direction needed
quiz.explain: One-directional updates over plain HTTP: less machinery than WebSockets for the same job.

quiz.q: Stale-while-revalidate improves perceived performance by:
choices: Serving cached data instantly while revalidating in the background
quiz.explain: Instant render from cache, fresh data moments later — the best of both latencies.

quiz.q: Generating multiple thumbnail sizes at upload time is worth it because:
choices: Clients download exactly the size they display — no wasted bytes or client-side scaling
quiz.explain: Serve-the-right-size beats serve-one-size: bandwidth follows the display, not the source.

modules.title: Machine Coding Build
modules.summary: Welcome to the Machine Coding Build — module 6 of the Frontend path. I'm your instructor, and this is machine coding as a sport: three builds under a timer with tests and accessible markup — the round that decides most frontend offers. We build a typeahead from scratch, a carousel with accessibility, and a Kanban with drag and drop; we practice clean component APIs under time and testing the build with Testing Library. By the end, the 90-minute cadence will be muscle memory.
objectives: Build and demonstrate: building a typeahead from scratch
Build and demonstrate: building a carousel with accessibility
Build and demonstrate: building a Kanban with drag and drop
Build and demonstrate: clean component APIs under time
Build and demonstrate: testing the build with Testing Library

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **90-minute cadence** — 10 clarify + plan the component API, 60 build working-first, 20 edge cases + tests — clean props interfaces over pixel perfection.
- **Working-first** — Happy path functional before polish and edge cases — a demoable build beats a perfect fragment; interviewers score working builds with clean APIs.
- **Component API design** — Props as the contract: minimal, typed, intention-revealing — the design judgment interviewers read in your code.
- **Typeahead build** — Debounced input, cancellable requests, keyboard navigation, ranked suggestions — the canonical machine-coding problem.
- **Accessible carousel** — Semantic structure, keyboard controls, visible focus, announced slide changes — accessibility as a correctness requirement.
- **Kanban drag-and-drop** — Data model first (columns → cards, normalized), drag via HTML5 or pointer events, optimistic updates, keyboard-accessible fallback.
- **Testing Library philosophy** — Test user-visible behavior (roles, text), not implementation details — role-based queries align tests with the accessible experience.
- **Edge cases under time** — Empty states, errors, loading — the 20-minute block that separates a demo from a build.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Build the typeahead in 90 minutes on a timer: 10 plan the component API, 60 working-first, 20 edge cases + tests — then score yourself on API cleanliness.
2. Build the accessible carousel in 90 minutes: keyboard operable, focus visible, slide changes announced — test it keyboard-only at the end.
3. Build the Kanban in 90 minutes: normalized data model first, drag-and-drop second, keyboard fallback third — narrate the API choices as you go.
4. Write Testing Library tests for one build: happy path plus two edge cases, role-based queries only — verify the tests break when accessibility breaks.
5. Review all three builds against the rubric: working-first? clean APIs? tests? accessibility? — log the pattern in your misses.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Machine-coding portfolio. The three timed builds — typeahead, carousel, Kanban — each with tests and an accessibility self-check, plus a one-page build narrative per build (decisions, rejected alternatives, what you'd do with more time). Deliverable: three builds, tests, and narratives — the round that decides offers, rehearsed.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: machine-coding rounds vary wildly — some companies grade polish, others grade API design, and this course confers no certificate. Timed builds train the cadence; the real round still depends on the prompt and the grader. What transfers is the working-first discipline.

cards.front: Design typeahead/autocomplete: the key decisions?
cards.back: Debounce input (~200–300ms), prefix index (trie or indexed prefix column), rank by popularity/recency, cache hot prefixes aggressively. Client: cancel stale in-flight requests so slow responses don’t overwrite fresh ones.

cards.front: What accessibility points score in frontend interviews?
cards.back: Semantic HTML first (buttons are <button>), visible focus states, color contrast, labels for inputs, alt text that conveys function, and keyboard operability. The line: ‘accessibility is a correctness requirement, tested like any other.’

cards.front: How do you approach a Kanban-with-drag-and-drop machine-coding task?
cards.back: Data model first (columns → cards, normalized), HTML5 drag events or pointer events, optimistic state updates with keyboard-accessible fallback, and clean component APIs. The interview line: ‘the data model is the app — drag-and-drop is just the input method.’

cards.front: How do you win a machine-coding round?
cards.back: The 90-minute cadence: 10 min clarify + plan the component API, 60 min build working-first (happy path before polish), 20 min edge cases + tests. Clean props interfaces matter more than pixel perfection — interviewers read your API design.

cards.front: How do you test a machine-coding build?
cards.back: Testing Library philosophy: test user-visible behavior (roles, text), not implementation details. Happy path + key edge cases (empty states, errors), accessible queries as a bonus a11y check. The interview line: ‘my tests describe what the user can do.’

quiz.q: Testing Library prefers role-based queries because:
choices: They test the accessible experience — the test breaks when accessibility breaks
quiz.explain: Querying by role aligns tests with how users (and assistive tech) find elements.

quiz.q: In machine coding, ‘working first’ means:
choices: Happy path functional before polish and edge cases — a demoable build beats a perfect fragment
quiz.explain: Interviewers score a working build with clean APIs; polish without function scores nothing.

quiz.q: Keyboard-accessible drag-and-drop matters because:
choices: Pointer-only interaction excludes keyboard users — accessibility is a correctness requirement
quiz.explain: Every pointer interaction needs a keyboard equivalent; interviewers check.

quiz.q: Using a <div> with onClick instead of <button> harms accessibility because:
choices: It loses built-in keyboard support, focus, and screen-reader semantics
quiz.explain: Native controls carry keyboard handling and ARIA roles for free; divs need all of it rebuilt.

modules.title: Frontend Mock Circuit
modules.summary: Welcome to the Frontend Mock Circuit — the final module of the Frontend path. I'm your instructor, and these are frontend-flavored mocks across all three round types — timed JS deep-dives, machine coding on camera, frontend system-design rounds — plus the behavioral ledger, debriefed into a punch list. By the end, the onsite will feel like repetition, not discovery.
objectives: Apply in professional practice: timed JS deep-dives
Apply in professional practice: machine-coding on camera
Apply in professional practice: frontend system design rounds
Apply in professional practice: behavioral ledger
Apply in professional practice: debrief and triage

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Layered deep-dive answers** — The 30-second correct answer, then the mechanism, then the edge case — 'the classic bug here is…' before they ask.
- **Machine-coding on camera** — The 90-minute cadence under observation: narrate the API plan, build working-first, test — composure as a scored skill.
- **Frontend design round** — Same walkthrough, client-side components: state architecture, caching/sync, rendering performance, real-time updates.
- **Behavioral ledger** — Story bank, stories-told-where, feedback, stumping questions — every behavioral touchpoint fresh and improving.
- **Debrief and triage** — Within the hour: what leaked, what held, biggest leak by frequency × weight, the 48-hour redrill — the mock is the test, the debrief is the studying.
- **Taper plan** — No new material, redrill from the debrief log, timed mocks, rest — the final two weeks.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Run a timed JS deep-dive mock (30 min): layered answers, 'the question behind the question' — log where you rambled versus where you landed.
2. Run a machine-coding mock on camera (90 min): narrate the component API plan, build working-first, test — review the recording for silent stretches.
3. Run a frontend system-design mock (45 min): client architecture with state, caching/sync, rendering, real-time — end with tradeoffs.
4. Run one behavioral round from your ledger: two-minute STAR answers, no repeated stories — log the follow-ups that stumped you.
5. Debrief all four within the hour: template, ranked leaks, 48-hour redrills, updated ledger — then write the taper plan.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Frontend mock portfolio. The four-mock circuit over two weeks — JS deep dive, machine coding on camera, frontend system design, behavioral — each debriefed (leaks, holds, biggest leak, redrill plan) with the ledger updated. Close with the taper schedule for your real loop. Deliverable: four debriefs, the ledger, the taper — the onsite as repetition.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: mocks can't reproduce the real loop's stakes or its interviewers — and this course confers no certificate. What the circuit removes is surprise: the format, the timing, and your own leak patterns, all discovered while fixes are still cheap.

cards.front: How do you handle timed language deep-dives?
cards.back: Answer in layers: the 30-second correct answer, then the mechanism, then the edge case — and say ‘the classic bug here is…’ before they ask. The interview line: ‘I answer the question, then the question behind the question.’

cards.front: How do you win a machine-coding round?
cards.back: The 90-minute cadence: 10 min clarify + plan the component API, 60 min build working-first (happy path before polish), 20 min edge cases + tests. Clean props interfaces matter more than pixel perfection — interviewers read your API design.

cards.front: How does a frontend system-design round differ?
cards.back: Same walkthrough (requirements → API → data → scale), but the components are client-side: state architecture, caching/sync strategy, rendering performance, and real-time updates. The interview line: ‘I design the client as a system, not a page.’

cards.front: What’s a behavioral ledger?
cards.back: Your running record: story bank entries, which stories you’ve told where, feedback received, and follow-up questions that stumped you. It stops you from repeating the same story and turns each behavioral round into training data.

cards.front: How do you debrief and triage after a mock?
cards.back: Within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), rank leaks by frequency × interview weight, and redrill the top one within 48 hours. The interview line: ‘the mock is the test; the debrief is the studying.’

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: Weak-spot triage should prioritize leaks by:
choices: Frequency × interview weight — what costs the most points most often
quiz.explain: Expected value: fix what loses you the most points most often.

quiz.q: A behavioral ledger prevents:
choices: Repeating the same story across rounds and losing track of feedback
quiz.explain: Loops have multiple behavioral touchpoints; the ledger keeps each one fresh and improving.

quiz.q: A frontend design round emphasizes:
choices: Client architecture: state, caching/sync, rendering perf, real-time
quiz.explain: The graded system is the client: how it manages state, data, and performance at scale.

modules.title: Fullstack Architecture
modules.summary: Welcome to Fullstack Architecture — the opening module of the Fullstack Engineering Interview Prep path. I'm your instructor, and we hold the whole path in one head here: every hop a request takes, the rendering strategies that shape it, and the architecture vocabulary fullstack loops demand. We cover the request path from DNS to render; monolith, modular monolith, and services; the BFF pattern; SSR, SSG, and ISR; and edge/CDN placement. By the end, you will draw the whole path before diving deep — because the diagram is the map.
objectives: Understand and apply: the request path: DNS to render
Understand and apply: monolith, modular monolith, services
Understand and apply: BFF (backend-for-frontend) pattern
Understand and apply: SSR, SSG, ISR: rendering strategies
Understand and apply: edge and CDN placement

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Request path** — DNS → TCP → TLS → CDN/edge → load balancer → app server → (cache → DB) → response → parse → render — saying the full path aloud is the fullstack flex.
- **Monolith** — One deployable, simplest ops — the honest starting point until a seam proves otherwise.
- **Modular monolith** — Bounded-context modules inside one deployable — the discipline without the distributed tax.
- **Microservices** — Independent deployables — the distributed-systems cost paid only when proven seams demand it.
- **BFF** — Backend-for-Frontend: a thin service per client type aggregating downstream services into exactly the shapes each UI needs — killing over-fetching without leaking topology.
- **SSR** — Render per request: fresh, slower TTFB — personalized dashboards, authenticated content.
- **SSG** — Render at build: fastest, stale until rebuild — marketing pages, docs.
- **ISR** — Static with timed revalidation: fresh without rebuilds — the middle path for mostly-static content that changes.
- **Edge placement** — Static and cacheable dynamic content at CDN PoPs; compute at the edge only when latency demands it; origin as the source of truth.
- **Draw-before-dive** — Establishing shared context first — then both you and the interviewer know where the deep dive lives.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Draw the full request path for an app you know, hop by hop, from DNS to render — then narrate it aloud in under three minutes.
2. For one product, choose the architecture: monolith, modular monolith, or services — write the seam analysis that justifies the call and the condition that would flip it.
3. Decide the rendering strategy per page of a sample site (landing, dashboard, docs, feed): SSG, SSR, or ISR — with the freshness argument for each.
4. Place the edge: mark on your request-path diagram what lives at the CDN, what computes at the edge, and what stays at the origin — with the latency argument per placement.
5. Present the whole-path diagram in 10 minutes to a partner: map first, then one deep dive where they point — practice the draw-before-dive discipline.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Whole-path architecture brief. For a product you choose: the request-path diagram with every hop labeled, the architecture decision (monolith → services spectrum) with the seam analysis, per-page rendering strategy with freshness arguments, and the edge-placement map. Deliverable: the brief — the artifact you will adapt live when a fullstack loop asks you to 'design the whole thing.'

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: 'fullstack' depth is breadth by design — no one is expert at every hop, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers test whether you can reason across the path and know where your depth ends; claiming depth everywhere is the fastest way to lose credibility.

cards.front: Walk the request path: DNS to render.
cards.back: DNS resolve → TCP handshake → TLS → request hits CDN/edge → load balancer → app server → (cache → DB) → response → browser parses HTML/CSS/JS → render. Saying the full path out loud is the fullstack flex — then zoom into wherever the question points.

cards.front: Monolith vs modular monolith vs microservices?
cards.back: Monolith: one deployable, simplest ops. Modular monolith: bounded-context modules inside one deployable — the discipline without the distributed tax. Microservices: independent deployables — pay the distributed-systems cost only when seams demand it. The interview line: ‘I evolve toward distribution, I don’t start there.’

cards.front: What’s the BFF pattern?
cards.back: Backend-for-Frontend: a thin service per client type (web, mobile) that aggregates downstream microservices into exactly the shapes each UI needs — killing over-fetching without leaking service topology to clients.

cards.front: SSR vs SSG vs ISR?
cards.back: SSR: render per request (fresh, slower TTFB). SSG: render at build (fastest, stale until rebuild). ISR: static with timed revalidation (the middle path). Choose by freshness needs: marketing page → SSG; personalized dashboard → SSR.

cards.front: How do you reason about edge and CDN placement?
cards.back: Push static and cacheable dynamic content to the edge (CDN PoPs), compute at the edge only when latency demands it (edge functions), origin for the source of truth. The interview line: ‘every mile between the user and the byte is latency I can buy off.’

quiz.q: Drawing before diving deep is strong because:
choices: It establishes shared context — then both of you know where the deep dive lives
quiz.explain: The diagram is the map; deep dives are the territory. Maps first.

quiz.q: Edge computing earns its keep when:
choices: Latency is the constraint and the work is cacheable or lightweight per request
quiz.explain: Edge pays for latency-sensitive, lightweight work — not for heavy computation.

quiz.q: ISR’s advantage over pure SSG is:
choices: Pages revalidate in the background on an interval — fresh without rebuilds
quiz.explain: Stale-while-revalidate at the page level: serve cached, regenerate on schedule.

quiz.q: A BFF mainly solves:
choices: Over/under-fetching by shaping responses per client
quiz.explain: Each client gets an aggregation layer tuned to its screens instead of N chatty service calls.

modules.title: REST and GraphQL
modules.summary: Welcome to REST and GraphQL — module 2 of the Fullstack path. I'm your instructor, and we take both API styles to decision depth: when REST's cacheability wins, when GraphQL's client-shaped queries win, and how to argue it. We cover REST resource modeling, GraphQL schema/queries/mutations, the honest over/under-fetching comparison, why caching GraphQL is harder, and subscriptions for real-time. By the end, you will choose per surface — because client constraints differ.
objectives: Understand and apply: REST resource modeling
Understand and apply: graphQL schema, queries, mutations
Understand and apply: over- and under-fetching: the honest comparison
Understand and apply: caching GraphQL (and why it is harder)
Understand and apply: subscriptions and real-time

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **REST resource modeling** — Resources as nouns, verbs as actions, status codes as the contract — the cacheable, toolable default.
- **GraphQL schema** — Types, queries, mutations: the typed contract clients shape per request — exact fields, one round trip.
- **Over-fetching** — REST endpoints returning fields the client ignores — wasted bytes, the cost GraphQL eliminates.
- **Under-fetching** — Needing N requests for one screen — chatty on high-latency networks, the cost GraphQL eliminates.
- **GraphQL caching cost** — A single endpoint with arbitrary query shapes defeats HTTP caching and simple per-route limits — the price of client-shaped queries; query-cost analysis required.
- **N+1 resolvers** — Per-field resolvers firing per row — the GraphQL performance trap, fixed by batching (dataloaders).
- **Subscriptions** — GraphQL's real-time primitive — server-pushed updates over a persistent connection for live data.
- **Per-surface choice** — Client constraints (bandwidth, latency, capabilities) decide the contract shape — not architectural purity.
- **Caching as a tradeoff** — What to cache, where, the invalidation strategy, the failure story — 'caching is a tradeoff with an invalidation plan, not a speedup.'
- **Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets** — Polling: simple, wasteful. SSE: server→client stream, auto-reconnect. WebSockets: full duplex — weakest sufficient tool per direction and frequency.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Model one screen's data needs twice: as REST endpoints (count the requests and wasted fields) and as one GraphQL query — write the over/under-fetching ledger for both.
2. Write the caching plan for the REST version (HTTP cache semantics, CDN, invalidation) and then for the GraphQL version (query hashing, persisted queries, cost limits) — compare the machinery.
3. Diagnose an N+1 resolver scenario on paper: per-row field resolvers, the query count explosion, then the dataloader batching fix — state the before/after query counts.
4. Choose the real-time mechanism for three features (notifications, chat, live dashboard): direction, frequency, weakest sufficient tool — with the rejected options named.
5. Argue one per-surface decision aloud in two minutes: 'mobile feed → GraphQL because…, public API → REST because…' — verdict plus the flip condition.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: API-strategy brief. For a two-client product (web + mobile): the REST surface (resources, caching plan, invalidation) and the GraphQL surface (schema sketch, caching strategy, query-cost limits, dataloader plan), the per-surface decision with client-constraint arguments, and the real-time choice per live feature. Deliverable: the brief — both styles at decision depth, argued not assumed.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: the REST/GraphQL debate is context-shaped — team skill, client mix, and existing infrastructure decide more than theory, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers score the honest comparison; partisanship for either style reads as inexperience.

cards.front: What makes an API ‘RESTful’ in an interview answer?
cards.back: Resources as nouns in URLs, HTTP verbs as actions, status codes as the contract (200/201/400/401/403/404/429/500), stateless requests, and versioning — then the judgment calls: pagination, filtering, and idempotency.

cards.front: When do queries beat endpoints — your GraphQL judgment call?
cards.back: When clients need varied, nested data and over/under-fetching hurts (mobile, aggregations): one query, exact fields, typed schema. The costs you must name: caching is harder, query complexity needs limits, and N+1 resolvers need batching (dataloaders).

cards.front: Over-fetching vs under-fetching — the honest comparison?
cards.back: Over-fetching: REST endpoints returning fields the client ignores (wasted bytes). Under-fetching: needing N requests for one screen (chatty). GraphQL fixes both per-query; the cost is caching complexity. The interview line: ‘I measure the waste before I prescribe the cure.’

cards.front: How do you discuss caching in a cloud interview?
cards.back: What to cache (read-heavy, slow-changing), where (CDN edge, app cache, DB query cache), invalidation strategy, and the failure story (thundering herd, stale reads). The interview line: ‘caching is a tradeoff with an invalidation plan, not a speedup.’

cards.front: Polling vs SSE vs WebSockets?
cards.back: Polling: simple, wasteful (empty responses). SSE: server→client stream over HTTP, auto-reconnect — perfect for notifications/feeds. WebSockets: full duplex — chat, games, collaboration. Choose the weakest tool that satisfies the direction and frequency.

quiz.q: Per-surface API choice is justified because:
choices: Client constraints differ (bandwidth, latency, capabilities) — the contract should fit the consumer
quiz.explain: The consumer’s constraints decide the contract shape, not architectural purity.

quiz.q: Server-Sent Events fit a live notification feed because:
choices: They’re a simple server-to-client stream with auto-reconnect — exactly the direction needed
quiz.explain: One-directional updates over plain HTTP: less machinery than WebSockets for the same job.

quiz.q: Every caching decision must name:
choices: The invalidation strategy — stale data is caching’s permanent tax
quiz.explain: Cache without an invalidation story is a future incident.

quiz.q: Under-fetching hurts mobile clients most because:
choices: Many sequential round trips compound on high-latency networks
quiz.explain: Chatty APIs multiply round-trip latency — the scarcest resource on mobile networks.

modules.title: Auth and Identity
modules.summary: Welcome to Auth and Identity — module 3 of the Fullstack path. I'm your instructor, and this is auth without hand-waving: the flows, the token lifecycle, and the storage decisions — the topic where bluffing is most visible and most punished. We cover sessions versus tokens, JWT structure and validation, the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow, OpenID Connect on top, and password hashing with bcrypt and Argon2. By the end, you will answer auth with threat models, not library names.
objectives: Understand and apply: sessions vs tokens
Understand and apply: JWT structure and validation
Understand and apply: oAuth 2.0 flows: authorization code
Understand and apply: openID Connect on top
Understand and apply: password hashing: bcrypt and argon2

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Sessions** — Server-side state keyed by cookie — revocable instantly, needs a shared store at scale; the stateful default.
- **Tokens (JWT)** — Stateless, self-contained — scales horizontally, but revocation needs denylists or short expiry; the stateless tradeoff.
- **JWT structure** — header.payload.signature, base64url — claims like sub, exp, iat; signed, not encrypted: never put secrets in claims.
- **JWT validation** — Signature with the right key and algorithm (never 'none'), expiry, issuer, audience — every one checked, every time.
- **OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow** — User → client redirects to auth server → approval → short-lived single-use code → code (+ secret, PKCE for public clients) exchanged for tokens; tokens never touch the browser URL.
- **PKCE** — code_verifier/code_challenge pair protecting public clients (mobile/SPA) that can't keep a secret — prevents authorization-code interception.
- **OpenID Connect** — The identity layer on top of OAuth 2.0: standardized ID tokens for 'who is this user' — SSO's building block.
- **Password hashing** — Never encrypt (reversible) — hash with a memory-hard salted function: Argon2id preferred, bcrypt acceptable; per-user salt; work factor tuned so login takes hundreds of milliseconds.
- **Refresh token storage** — httpOnly secure cookies, rotated on use — the answer to 'where do refresh tokens live.'
- **JWT revocation** — The honest answer: short-lived access tokens plus refresh-token rotation and denylists — statelessness means bounding the exposure window, not central killing.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Draw the authorization code flow with PKCE end to end: every redirect, the code exchange, where each token lives — then narrate it aloud in three minutes.
2. Write the JWT validation checklist for a resource server: algorithm, signature key, exp, iss, aud — then list what breaks if each check is skipped.
3. Compare sessions vs tokens for two products (a bank dashboard, a content API): revocation needs, scale needs, the verdict per product with reasons.
4. Write the password-storage spec: algorithm choice, salt strategy, work-factor target, and the 'never roll your own crypto' rule — as you'd state it in an interview.
5. Answer the three senior-loop auth questions aloud: 'how do you revoke a JWT?', 'where do refresh tokens live?', 'how do you do SSO?' — threat model first, mechanism second.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Auth design brief. For a two-client product: the flow choice (sessions vs tokens, with the revocation analysis), the OAuth/OIDC integration sketch, the JWT validation checklist, refresh-token storage and rotation policy, and the password-hashing spec. Include the threat model: what each decision defends against. Deliverable: the brief — auth argued from threat models.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: auth is the topic where overconfidence is dangerous — real systems add key rotation, breach response, and compliance that interviews skip, and this course confers no certificate. State the threat model honestly; 'it depends on the threat model' is a senior answer, not evasion.

cards.front: Sessions vs tokens?
cards.back: Sessions: server-side state keyed by cookie — revocable instantly, needs sticky/shared store at scale. Tokens (JWT): stateless, self-contained — scales horizontally, but revocation needs denylists/short expiry. Choose by revocation needs.

cards.front: What’s inside a JWT, and what must you validate?
cards.back: Header.payload.signature, base64url: claims like sub, exp, iat. Validate: signature with the right key/algorithm (never ‘none’), expiry, issuer/audience. And the warning: JWTs are signed, not encrypted — never put secrets in claims.

cards.front: Walk the OAuth 2.0 authorization code flow.
cards.back: User → client redirects to auth server → user approves → auth code returned → client exchanges code (+ secret, PKCE for public clients) for tokens at the token endpoint. The code is short-lived and single-use; tokens never touch the browser URL.

cards.front: How do you store passwords — the interview answer?
cards.back: Never encrypt (reversible); hash with a memory-hard, salted function: Argon2id preferred, bcrypt acceptable. Per-user random salt, work factor tuned so login takes ~hundreds of ms. And never roll your own crypto.

cards.front: Which auth questions decide senior loops?
cards.back: ‘How do you revoke a JWT?’ (short expiry + denylist/rotation), ‘where do refresh tokens live?’ (httpOnly secure cookies, rotated), ‘how do you do SSO?’ (OIDC). The interview line: ‘I answer auth with threat models, not library names.’

quiz.q: JWT revocation’s honest answer is:
choices: Short-lived access tokens + refresh-token rotation and denylists — statelessness has a revocation cost
quiz.explain: Stateless tokens can’t be centrally killed; the design bounds the exposure window instead.

quiz.q: Passwords must be hashed, not encrypted, because:
choices: Encryption is reversible — a key leak exposes every password; hashing is one-way
quiz.explain: One-way hashing means even a full database theft doesn’t yield passwords (beyond cracking).

quiz.q: PKCE exists to protect:
choices: Public clients (mobile/SPA) that can’t keep a secret — the code exchange is bound to the original request
quiz.explain: Without a client secret, PKCE’s code_verifier/code_challenge pair prevents authorization-code interception.

quiz.q: A JWT is ___ not ___:
quiz.explain: Anyone can read the payload; the signature only proves it wasn’t tampered with.

modules.title: Data Across the Stack
modules.summary: Welcome to Data Across the Stack — module 4 of the Fullstack path. I'm your instructor, and this is data end to end: validation at every boundary, the ORM/SQL tradeoff, and keeping client state and the database telling the same story. We cover validation layers from form to row, ORMs versus query builders versus raw SQL, migrations in a deployed app, full-text search basics, file uploads with object storage, and client-cache/DB consistency. By the end, you will trace a datum from the form field to the row — and back.
objectives: Understand and apply: from form to row: validation layers
Understand and apply: oRMs vs query builders vs SQL
Understand and apply: migrations in a deployed app
Understand and apply: search: full-text basics
Understand and apply: file uploads and object storage

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Validation layers** — Client for UX, API boundary for trust, database constraints for the last line of defense — never trust the client alone.
- **ORM tradeoff** — Speed of development with relationships as objects — watch N+1 and leaky abstractions on complex queries; 'ORM for CRUD, SQL where it earns it.'
- **Query builders** — Composable SQL without string soup — the middle path between ORM magic and raw strings.
- **Migrations in production** — Expand-contract: backward-compatible steps, old and new code coexisting, old shape removed after readers move.
- **Inverted index** — Terms → documents: tokenization, stemming, ranking (TF-IDF/BM25) — Postgres tsvector for the simple case, dedicated engines at scale.
- **Presigned uploads** — Clients upload straight to object storage — app servers never proxy the bytes; async processing (thumbnails, scans) via queues.
