- **Optimistic updates** — UI applies the mutation immediately with a rollback path for server rejection — optimism as a UX bet, the rollback as the hedge.
- **Client/DB consistency** — Server as source of truth; client cache as a performance layer with invalidation tied to mutations — allowed to be briefly wrong, never permanently.
- **Senior answer structure** — Three beats for any deep-dive: one-sentence definition, the mechanism, when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Trace one form submission end to end: client validation, API validation, DB constraints — write what each layer catches that the others can't.
2. Take an ORM query with an N+1 smell: find it, fix it with eager loading, then drop to raw SQL for the reporting query — state the layer choice each time.
3. Write the expand-contract migration for renaming a column on a live table: the steps, the dual-read period, the cleanup — with the rollback at each step.
4. Sketch full-text search for a product catalog: tsvector vs dedicated engine — the scale and faceting arguments that decide.
5. Design the upload flow: presigned URL, direct-to-storage, async processing queue, CDN reads — draw the bytes' path and name what never touches the app server.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Data-flow brief. For your capstone-shaped app: the validation map (what each layer enforces), the ORM/SQL layering with the N+1 audit, the migration plan for the first three schema changes, the search approach with the scale argument, and the upload pipeline. Deliverable: the brief — data traced from form to row, every layer justified.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: data-layer taste is workload-shaped — the ORM/SQL split, the search engine, the migration strategy all answer to scale and team, and this course confers no certificate. The interview tests the reasoning chain; production adds the constraints of the system you inherited.

cards.front: ORMs vs query builders vs raw SQL?
cards.back: ORMs: speed of development, relationships as objects — watch N+1 and leaky abstraction on complex queries. Query builders: composable SQL without string soup. Raw SQL: full control for reporting/analytics. The senior line: ‘I use the ORM for CRUD and drop to SQL where it earns it.’

cards.front: How do you discuss full-text search basics?
cards.back: Inverted index: terms → documents, with tokenization, stemming, and ranking (TF-IDF/BM25). For interview depth: Postgres tsvector covers the simple case; dedicated engines (OpenSearch/Elasticsearch) earn their keep at scale, faceting, and relevance tuning.

cards.front: How do you handle file uploads at scale?
cards.back: Direct-to-object-storage uploads (presigned URLs — the app server never proxies bytes), async processing (thumbnails, virus scan) via queues, CDN in front for reads. The interview line: ‘bytes never touch my app servers.’

cards.front: How do you keep client cache and DB consistent?
cards.back: Server as source of truth; client cache as a performance layer with invalidation tied to mutations (optimistic updates + rollback on error, or refetch-on-mutation). The interview line: ‘the client cache is allowed to be wrong briefly, never permanently.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'From form to row: validation layers'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: Optimistic updates need a rollback path because:
choices: The server can reject the mutation — the UI must revert to truth
quiz.explain: Optimism is a UX bet; the rollback is the hedge when the bet loses.

quiz.q: Presigned URLs for uploads are preferred because:
choices: Clients upload straight to object storage — app servers never proxy the bytes
quiz.explain: Offloading byte transfer removes the app tier from the bandwidth path entirely.

quiz.q: An inverted index maps:
choices: Terms to the documents containing them — enabling fast keyword lookup
quiz.explain: Search flips the document: instead of scanning text, you look up precomputed term postings.

quiz.q: An ORM’s classic performance trap is:
choices: N+1 queries from lazy-loaded relationships in loops
quiz.explain: Accessing relations per-row in a loop fires a query each — eager loading is the fix.

modules.title: Deployment Literacy
modules.summary: Welcome to Deployment Literacy — module 5 of the Fullstack path. I'm your instructor, and this is enough operations to be dangerous in the good way: pipelines, environments, containers, and rollbacks — the literacy fullstack interviews assume. We cover CI/CD (build, test, deploy), environments and feature flags, what Docker actually gives you, observability (logs, metrics, traces), and rollback strategies. By the end, you will describe a deployment the way an owner does.
objectives: Understand and apply: CI/CD: build, test, deploy
Understand and apply: environments and feature flags
Understand and apply: containers: what Docker gives you
Understand and apply: observability: logs, metrics, traces
Understand and apply: rollback strategies

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **CI** — Every push builds, lints, tests, scans — fast feedback on main; the definition of done, enforced mechanically.
- **CD** — Artifacts promoted through environments with automated deployments (blue-green/canary/rolling) and one-command rollback — lead time and change-failure rate as the metrics.
- **Feature flags** — Decouple deploy from release: merge dark, release to 1%, kill-switch without redeploying — with flag hygiene (owner + removal date) or flag spaghetti.
- **Environments** — Dev → staging → production with promotion discipline — staging that mirrors production is the point, not the checkbox.
- **Docker** — Portable, reproducible runtime: image bundles code + dependencies + OS userland — containers share the host kernel (lighter than VMs, weaker isolation).
- **Blue-green rollback** — Instant: flip the router back to the still-running previous environment — rollback as a route change, rehearsed not hoped.
- **Observability trio** — Metrics alert, traces show where, logs tell why — 'metrics alert me, traces show me where, logs tell me why.'
- **Rollback rehearsal** — Immutable artifacts, previous version one command away, backward-compatible migrations — an untested rollback plan is a hope.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Sketch the CI/CD pipeline for your capstone: triggers, parallel jobs (lint/test/build/scan), artifact promotion, environments — with the gate that blocks a bad merge.
2. Write the feature-flag plan for one risky launch: flag name, owner, rollout percentages, kill-switch procedure, removal date — the hygiene, not just the flag.
3. Containerize a toy app: write the Dockerfile, note the layer-caching order, shrink the image — then state what Docker did and didn't give you versus a VM.
4. Design the rollback for one deploy: immutable artifact, blue-green or canary, the router flip, the migration-compatibility check — then rehearse it on paper.
5. Write the observability starter set: three alerting metrics, what each log line carries, where you'd add the first trace — the owner's minimum.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Deployment runbook. For your capstone app: the CI/CD pipeline definition, environment promotion rules, the feature-flag register (with owners and removal dates), the container strategy, and the rollback runbook — including the migration-compatibility rule and the rehearsal log. Deliverable: the runbook — deployment literacy written down.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: 'deployment literacy' is literacy, not operations expertise — real on-call involves incidents, cost, and compliance this module doesn't simulate, and this course confers no certificate. The interview tests whether you think like an owner; the pager teaches the rest.

cards.front: What does a good CI/CD pipeline do?
cards.back: CI: every push builds, lints, tests, scans — fast feedback on main. CD: artifacts promoted through environments, deployments automated (blue-green/canary/rolling), rollback one command. The interview metrics: lead time and change-failure rate.

cards.front: Why do fullstack interviews love feature flags?
cards.back: They decouple deploy from release: merge dark code, release to 1%, kill-switch bad launches without redeploying. The discipline to name: flag hygiene — every flag gets an owner and a removal date, or you inherit flag spaghetti.

cards.front: What does Docker actually give you?
cards.back: A portable, reproducible runtime: the image bundles code + dependencies + OS userland, so ‘works on my machine’ dies. Containers share the host kernel (lighter than VMs, weaker isolation) — and the interview follow-up is always about image size and layer caching.

cards.front: Logs, metrics, traces — when do you reach for each?
cards.back: Metrics: ‘is something wrong’ (alerts, dashboards). Logs: ‘what happened’ (discrete events with context). Traces: ‘where did the request go’ (latency across services). The interview line: ‘metrics alert me, traces show me where, logs tell me why.’

cards.front: What’s a real rollback strategy?
cards.back: Deploy immutable artifacts, keep the previous version one command away (or N−1 running in blue-green), database migrations backward-compatible (expand-contract), and rehearse the rollback — an untested rollback plan is a hope.

quiz.q: Blue-green deployment’s rollback is:
choices: Instant: flip the router back to the still-running green environment
quiz.explain: The old environment stays live behind the router until cutover is verified — rollback is a route change.

quiz.q: A distributed trace’s primary value is:
choices: Following one request across services to find where latency/errors originate
quiz.explain: Trace spans stitch the request path across service boundaries — the only view that crosses them.

quiz.q: Containers differ from VMs in that they:
choices: Share the host OS kernel instead of virtualizing hardware
quiz.explain: No guest kernel per container: faster startup, denser packing, but a shared kernel attack surface.

quiz.q: Feature flags decouple:
choices: Deploying code from releasing features to users
quiz.explain: Code ships dark; the flag controls who sees it — enabling progressive rollout and instant kill-switches.

modules.title: Fullstack Capstone
modules.summary: Welcome to the Fullstack Capstone — module 6 of the Fullstack path. I'm your instructor, and this is the artifact that answers 'show me you can own the whole path': one deployed app, contract-first, with auth and CI. We scope a shippable app, write the API contract first, build auth and the data model, deploy with CI, and write the README and demo script — then present the build. By the end, you will demo value and narrate judgment.
objectives: Demonstrate end to end: scoping a shippable app
Demonstrate end to end: API contract first
Demonstrate end to end: auth and data model
Demonstrate end to end: deployed with CI
Demonstrate end to end: README and demo script

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Shippable scope** — The thinnest slice demonstrating the skill: contract first, auth + data model, deployed with CI, README and demo script — shipped and demoable beats ambitious and half-built.
- **Contract-first** — Interface decisions early when they're cheap — frontend and backend evolve independently against the contract.
- **Auth in the capstone** — Real login with the threat model stated: what you chose (sessions vs tokens) and what it defends against.
- **CI on the capstone** — The pipeline as proof of process: every push tested, every deploy gated — the definition of done, visible.
- **README as interview** — 'The README is the interview before the interview': what it does, how to run it, architecture in one diagram, decisions and tradeoffs.
- **Demo script** — The 3-minute happy path with one 'and here's the interesting part' beat — rehearsed, not improvised.
- **Presenting the build** — Live demo, then architecture (one diagram), then the two hardest decisions with alternatives, then 'what I'd do with more time.'
- **Scope discipline** — 'What I'd do with more time' proves the build was scoped deliberately, not abandoned — a senior signal.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Scope the capstone in one page: the thinnest shippable slice, the explicit non-goals, the contract-first order of work — get the scope signed off (by a peer or yourself, in writing).
2. Write the API contract before any code: endpoints, schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits — the interface the build must satisfy.
3. Build vertical slices: auth + one full feature path end to end (UI → API → DB → deploy) before adding breadth — demoable at every commit.
4. Wire CI on day one: every push builds and tests, deploys gated — the pipeline grows with the app, not after it.
5. Write the README and demo script, then present: live demo, one architecture diagram, two hardest decisions, 'what I'd do with more time' — record it.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: The capstone itself. Ship it: scoped app, contract-first API, auth with a stated threat model, data model with migrations, CI/CD, deployed and demoable — plus the README (run instructions, one architecture diagram, decisions and tradeoffs) and the 3-minute demo script. Deliverable: the deployed app, the repo, the README, and the recorded demo — the artifact that answers 'show me.'

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: a capstone proves you can ship a scoped thing well — it doesn't prove production experience (no real users, no incidents, no legacy), and this course confers no certificate. Present it as what it is: evidence of craft and judgment, sized honestly.

cards.front: How do you scope a shippable capstone app?
cards.back: Thinnest slice that demonstrates the skill: API contract first, auth + data model, deployed with CI, README and demo script. The interview line: ‘shipped and demoable beats ambitious and half-built.’

cards.front: What goes in an API contract / OpenAPI sketch?
cards.back: Endpoints, methods, request/response schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits, and versioning — enough that a client team could build against it. The interview line: ‘the contract is the interface; code is the implementation.’

cards.front: What makes a capstone README and demo script work?
cards.back: README: what it does, how to run it, architecture in one diagram, decisions and tradeoffs. Demo script: the 3-minute happy path with one ‘and here’s the interesting part’ beat. The interview line: ‘the README is the interview before the interview.’

cards.front: How do you present a build in an interview?
cards.back: Live demo of the happy path, then the architecture (one diagram), then the two hardest decisions with alternatives, then ‘what I’d do with more time.’ The interview line: ‘demo the value, narrate the judgment.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Scoping a shippable app'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: Ending with ‘what I’d do with more time’ is strong because:
choices: It shows you see the work’s limits and can prioritize — a senior signal
quiz.explain: Named next steps prove the build was scoped deliberately, not abandoned.

quiz.q: An architecture diagram in the README is worth it because:
choices: Reviewers grasp the system in 30 seconds — before reading a line of code
quiz.explain: Hiring managers skim; the diagram carries the design when they won’t read prose.

quiz.q: Writing the contract before the implementation is strong because:
choices: It forces interface decisions early, when they’re cheap — and enables parallel client/server work
quiz.explain: Contract-first surfaces disagreements before code cements them.

quiz.q: API-contract-first in a capstone is strong because:
choices: It proves interface thinking and lets frontend/backend evolve independently
quiz.explain: Contracts before code: the habit interviewers want to see generalized.

modules.title: Fullstack Mock Circuit
modules.summary: Welcome to the Fullstack Mock Circuit — the final module of the Fullstack path. I'm your instructor, and these are mocks that cross the stack in one round: API design, data model, a UI sketch, auth deep dives, live coding across the stack — debriefed into the final study plan. By the end, you will timebox visibly, demo thin working slices, and convert every mock into the plan.
objectives: Apply in professional practice: timed full-path design rounds
Apply in professional practice: API and auth deep dives
Apply in professional practice: live coding across the stack
Apply in professional practice: behavioral ledger
Apply in professional practice: debrief and triage

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Full-path design round** — Design the path first (10 min), then code the thinnest vertical slice (API + one screen) — 'a thin working slice beats a thick imaginary one.'
- **Timed API-design round** — 5 requirements, 10 resources + verbs + status codes, 10 edge cases, 5 tradeoffs — the contract a client could program against.
- **Auth deep dive** — Threat model first, mechanism second: the senior-loop auth questions answered with the storage and lifecycle reasoning.
- **Live coding across the stack** — Timeboxed visibly: design, then the thinnest slice, narrating tradeoffs — breadth demonstrated through the slice, not described.
- **Behavioral ledger** — Story bank, stories-told-where, feedback, stumping questions — every behavioral touchpoint fresh.
- **Debrief and triage** — Within the hour: leaks, holds, biggest leak by frequency × weight, 48-hour redrill — the mock is the test, the debrief is the studying.
- **Taper plan** — No new material, redrill from the log, timed mocks, rest — consolidation for the real loop.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Run a timed full-path design mock (45 min): 10 min path design, then the thinnest vertical slice — narrate tradeoffs, timebox visibly.
2. Run an API + auth deep-dive mock: defend the contract and the threat model against follow-ups — mechanism over buzzwords.
3. Run a live-coding-across-the-stack mock: one feature from UI to DB in the timebox — thin slice, working, narrated.
4. Run one behavioral round from the ledger: two-minute STAR answers, no repeated stories.
5. Debrief all four within the hour each: template, ranked leaks, 48-hour redrills, ledger update — then the taper plan.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Fullstack mock portfolio. The four-mock circuit over two weeks — full-path design, API/auth deep dive, live coding across the stack, behavioral — each debriefed with the template and the ledger updated. Close with the taper schedule for your real loop. Deliverable: four debriefs, the ledger, the taper — mocks converted into the final study plan.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: crossing the stack in a mock is still a simulation — real loops add unfamiliar interviewers, real nerves, and company-specific bars, and this course confers no certificate. What the circuit buys is the timeboxing habit and the leak log — the two things that compound.

cards.front: How do you handle full-stack live rounds (design + coding)?
cards.back: Timebox visibly: design the path first (10 min), then code the thinnest vertical slice (API + one screen), narrating tradeoffs. The interview line: ‘I’d rather demo a thin working slice than describe a thick imaginary one.’

cards.front: How do you handle timed API-design rounds?
cards.back: Budget: 5 min requirements, 10 min resources + verbs + status codes, 10 min edge cases (pagination, idempotency, versioning), 5 min tradeoffs. Think in resources and contracts — the interview line: ‘I design the contract a client could program against.’

cards.front: What’s a behavioral ledger?
cards.back: Your running record: story bank entries, which stories you’ve told where, feedback received, and follow-up questions that stumped you. It stops you from repeating the same story and turns each behavioral round into training data.

cards.front: How do you debrief and triage after a mock?
cards.back: Within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), rank leaks by frequency × interview weight, and redrill the top one within 48 hours. The interview line: ‘the mock is the test; the debrief is the studying.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: Weak-spot triage should prioritize leaks by:
choices: Frequency × interview weight — what costs the most points most often
quiz.explain: Expected value: fix what loses you the most points most often.

quiz.q: A behavioral ledger prevents:
choices: Repeating the same story across rounds and losing track of feedback
quiz.explain: Loops have multiple behavioral touchpoints; the ledger keeps each one fresh and improving.

quiz.q: In an API-design round, idempotency belongs in the discussion because:
choices: Clients retry — safe retries are a contract requirement, not an optimization
quiz.explain: Distributed clients will retry; the API must make retries safe.

modules.title: Swift Language Core
modules.summary: Welcome to Swift Language Core — the opening module of the iOS Engineering Interview Prep path. I'm your instructor, and this is Swift at interview depth: optionals without force-unwraps, value/reference discipline, and protocols — the language questions iOS loops open with. We cover optionals (binding, chaining, coalescing), value versus reference semantics, protocols and protocol extensions, generics and associated types, and closures with capture lists. By the end, you will write Swift that reads like you mean it.
objectives: Understand and apply: optionals: binding, chaining, coalescing
Understand and apply: value vs reference semantics
Understand and apply: protocols and protocol extensions
Understand and apply: generics and associated types
Understand and apply: closures and capture lists

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Optionals** — The type-level answer to null: binding (if let/guard let) over force-unwrapping, chaining for deep access, nil-coalescing for defaults — '!!' as a justified-only smell.
- **Optional map/flatMap** — Transforms over optionals without pyramid nesting — the functional spelling of 'if-let then transform.'
- **Value semantics** — Structs/enums copied on assignment — no shared-state bugs; the Swift default, chosen deliberately.
- **Reference semantics** — Classes with shared identity — for view controllers, shared services, and anywhere identity or inheritance is required.
- **Protocols** — Capabilities as contracts — the unit of abstraction Swift leans on hardest.
- **Protocol extensions** — Default implementations shared across conforming types — mixins without a base class: 'composition of protocols over class inheritance.'
- **Generics and associated types** — Constrained generic code over protocol requirements — the machinery behind Swift's standard library and your own reusable components.
- **Closures and capture lists** — Captured variables with explicit ownership: capture lists ([weak self]) breaking retain cycles — the memory-management interview core.
- **Error handling** — throws and Result: typed, explicit failure — try! justified only with a proof the call cannot fail, never with hope.
- **Retain cycles** — Strong reference loops (delegate patterns, closures capturing self) — broken with weak/unowned; the leak interviewers always probe.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Rewrite five force-unwraps from a sample file using binding, chaining, and coalescing — state aloud for each why the unwrap was unjustified.
2. Model one feature twice: as a struct and as a class — write the test that shows the value/reference difference, then state the choosing rule.
3. Design a small protocol hierarchy with protocol extensions for shared behavior: two conforming types, one extension, zero base classes.
4. Write a generic function with an associated-type constraint (a simple container or pipeline) — state the constraint's job in one sentence.
5. Fix a retain cycle in a closure-heavy sample: add the capture list, explain the cycle that existed, and verify the deinit fires.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Swift core portfolio. A playground or package demonstrating: optional-heavy API handling without force-unwraps, a struct-vs-class decision with the test proving the semantics, a protocol-oriented mini-design, one generic abstraction, and a retain-cycle fix with the before/after. Each with a one-paragraph interview-style explanation. Deliverable: the package plus explanations — language depth you can walk through.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: language depth is the opening of the iOS loop, not the loop — frameworks, concurrency, and architecture decide the rest, and this course confers no certificate. Swift also evolves yearly; verify details against the current language guide before interviewing.

cards.front: How do you show Optional mastery in a Swift interview?
cards.back: Binding (if let/guard let) over force-unwrapping, optional chaining for deep access, nil-coalescing for defaults, and ‘!!’ as a code smell you justify only with a proof. Map/flatMap on Optionals for transforms without pyramids.

cards.front: Value vs reference semantics — the Swift interview core?
cards.back: Structs/enums: copied on assignment (value semantics — no shared-state bugs). Classes: shared reference (identity matters: view controllers, shared services). Choose struct by default; reach for class when identity or inheritance is required.

cards.front: Why does Swift lean on protocols so hard?
cards.back: Protocol-oriented design: capabilities as protocols, shared behavior via protocol extensions with default implementations, generics constrained by protocols. The interview line: ‘prefer composition of protocols over class inheritance.’

cards.front: What TypeScript features do interviewers actually ask about?
cards.back: Narrowing (typeof/instanceof/discriminated unions — exhaustiveness checking with never), generics with constraints, and utility types (Partial, Pick, Omit, Record). The pitch: ‘types as executable documentation that the compiler checks.’

cards.front: Explain closures like the interviewer is testing depth.
cards.back: A function that captures variables from its enclosing scope — the variables live as long as the closure does. That’s the module pattern, private state, and also the classic bug: loop variables captured by reference (fixed with let in modern JS).

quiz.q: Using try! is acceptable only when:
choices: You can prove the call cannot fail (e.g. a bundled resource that ships with the app)
quiz.explain: try! converts failure into a crash — justifiable only with a proof, never with hope.

quiz.q: A closure lets a function:
choices: Access its outer scope’s variables after that scope has returned
quiz.explain: The captured environment outlives the enclosing call — that’s what makes private state possible.

quiz.q: A discriminated union’s power in TypeScript is:
choices: Exhaustive narrowing: the compiler proves you handled every variant
quiz.explain: Switching on the discriminant literal lets TS narrow each branch — and ‘never’ in default proves exhaustiveness.

quiz.q: Protocol extensions with default implementations enable:
choices: Shared behavior across conforming types without a base class
quiz.explain: Mixins via extensions: types gain behavior by conforming, no inheritance chain required.

modules.title: UIKit and SwiftUI
modules.summary: Welcome to UIKit and SwiftUI — module 2 of the iOS path. I'm your instructor, and we take both UI worlds honestly: UIKit's imperative lifecycle and SwiftUI's declarative state — plus the judgment to discuss either in an interview. We cover view controllers and their lifecycle, Auto Layout, SwiftUI's state trio and layout algorithm, UIKit–SwiftUI interop, and which framework fits which question. By the end, 'which framework?' will be a reasoned answer, not a religion.
objectives: Understand and apply: uIKit: view controllers, lifecycle
Understand and apply: auto Layout and constraints
Understand and apply: swiftUI: state, binding, observed objects
Understand and apply: the SwiftUI layout algorithm
Understand and apply: uIKit–SwiftUI interop

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **View controller lifecycle** — loadView → viewDidLoad (one-time setup) → viewWill/DidAppear (per-appearance work) → viewWill/DidDisappear → deinit — the traps: per-appearance work in viewDidLoad, leaked observers.
- **Auto Layout** — Constraints as linear equations the solver satisfies; intrinsic content size vs explicit constraints; ambiguity and conflicts read from the logs — 'I think in constraints, not frames.'
- **@State** — View-local value state — owned by the view, the simplest state.
- **@Binding** — A two-way lens on someone else's state: the child reads and writes without owning — parent owns, child edits through the lens.
- **@ObservedObject / @StateObject** — External reference-type models — StateObject owns the lifetime, ObservedObject borrows it.
- **SwiftUI layout algorithm** — Three steps, parent-driven: the parent proposes a size, the child chooses, the parent places — one pass, no solver; GeometryReader for the rest.
- **UIViewRepresentable** — Wrapping a UIView to live inside SwiftUI — the bridge for the imperative world.
- **UIHostingController** — Embedding SwiftUI inside UIKit — interop as a migration strategy: wrap the legacy, write new code declaratively.
- **State flows down, events flow up** — The unidirectional rule of SwiftUI data flow — ownership explicit at every level.
- **Per-screen pragmatism** — Choosing per screen, not per religion — each framework has real gaps; interop exists so teams can mix.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Trace a view controller's lifecycle for a push/pop/push sequence on paper: name what runs when, and place one per-appearance task correctly (not in viewDidLoad).
2. Build one screen twice: UIKit with constraints and SwiftUI with state — then write the honest comparison (what was easier, what fought you) for each.
3. Diagnose an Auto Layout conflict from a console log: find the conflicting constraints, name the ambiguity, fix it — state the reading method aloud.
4. Explain the SwiftUI layout algorithm for one custom layout: who proposes, who chooses, who places — then implement it and verify against the prediction.
5. Bridge one UIKit component into SwiftUI (representable) and one SwiftUI view into UIKit (hosting controller) — state the ownership/lifecycle rule at each boundary.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Two-worlds showcase. One feature built twice — UIKit and SwiftUI — with a shared view model where sensible, plus one interop bridge in each direction. Document: the lifecycle-correct UIKit version, the state-correct SwiftUI version, and the per-screen framework choice argued. Deliverable: the project plus the comparison write-up — both worlds, honestly held.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: the UIKit/SwiftUI balance shifts every year — teams are mid-migration everywhere, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers want the judgment to discuss both; claiming one world is 'done' reads as out of touch.

cards.front: What must you know about UIViewController lifecycle?
cards.back: loadView → viewDidLoad (one-time setup) → viewWill/DidAppear (per-appearance work, start/stop observations) → viewWill/DidDisappear → deinit. The interview traps: doing per-appearance work in viewDidLoad, and leaking via unreleased observers.

cards.front: How do you discuss Auto Layout?
cards.back: Constraints as linear equations the solver satisfies; intrinsic content size vs explicit constraints; ambiguity and conflicts (and how you read the logs); performance (flatten deep hierarchies). The interview line: ‘I think in constraints, not frames.’

cards.front: How do you explain SwiftUI’s state trio?
cards.back: @State: view-local value state. @Binding: a reference to someone else’s state (child writes up). @ObservedObject/@StateObject: external reference-type models (StateObject owns the lifetime). The interview line: ‘state flows down, events flow up, ownership is explicit.’

cards.front: How do you explain the SwiftUI layout algorithm?
cards.back: Three steps, parent-driven: the parent proposes a size, the child chooses its size, the parent places it. One pass, no constraint solver — which is why GeometryReader and alignment guides exist for the cases the simple flow can’t express.

cards.front: How do you bridge UIKit and SwiftUI?
cards.back: UIViewRepresentable/UIViewControllerRepresentable to embed UIKit in SwiftUI; UIHostingController to embed SwiftUI in UIKit. The interview line: ‘interop is a migration strategy — wrap the legacy, write new code in SwiftUI.’

quiz.q: Choosing per screen (not per religion) is the senior answer because:
choices: Each framework has real gaps — pragmatism ships, purity stalls
quiz.explain: Interop exists precisely so teams can mix; dogma ignores the gaps.

quiz.q: UIViewRepresentable exists to:
choices: Wrap a UIView so it can live inside a SwiftUI hierarchy
quiz.explain: The representable protocol bridges the imperative UIKit world into declarative SwiftUI.

quiz.q: In SwiftUI layout, the parent:
choices: Asks the child for its size first
Proposes a size; the child decides; the parent places it
quiz.explain: The negotiate-propose-place flow runs in a single pass — fast, but less flexible than Auto Layout.

quiz.q: @Binding exists so that:
choices: A child can read and write a parent’s state without owning it
quiz.explain: Bindings are two-way lenses: the parent owns, the child edits through the lens.

modules.title: Concurrency on iOS
modules.summary: Welcome to Concurrency on iOS — module 3 of the iOS path. I'm your instructor, and this is concurrency the iOS way: from GCD to Swift's structured concurrency and actors — plus the main-thread rule interviewers always check. We cover GCD (queues, QoS, dispatch groups), OperationQueues, async/await and structured concurrency, actors and data-race safety, and main-thread discipline for UI. By the end, the compiler will be your concurrency reviewer — and you'll be able to prove it.
objectives: Understand and apply: GCD: queues, QoS, dispatch groups
Understand and apply: operation queues and dependencies
Understand and apply: async/await and structured concurrency
Understand and apply: actors and data-race safety
Understand and apply: main-thread discipline for UI

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **GCD queues** — Serial vs concurrent queues; async vs sync dispatch — the iron rule: UI on main, work off main; the deadlock demo: sync onto the current serial queue.
- **QoS classes** — User-interactive down to background — priority as a scheduling hint the system actually honors.
- **Dispatch groups** — Fan-in: enter/leave across parallel work, notify on completion — the pre-async/await coordination primitive.
- **OperationQueue** — Higher-level: dependencies between operations, cancellation, priorities, max concurrency — 'dependencies and cancellation buy the abstraction; otherwise GCD.'
- **Structured concurrency** — async/await with task hierarchies where children can't outlive parents — lifetimes provable, no detached callbacks leaking.
- **@MainActor** — Compiler-enforced main-thread execution for UI-bound code — UI-touching code can't accidentally run elsewhere.
- **Actors** — Isolated mutable state with serialized, compiler-checked access — data races caught at build time: 'actors make the compiler my concurrency reviewer.'
- **Main-thread discipline** — UIKit/SwiftUI are not thread-safe: compute off main, hop back for every UI touch — undefined behavior otherwise.
- **Cooperative cancellation** — Tasks check for cancellation at suspension points — structured concurrency makes the propagation automatic.
- **Data-race safety** — The compile-time guarantee: shared mutable state without synchronization can't compile under strict concurrency.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write the GCD deadlock demo (sync onto the current serial queue), run it, then fix it — explain the mechanism aloud in under a minute.
2. Convert a dispatch-group fan-in to structured concurrency: task group with the same coordination, then state what the structure guarantees that the group didn't.
3. Isolate shared mutable state in an actor: show the data race the compiler now rejects, and the serialized access it enforces.
4. Audit a sample for main-thread violations: mark every UI touch, route them through @MainActor, and state the rule each fix enforces.
5. Build one screen's data load with async/await end to end: fetch off main, hop to main for UI, cancellation on disappear — the disciplined shape, complete.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Concurrency portfolio. A small app feature demonstrating: GCD done right (queues, QoS, groups), the structured-concurrency rewrite, an actor guarding shared state, and @MainActor-enforced UI updates — each with a before/after showing the hazard removed. Document the interview-style explanation per piece. Deliverable: the feature plus explanations — concurrency you can prove.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: Swift concurrency is still evolving — strict checking modes and best practices shift yearly, and this course confers no certificate. State which language mode your answers assume; interviewers respect the precision.

cards.front: GCD in an interview: what do you need cold?
cards.back: Serial vs concurrent queues, QoS classes (user-interactive down to background), async vs sync dispatch, dispatch groups for fan-in, and the iron rule: UI on main, work off main. Deadlock demo: sync onto the current serial queue.

cards.front: OperationQueue vs GCD?
cards.back: OperationQueue: higher-level — dependencies between operations, cancellation, priorities, max concurrency. GCD: lighter, C-level queues. The interview line: ‘dependencies and cancellation buy the Operation abstraction; otherwise GCD.’

cards.front: How do you explain Swift’s structured concurrency?
cards.back: async/await for sequential-looking async code, tasks in hierarchies where children can’t outlive parents, actors for isolated mutable state. The interview line: ‘structure makes lifetimes provable — no more detached callbacks leaking.’

cards.front: What do actors buy you?
cards.back: Isolated mutable state with compiler-enforced exclusive access: only one task touches the actor’s state at a time, and the compiler flags data races at build time. The interview line: ‘actors make the compiler my concurrency reviewer.’

cards.front: Why is main-thread discipline non-negotiable on iOS?
cards.back: UIKit/SwiftUI are not thread-safe: UI updates off the main thread cause undefined behavior — glitches, crashes, corruption. The rule: compute off main (@MainActor for UI-bound code), hop back to main for every UI touch.

quiz.q: @MainActor on a class guarantees:
choices: Its methods run on the main thread — safe for UI work
quiz.explain: The compiler enforces the hop: UI-touching code can’t accidentally run elsewhere.

quiz.q: Swift actors prevent data races by:
choices: Enforcing exclusive, serialized access to their isolated state
quiz.explain: Isolation is checked at compile time: shared mutable state without synchronization can’t compile.

quiz.q: Structured concurrency’s core guarantee is:
choices: Child tasks can’t outlive their parent scope
quiz.explain: The task tree bounds lifetimes: cancellation and completion propagate through the structure.

quiz.q: Operation dependencies give you:
choices: Declarative ordering (‘B after A’) without manual synchronization
quiz.explain: The queue topologically sorts the graph; you declare relationships, not locks.

modules.title: Persistence on iOS
modules.summary: Welcome to Persistence on iOS — module 4 of the iOS path. I'm your instructor, and this is the persistence ladder from UserDefaults to Core Data to Keychain: what each is for, and the selection reasoning design rounds expect. We cover UserDefaults (and what doesn't belong there), Codable and file storage, the Core Data stack, SwiftData at a glance, and the Keychain for secrets. By the end, you will choose the store from the access pattern — then justify the tradeoff.
objectives: Understand and apply: userDefaults: what belongs there
Understand and apply: codable and file storage
Understand and apply: core Data: stack, contexts, faults
Understand and apply: swiftData at a glance
Understand and apply: keychain for secrets

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **UserDefaults** — A preferences plist for small user settings — not secrets, not large data, not anything needing queries or migrations.
- **Codable** — Compiler-synthesized serialization for JSON/plist — custom keys and strategies for real-world APIs; the format layer.
- **App sandbox** — Documents vs caches vs tmp: the right directory per data lifetime, with the right file protection.
- **Core Data stack** — Persistent container → contexts (main for UI, background for work) → store coordinator → SQLite — faults as lazy loading; one context per queue.
- **Faults** — Lazily-loaded placeholders — data materializes on first access; memory-efficient by design.
- **Merge policies** — The conflict answer: what happens when background and main contexts disagree — named, not hoped.
- **SwiftData** — The modern API: @Model macro-driven, #Predicate queries, @Query in SwiftUI — backed by Core Data's storage; Core Data knowledge explains what's underneath.
- **@Query** — Live-updating fetch results bound to the view — declarative data that stays in sync automatically.
- **Keychain** — Encrypted, access-controlled secret storage (kSecAttrAccessible) surviving reinstall — 'if it's a secret, it's in the Keychain.'
- **Access-pattern-first choice** — Queries, relationships, and size decide the store — not habit.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Audit a sample app's storage: move every misplaced item (a token in UserDefaults, a queryable list in a plist) to its correct store — state the rule each move enforces.
2. Build the Codable layer for one API: custom keys, one custom strategy, file persistence in the right sandbox directory with protection set.
3. Stand up the Core Data stack for one entity: background import, main-context UI, a merge policy — then trigger a conflict and watch the policy decide.
4. Rebuild the same feature in SwiftData (@Model, #Predicate, @Query) and write the honest comparison: what the modern API hides, what Core Data knowledge still explains.
5. Store one secret correctly: Keychain with an explicit accessibility attribute — then state what UserDefaults would have exposed.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Persistence-ladder showcase. One app using every rung correctly: UserDefaults for preferences, Codable files for documents, SwiftData/Core Data for queryable data with a background import, Keychain for the token — each choice documented with the access-pattern argument. Deliverable: the app plus the choice log — the ladder, climbed deliberately.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: persistence advice is Apple-ecosystem-shaped — the APIs and best practices move with the platform, and this course confers no certificate. State the iOS version your answers assume; storage choices also answer to sync, backup, and privacy requirements interviews skip.

cards.front: What belongs in UserDefaults — and what doesn’t?
cards.back: Small user preferences (toggles, last-selected tab). NOT secrets (that’s Keychain), NOT large data, NOT anything needing queries or migrations. The interview line: ‘UserDefaults is a preferences plist, not a database.’

cards.front: How do you discuss Codable and file storage?
cards.back: Codable: compiler-synthesized serialization for JSON/plist — custom keys and strategies for real-world APIs. File storage: app sandbox directories (documents vs caches vs tmp) with the right protection. The interview line: ‘Codable for the format, the sandbox for the place.’

cards.front: Core Data stack in 60 seconds?
cards.back: Persistent container → managed object contexts (main for UI, background for work) → persistent store coordinator → SQLite. Faults are lazy loading; the interview traps are threading (one context per queue) and merge policies on conflicts.

cards.front: SwiftData at a glance — how do you position it?
cards.back: Apple’s modern persistence: @Model macro-driven, Swift-native queries with #Predicate, SwiftUI-integrated via @Query — backed by Core Data’s storage. The interview line: ‘SwiftData is the modern API; Core Data knowledge still explains what’s underneath.’

cards.front: Where do secrets go on iOS?
cards.back: Keychain — encrypted, access-controlled (kSecAttrAccessible), surviving app reinstall on the device. The interview line: ‘if it’s a secret, it’s in the Keychain; UserDefaults is a plist anyone can read.’

quiz.q: The choosing rule’s core is:
choices: Access pattern first — queries, relationships, and size decide the store
quiz.explain: Storage choice follows how data is read, written, and related — not habit.

quiz.q: Keychain items vs UserDefaults for a refresh token:
choices: Keychain: encrypted storage with access control; UserDefaults is plaintext-adjacent
quiz.explain: Refresh tokens are long-lived credentials — they get the strongest storage available.

quiz.q: SwiftData’s @Query in SwiftUI provides:
choices: Live-updating fetch results bound to the view — the UI refreshes as data changes
quiz.explain: Declarative data: the view describes what it needs and stays in sync automatically.

quiz.q: Core Data faults are:
choices: Lazily-loaded placeholders — data materializes on first access
quiz.explain: Faulting defers loading until the property is touched — memory-efficient by design.

modules.title: App Architecture Patterns
modules.summary: Welcome to App Architecture Patterns — module 5 of the iOS path. I'm your instructor, and this is architecture as an interview topic: MVVM versus coordinators versus unidirectional flows, dependency injection, and testability — argued with tradeoffs, not slogans. We cover MVC/MVVM and where they break, coordinators and navigation, DI on iOS, unidirectional data flow, and testing layers. By the end, every architecture you name will be a bet with stated odds.
objectives: Understand and apply: MVC, MVVM, and where they break
Understand and apply: coordinators and navigation
Understand and apply: dependency injection on iOS
Understand and apply: unidirectional data flow
Understand and apply: testing: unit, UI, snapshot

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Massive View Controller** — UIKit MVC's decay mode: the view controller absorbs networking, logic, and navigation — the problem MVVM and coordinators solve.
- **MVVM** — State and logic extracted into testable view models; the view as a binding layer — testability as the payoff.
- **Coordinators** — Navigation owned outside view controllers — screens stop knowing about each other; flows become testable objects.
- **Dependency injection** — Classes declare needs, something else supplies them — constructor injection, testable with fakes, no manual singletons.
- **Unidirectional data flow** — State down, events up: one source of truth, one traceable path — 'one direction, one truth, no mysteries.'
- **Test pyramid (mobile)** — Unit: view models and logic with fakes — fast, many. UI (XCUITest): critical journeys — slow, few. Snapshot: visual regressions on components.
- **Seams** — The interfaces between layers — where testability and changeability live; 'I design the seams first — the code follows the seams.'
- **Conditional choices** — 'I chose X because [conditions]; I'd switch to Y if [change]' — the sentence that proves judgment over dogma.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Refactor one Massive View Controller into MVVM + coordinator: extract the view model, move navigation to the coordinator — state what each move bought.
2. Add DI to the refactored feature: constructor injection with fakes in tests — show the test that was impossible before.
3. Trace one user action through unidirectional flow: event up, state down — then break it deliberately (two-way binding) and observe the debugging cost.
4. Write the three test layers for one feature: unit tests on the view model, one UI test on the critical journey, one snapshot — state what each layer proves.
5. Argue one architecture choice aloud in two minutes: forces, options with costs, choice, and the condition that would change it — the bet with stated odds.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Architecture brief. For a two-screen feature: the pattern choice (MVVM + coordinators + repository, or your argued alternative) with the forces analysis, the DI map, the unidirectional flow diagram, and the test plan across the three layers. Include the conditional: what would change your choice. Deliverable: the brief — architecture argued, not asserted.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: architecture taste is team- and app-shaped — the 'right' pattern depends on size, longevity, and who's maintaining it, and this course confers no certificate. Interviewers reward the tradeoff argument; the codebase you inherit will have opinions of its own.

cards.front: MVC vs MVVM on iOS — the honest comparison?
cards.back: MVC in UIKit decays into Massive View Controller; MVVM extracts state and logic into testable view models with the view as a binding layer. Coordinators own navigation so view controllers stop knowing about each other.

cards.front: Why Hilt (DI) in Android interviews?
cards.back: Constructor injection with generated components: testable (swap fakes), lifecycle-aware scoping, no manual singletons. The interview line: ‘DI inverts control — the class declares needs, Hilt supplies them.’

cards.front: What is unidirectional data flow?
cards.back: State flows down, events flow up: a single source of truth, views render from it, user actions dispatch events that produce new state. Debugging becomes ‘what event produced this state?’ The interview line: ‘one direction, one truth, no mysteries.’

cards.front: How do you layer mobile tests?
cards.back: Unit: view models/logic with fakes — fast, many. UI (XCUITest/Espresso): critical journeys — slow, few. Snapshot: visual regressions on components. The interview line: ‘I test logic in units and reserve devices for what only devices prove.’

cards.front: How do you discuss architecture tradeoffs in an interview?
cards.back: Name the forces (testability, team size, app complexity, longevity), the options with their costs, and your choice with the condition that would change it. The interview line: ‘every architecture is a bet — I state the odds.’

quiz.q: Stating what would change your architecture choice is strong because:
choices: It proves the choice was reasoned from conditions, not dogma
quiz.explain: Conditional choices show engineering judgment; unconditional ones show fashion.

quiz.q: Snapshot tests catch:
choices: Unintended visual changes — pixel-level regressions in components
quiz.explain: Rendered-output comparison: the safety net for UI refactors.

quiz.q: Unidirectional flow’s debugging win is:
choices: State changes have a single traceable path — events in, state out
quiz.explain: Two-way bindings create update cycles; one direction makes every change explainable.

quiz.q: Dependency injection’s testability win is:
choices: Dependencies can be replaced with fakes in tests
quiz.explain: Injected interfaces seam the code: tests substitute fakes without touching production wiring.

modules.title: Guided iOS App Build
modules.summary: Welcome to the Guided iOS App Build — module 6 of the iOS path. I'm your instructor, and this is a complete small app — networking, persistence, tests — built to be walked through in an interview as proof of platform fluency. We build a list-detail app with cache: the spec, a networking layer with async/await, SwiftUI views with view models, persistence with SwiftData, and unit tests for the view models. By the end, you will have the build narrative, not just the build.
objectives: Build and demonstrate: app spec: a list-detail app with cache
Build and demonstrate: networking layer with async/await
Build and demonstrate: swiftUI views with view models
Build and demonstrate: persistence with SwiftData
Build and demonstrate: unit tests for the view models

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **List-detail spec** — The canonical interview app: list, detail, cache — every layer exercised, nothing extraneous.
- **Networking layer** — Typed endpoints, async suspension, centralized error mapping, auth via interceptors, lifecycle-tied cancellation — 'the UI never sees HTTP.'
- **Repository** — Network + local cache behind one data API — 'the only class that knows where data lives.'
- **View models** — State holders the UI observes — testable without the UI; the seam the unit tests target.
- **SwiftData persistence** — @Model, #Predicate, @Query — the cache layer with live-updating UI binding.
- **Build narrative** — Problem → constraints → key decisions (with rejected alternatives) → result → 'what I'd do with more time' — the delivery vehicle for the proof.
- **Senior answer structure** — Definition, mechanism, fit-and-tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up; structure separating senior answers from recitation.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write the spec in one page: screens, data, cache policy, the explicit non-goals — sign it off before coding.
2. Build the networking layer first: typed endpoints, error mapping, cancellation — test it in isolation before any UI exists.
3. Add the repository: network + SwiftData cache, single source of truth — write the test proving the cache policy.
4. Build the SwiftUI views on view models: state down, events up — keep every decision in the view model, testable.
5. Write the unit tests for the view models, then rehearse the build narrative aloud: decisions first, the probe-fodder you chose to lead with.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: The guided build, complete. The list-detail app with cache: networking layer, repository, SwiftUI + view models, SwiftData persistence, view-model unit tests — plus the one-page spec and the build narrative (decisions, rejected alternatives, 'what I'd do with more time'). Deliverable: the app, the tests, the narrative — platform fluency you can walk through.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: a guided build proves you can execute a known shape well — real apps add product ambiguity, legacy, and scale this build doesn't simulate, and this course confers no certificate. Present it as craft evidence, sized honestly.

cards.front: How do you attack a ‘list-detail with cache’ app spec?
cards.back: Layers: networking (async, cancellable) → repository (network + local cache, single source of truth) → view models (state) → UI. The interview line: ‘the repository is the only class that knows where data lives.’

cards.front: What does a good networking layer look like?
cards.back: Typed endpoints (Retrofit/URLSession), coroutine/async suspension, centralized error mapping, auth injection via interceptors, and cancellable requests tied to lifecycle. The interview line: ‘the UI never sees HTTP — it sees domain results.’

cards.front: SwiftData at a glance — how do you position it?
cards.back: Apple’s modern persistence: @Model macro-driven, Swift-native queries with #Predicate, SwiftUI-integrated via @Query — backed by Core Data’s storage. The interview line: ‘SwiftData is the modern API; Core Data knowledge still explains what’s underneath.’

cards.front: How do you turn a guided build into an interview narrative?
cards.back: Problem → constraints → key decisions (with rejected alternatives) → result → what you’d do with more time. The build is proof; the narrative is the delivery vehicle — interviewers probe decisions, so lead with them.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'App spec: a list-detail app with cache'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: A build narrative should lead with:
choices: The problem, constraints, and key decisions with alternatives
quiz.explain: Decisions are what get probed; leading with them controls the conversation.

quiz.q: SwiftData’s @Query in SwiftUI provides:
choices: Live-updating fetch results bound to the view — the UI refreshes as data changes
quiz.explain: Declarative data: the view describes what it needs and stays in sync automatically.

quiz.q: Centralizing auth in an interceptor beats per-call headers because:
choices: Token refresh and injection happen once — every call inherits it correctly
quiz.explain: Cross-cutting concerns in one place: no call site can forget the token.

quiz.q: The repository’s job in the list-detail spec is:
choices: Mediating network and cache — one data API for the view models
quiz.explain: View models stay source-agnostic; caching policy lives in one seam.

modules.title: iOS Mock Circuit
modules.summary: Welcome to the iOS Mock Circuit — the final module of the iOS path. I'm your instructor, and these are iOS-flavored mocks across language, UI, and architecture rounds: timed Swift deep-dives, UIKit/SwiftUI whiteboard rounds, app-architecture design — plus the behavioral ledger — debriefed into targeted reps before the real loop. By the end, your leaks will be found while fixes are cheap.
objectives: Apply in professional practice: timed Swift deep-dives
Apply in professional practice: uIKit/SwiftUI whiteboard rounds
Apply in professional practice: iOS system design (app architecture)
Apply in professional practice: behavioral ledger
Apply in professional practice: debrief and triage

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Timed Swift deep-dives** — Layered answers: 30-second correct, mechanism, edge case — 'the classic bug here is…' before they ask.
- **Framework whiteboard rounds** — Narrate the architecture as you draw: components, lifecycles, data flow — then zoom into the probed area.
- **App-architecture design** — Requirements → layers → patterns → concurrency and persistence choices → testing story — 'I design the seams first.'
- **Behavioral ledger** — Story bank, stories-told-where, feedback, stumping questions — every round fresh.
- **Debrief and triage** — Within the hour: leaks, holds, biggest leak by frequency × weight, 48-hour redrill.
- **Taper plan** — No new material, redrill from the log, timed mocks, rest.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Run a timed Swift deep-dive mock (30 min): layered answers on optionals, value/reference, concurrency — log the ramble points.
2. Run a UIKit/SwiftUI whiteboard mock: draw-then-zoom on lifecycles and state flow — review for silent stretches.
3. Run an app-architecture design mock (45 min): seams-first design with the testing story — end with tradeoffs.
4. Run one behavioral round from the ledger: two-minute STAR answers, no repeats.
5. Debrief all four within the hour: template, ranked leaks, 48-hour redrills, ledger update — then the taper.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: iOS mock portfolio. The four-mock circuit over two weeks — Swift deep dive, framework whiteboard, app-architecture design, behavioral — each debriefed with the template and the ledger updated. Close with the taper schedule. Deliverable: four debriefs, the ledger, the taper — the real loop as repetition.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: mocks simulate format, not stakes — and this course confers no certificate. iOS loops also vary by team (UIKit-heavy vs SwiftUI-forward); the circuit trains the format, and your research on the specific team covers the rest.

cards.front: How do you handle timed language deep-dives?
cards.back: Answer in layers: the 30-second correct answer, then the mechanism, then the edge case — and say ‘the classic bug here is…’ before they ask. The interview line: ‘I answer the question, then the question behind the question.’

cards.front: How do you handle framework whiteboard rounds?
cards.back: Narrate the architecture as you draw: components, lifecycles, data flow — then zoom into the probed area. The interview line: ‘I draw the system first so we both know where the deep dive lives.’

cards.front: How do you do app-architecture design in an iOS interview?
cards.back: Requirements → layers (UI, domain, data) → patterns (MVVM + coordinators + repository) → concurrency and persistence choices → testing story. The interview line: ‘I design the seams first — the code follows the seams.’

cards.front: What’s a behavioral ledger?
cards.back: Your running record: story bank entries, which stories you’ve told where, feedback received, and follow-up questions that stumped you. It stops you from repeating the same story and turns each behavioral round into training data.

cards.front: How do you debrief and triage after a mock?
cards.back: Within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), rank leaks by frequency × interview weight, and redrill the top one within 48 hours. The interview line: ‘the mock is the test; the debrief is the studying.’

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: Weak-spot triage should prioritize leaks by:
choices: Frequency × interview weight — what costs the most points most often
quiz.explain: Expected value: fix what loses you the most points most often.

quiz.q: A behavioral ledger prevents:
choices: Repeating the same story across rounds and losing track of feedback
quiz.explain: Loops have multiple behavioral touchpoints; the ledger keeps each one fresh and improving.

quiz.q: Leading with the seams (interfaces between layers) is strong because:
choices: Seams are where testability and changeability live — implementations follow
quiz.explain: Architecture is the shape of the boundaries; code fills them in.

modules.title: Kotlin Language Core
modules.summary: Welcome to Kotlin Language Core — the opening module of the Android Engineering Interview Prep path. I'm your instructor, and this is Kotlin at interview depth: null safety without the double-bang, sealed hierarchies, and the coroutine mental model — the language half of every Android loop. We cover null safety (?., ?:, and the justified-only !!), data/sealed classes and objects, the coroutines mental model, extension and scope functions, delegation (by lazy, observable), and Java interop costs. By the end, you will write Kotlin that defends itself at the boundaries.
objectives: Understand and apply: null safety: ?, ?., ?:, !!
Understand and apply: data classes, sealed classes, objects
Understand and apply: coroutines: the mental model
Understand and apply: extension functions and scope functions
Understand and apply: delegation: by lazy, observable

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Null safety** — Nullable types (?), safe calls (?.), Elvis (?:) for defaults — with !! as a justified-only escape hatch and platform types from Java interop still able to hand you null.
- **Data classes** — Value holders with generated equals/hashCode/copy — UI state, DTOs; the boring-correct choice for data.
- **Sealed classes/interfaces** — Closed hierarchies for states and results (Loading/Success/Error) with exhaustive when — UI state modeled safely.
- **Coroutines mental model** — 'Sequential code, asynchronous execution': suspend functions pause without blocking threads; structured concurrency ties child lifetimes to scopes; dispatchers choose the pool (Main/IO/Default).
- **Extension functions** — Behavior added without inheritance — nullable receivers included; the API-shaping tool.
- **Scope functions** — let (transform nullable), apply (configure), run/with (compute on receiver), also (side effects) — picked by what they return and what 'it' is.
- **by lazy** — Thread-safe lazy init — expensive immutable values created once on first access; preferred over lateinit var when the value is a val.
- **Delegation (by)** — Class delegation as composition without boilerplate — the ceremony remover for common patterns.
- **Platform types** — Java interop's nullability blind spot: annotate and defend at the boundaries — the compiler can't see what Java didn't declare.
- **Suspend vs blocking** — Suspension frees the thread for other coroutines; blocking pins it — the distinction the whole concurrency model rests on.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Rewrite five !! usages with safe calls, Elvis, and let-scoping — justify the one you keep (if any) with the proof it can't fail.
2. Model one screen's UI state as a sealed hierarchy (Loading/Success/Error): write the exhaustive when, then add a state and watch the compiler demand handling.
3. Convert a callback-based repository call to suspend functions: sequential-looking code, dispatcher made explicit — state what changed about threading.
4. Pick the scope function for five snippets (transform, configure, compute, side-effect, nullable chain) — state the return-and-receiver rule each time.
5. Draw the Java-interop boundary for one module: mark every platform type, add the nullability annotations, and write the defensive check at the seam.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Kotlin core portfolio. A small module demonstrating: null-safe API handling with the boundary defenses marked, a sealed UI-state hierarchy with exhaustive handling, a suspend-based data call, scope functions chosen by the rule, and one by-lazy expensive init with the lateinit comparison. Each with the interview-style explanation. Deliverable: the module plus explanations — language depth, defended.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: Kotlin evolves — coroutines and language features gain new idioms yearly, and this course confers no certificate. State the version your answers assume; interviewers respect current knowledge over memorized snapshots.

cards.front: How do you demonstrate Kotlin null-safety depth?
cards.back: Nullable types (?), safe calls (?.), Elvis (?:) for defaults, !! as a justified-only escape hatch, and let/run scoping for non-null blocks. The platform-types warning: Java interop can still hand you null — annotate and defend at boundaries.

cards.front: Data classes vs sealed classes — when each?
cards.back: Data class: value holders with generated equals/hashCode/copy — UI state, DTOs. Sealed class/interface: closed hierarchies for states and results (Loading/Success/Error) with exhaustive when. Together they model UI state safely.

cards.front: What’s the coroutines mental model you’d state?
cards.back: Lightweight sequential-looking async: suspend functions pause without blocking threads, structured concurrency ties child lifetimes to scopes, dispatchers choose the thread pool (Main/IO/Default). ‘Sequential code, asynchronous execution.’

cards.front: Extension functions and scope functions — the interview version?
cards.back: Extensions add behavior without inheritance (nullable receivers included). Scope functions: let (transform nullable), apply (configure), run/with (compute on receiver), also (side effects). The interview line: ‘I pick the scope function by what it returns and what ‘it’ is.’

cards.front: What does Kotlin delegation give you?
cards.back: by lazy: thread-safe lazy init — expensive objects created once on first use. observable/vetoable: react to property changes. Class delegation (by): composition without boilerplate. The interview line: ‘delegation removes the ceremony around common patterns.’

quiz.q: UIViewRepresentable exists to:
choices: Wrap a UIView so it can live inside a SwiftUI hierarchy
quiz.explain: The representable protocol bridges the imperative UIKit world into declarative SwiftUI.

quiz.q: by lazy is preferred over lateinit var when:
choices: The value is immutable and expensive — initialized once, safely, on first access
quiz.explain: lazy gives val semantics with deferred cost; lateinit is a var promise the compiler can’t verify.

quiz.q: let is the right scope function when you want to:
choices: Transform a (possibly null) value and return the result
quiz.explain: let’s lambda returns its last expression — the transform-and-return shape.

quiz.q: A suspend function differs from a blocking call in that it:
choices: Suspends without blocking the underlying thread
quiz.explain: Suspension frees the thread for other coroutines; blocking would pin it.

modules.title: The Android Framework
modules.summary: Welcome to The Android Framework — module 2 of the Android path. I'm your instructor, and this is the framework without folklore: lifecycles, the back stack, and background work — the platform facts Android interviews assume cold. We cover activities, fragments, and lifecycles; intents and the task back stack; views, ViewGroups, and measurement; services, broadcast receivers, and WorkManager; and the permissions model. By the end, the lifecycle will be a contract you code against.
objectives: Understand and apply: activities, fragments, and lifecycles
Understand and apply: intents and the task back stack
Understand and apply: views, ViewGroups, and measurement
Understand and apply: services, broadcast receivers, WorkManager
Understand and apply: permissions model

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Lifecycle as contract** — Init in onCreate, symmetric cleanup in onDestroy — code against the callbacks, not around them; ViewModels survive what activities don't.
- **Configuration changes** — Destroy-and-recreate on rotation — the reason state lives in ViewModels, not activities.
- **Intents** — The messaging primitive: explicit (targeted at a component) vs implicit (resolved by the system via intent filters) — deep links are intents from outside.
- **Task back stack** — The ordered activities behind the back button — shaped by launch modes and intent flags; the navigation model interviews assume.
- **Measure/layout passes** — Measure negotiates size (MeasureSpec: EXACTLY/AT_MOST/UNSPECIFIED), layout assigns position — custom views implement onMeasure/onLayout.
- **Foreground service** — User-visible long work (playback) — the only long-running background shape the user consents to.
- **WorkManager** — Deferrable guaranteed work (sync, uploads): battery-aware, survives restarts, respects Doze — the modern default for background work.
- **Broadcast receivers** — System-event hooks — for reacting to the outside world, not for doing the work itself.
- **Permissions model** — Install-time vs runtime, groups, one-time and while-in-use grants — 'permissions are a trust negotiation, not a manifest entry.'
- **In-context permission requests** — Ask when the feature needs it, with a rationale, handle denial gracefully — the UX rule that decides grant rates.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Trace an activity through rotation, back-press, and process death on paper: name every callback and what state survives each — then verify with logging.
2. Route three navigations (in-app, deep link, share intent): explicit vs implicit, the intent flags shaping the back stack — state the resolution rule each time.
3. Implement a custom view's onMeasure/onLayout for a simple layout: predict the MeasureSpec modes, verify with logging, fix the AT_MOST wrap_content case.
4. Schedule one deferrable job three ways (raw service, receiver, WorkManager): write the honest comparison — then keep the WorkManager version and state why.
5. Implement one runtime-permission flow in context with rationale and graceful denial — the trust-negotiation shape, complete.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Framework fluency portfolio. A sample app exercising: lifecycle-correct state (survives rotation), deep-link routing, a custom view with correct measurement, WorkManager-scheduled sync, and an in-context permission flow — each with the one-paragraph 'platform fact' it demonstrates. Deliverable: the app plus the fact log — the framework, without folklore.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: the framework is a moving target — APIs deprecate, recommendations shift (Compose, anyone), and this course confers no certificate. Learn the current guidance alongside these fundamentals; interviewers test both the facts and your awareness that they change.

cards.front: Activities, fragments, lifecycles — what must you know cold?
cards.back: The lifecycle callbacks and what belongs in each (init in onCreate, cleanup symmetric in onDestroy), configuration changes destroying and recreating, and why ViewModels survive them. The interview line: ‘the lifecycle is a contract — I code against the callbacks, not around them.’

cards.front: How do you explain intents and the back stack?
cards.back: Intents: the messaging primitive — explicit (targeted) vs implicit (resolved by the system). The task back stack orders activities for back navigation; launch modes and intent flags shape it. Deep links are intents from the outside world.

cards.front: What must you know about Android view measurement?
cards.back: Measure pass (parent proposes, child measures via MeasureSpec: EXACTLY/AT_MOST/UNSPECIFIED) → layout pass (parent positions). Custom views implement onMeasure/onLayout. The interview line: ‘measure negotiates size; layout assigns position.’

cards.front: Services, broadcast receivers, WorkManager — when each?
cards.back: Foreground service: user-visible long work (playback). WorkManager: deferrable guaranteed work (sync, uploads) — the modern default. Broadcast receivers: system events. The interview line: ‘background work goes through WorkManager unless the user is actively engaged.’

cards.front: How do you discuss Android’s permissions model?
cards.back: Install-time vs runtime permissions, permission groups, one-time and while-in-use grants, and the UX rule: ask in context with a rationale, handle denial gracefully. The interview line: ‘permissions are a trust negotiation, not a manifest entry.’

quiz.q: Requesting a runtime permission should happen:
choices: In context, when the feature needs it, with a clear rationale
quiz.explain: In-context requests with rationale get granted; upfront bulk requests get denied.

quiz.q: WorkManager is preferred over a background service for deferrable work because:
choices: It’s battery-aware, survives app restarts, and respects Doze — guaranteed execution
quiz.explain: The OS cooperates with WorkManager scheduling; raw background services get killed.

quiz.q: MeasureSpec.AT_MOST means:
choices: The child can be up to this size — wrap_content’s mode
quiz.explain: AT_MOST bounds the child; EXACTLY fixes it; UNSPECIFIED leaves it free.

quiz.q: An explicit intent differs from an implicit intent in that it:
choices: Names its target component directly; implicit intents are resolved by the system
quiz.explain: Explicit = ‘open this screen’; implicit = ‘who can handle this action?’ — resolved via intent filters.

modules.title: Coroutines and Concurrency
modules.summary: Welcome to Coroutines and Concurrency — module 3 of the Android path. I'm your instructor, and this is concurrency the modern Android way: structured coroutines, Flows, and lifecycle-aware scopes — plus RxJava literacy for the legacy code you will inherit. We cover suspend functions and dispatchers, structured concurrency and scopes, cold/hot Flows with StateFlow and SharedFlow, viewModelScope, and cancellation with exception handling. By the end, lifecycle bugs will be impossible by construction — and you'll be able to prove it.
objectives: Understand and apply: suspend functions and dispatchers
Understand and apply: structured concurrency and scopes
Understand and apply: flows: cold, hot, StateFlow and SharedFlow
Understand and apply: viewModelScope and lifecycle awareness
Understand and apply: cancellation and exception handling

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Suspend functions** — Sequential-looking async that pauses without blocking threads — the unit of coroutine work.
- **Dispatchers** — Main (UI), IO (blocking I/O), Default (CPU work) — the pool choice made explicit per call.
- **Structured concurrency** — Child lifetimes tied to scopes: cancellation and completion propagate through the structure — no detached work leaking.
