- **coroutineScope vs supervisorScope** — coroutineScope: a child's failure cancels siblings. supervisorScope: failures isolated — 'failure policy is a design choice, stated up front.'
- **Cold flows** — Start work per collector — the stream that doesn't exist until observed.
- **StateFlow** — Hot, holds the latest value, replays to new collectors — UI state; rotation-safe by construction.
- **SharedFlow** — Hot, configurable replay/buffer — one-shot events (with the caveat that events are often better modeled as state).
- **viewModelScope** — A CoroutineScope tied to the ViewModel lifecycle — cancelled automatically on clearance; no leaked coroutines on rotation.
- **Cooperative cancellation** — Checkpoints at suspension points — cancellation propagates through structured scopes automatically.
- **RxJava literacy** — Disposables as the Jobs/scopes equivalent — the legacy vocabulary for the codebases you'll inherit.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Convert a callback chain to suspend functions with explicit dispatchers: state the thread each part runs on before and after.
2. Build a task hierarchy with coroutineScope, fail one child, observe the sibling cancellation — then switch to supervisorScope and observe the isolation.
3. Model one screen's state in StateFlow and its one-shot events in SharedFlow: rotate the device and verify the state replay; state the events-as-state caveat.
4. Launch work in viewModelScope, rotate, and verify cancellation — then write the sentence: 'structured concurrency makes this leak impossible by construction.'
5. Translate one RxJava chain (map/filter/dispose) to coroutines/Flow: name the Disposable→Job mapping at each step — the literacy drill for legacy code.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Concurrency portfolio. A feature demonstrating: suspend-based data loading with explicit dispatchers, a StateFlow UI state with SharedFlow events, viewModelScope lifecycle safety (with the rotation test), and one RxJava-to-coroutines translation with the mapping documented. Deliverable: the feature plus explanations — modern concurrency, proven.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: coroutines are the current idiom, not the eternal one — RxJava still runs production code you'll inherit, and this course confers no certificate. Literacy in both is the honest position; fluency in the modern one is the interview position.

cards.front: What’s the coroutines mental model you’d state?
cards.back: Lightweight sequential-looking async: suspend functions pause without blocking threads, structured concurrency ties child lifetimes to scopes, dispatchers choose the thread pool (Main/IO/Default). ‘Sequential code, asynchronous execution.’

cards.front: How do you explain Swift’s structured concurrency?
cards.back: async/await for sequential-looking async code, tasks in hierarchies where children can’t outlive parents, actors for isolated mutable state. The interview line: ‘structure makes lifetimes provable — no more detached callbacks leaking.’

cards.front: StateFlow vs SharedFlow?
cards.back: StateFlow: hot, holds the latest value, replays to new collectors — UI state. SharedFlow: hot, configurable replay/buffer — one-shot events (with the caveat that events are better modeled as state where possible). Both respect structured concurrency.

cards.front: Why viewModelScope?
cards.back: It’s a CoroutineScope tied to the ViewModel’s lifecycle — cancelled automatically on ViewModel clearance. No leaked coroutines on rotation, no manual cleanup. The interview point: structured concurrency makes lifecycle bugs impossible by construction.

cards.front: How do cancellation and exceptions interact in coroutines?
cards.back: Cancellation is cooperative (checkpoints at suspension points); a child’s failure cancels the scope by default — supervisorScope isolates sibling failures. CoroutineExceptionHandler catches uncaught exceptions in root coroutines. The interview line: ‘failure policy is a design choice, stated up front.’

quiz.q: RxJava Disposables correspond to coroutine:
choices: Jobs/scopes — the thing you cancel to stop the work
quiz.explain: Both represent cancellable async work; disposing is Rx’s structured-concurrency equivalent.

quiz.q: supervisorScope differs from coroutineScope in that:
choices: A child’s failure doesn’t cancel its siblings
quiz.explain: Supervision isolates failures: one failing child doesn’t take down independent siblings.

quiz.q: viewModelScope’s cancellation guarantee means:
choices: Launched coroutines are cancelled when the ViewModel is cleared — no leaks on rotation
quiz.explain: Scope cancellation propagates to children: rotation can’t strand work anymore.

quiz.q: StateFlow suits UI state because:
choices: It always holds the latest value and replays it to new collectors
quiz.explain: New collectors (e.g. after rotation) immediately get current state — no missed updates.

modules.title: Persistence on Android
modules.summary: Welcome to Persistence on Android — module 4 of the Android path. I'm your instructor, and this is the Android persistence ladder: DataStore, Room, scoped storage, and encrypted prefs — selected with reasons, not habit. We cover SharedPreferences versus DataStore, Room (entities, DAOs, migrations), SQLite under Room, files and scoped storage, and encrypted storage for secrets. By the end, 'why this store?' will be your reflex.
objectives: Understand and apply: sharedPreferences vs DataStore
Understand and apply: room: entities, DAOs, migrations
Understand and apply: sQLite under Room
Understand and apply: files and scoped storage
Understand and apply: encrypted storage for secrets

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **SharedPreferences** — Synchronous-ish XML, no type safety, main-thread reads risk ANRs — legacy you migrate, not code you write.
- **DataStore** — Preferences/Proto: coroutine/Flow-based, async, transactional, typed schemas — the modern preferences store.
- **Room** — SQLite with compile-time safety: @Entity tables, @Dao interfaces with build-time query checking, migrations — 'Room doesn't replace SQLite, it civilizes it.'
- **DAO** — The data-access seam: queries declared as interface methods, validated at compile time — bad queries fail the build.
- **Migrations** — Schema changes as versioned steps — never destructive in production; the upgrade path is part of the design.
- **SQLite under Room** — The same relational engine underneath — migrations, complex queries, and debugging all bottom out at SQL.
- **Scoped storage** — App-specific directories need no permissions; shared media via MediaStore — no more broad external-storage access.
- **Encrypted storage** — EncryptedSharedPreferences/DataStore backed by the Android Keystore — secrets never in plaintext.
- **Android Keystore** — Hardware-backed key storage — keys that never leave secure hardware can't be extracted from a stolen file.
- **Access-pattern-first choice** — Preferences → DataStore; relational → Room; documents → files; secrets → Keystore; blobs → files with DB metadata.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Migrate a SharedPreferences usage to DataStore: convert the reads to Flows, handle the async, and state what the migration bought.
2. Build a Room database for two entities with a relation: write the DAO, trigger a compile-time query error deliberately, fix it — the safety, demonstrated.
3. Write a migration for adding a column: version bump, the migration object, the test — then state the 'never destructive in prod' rule it enforces.
4. Store three data kinds correctly (a setting, a relational dataset, a secret): DataStore, Room, encrypted prefs — state the access-pattern rule per choice.
5. Write one raw SQL query Room can't express cleanly, run it through the DAO, and explain when you drop below the abstraction.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Persistence-ladder showcase. One app using every rung correctly: DataStore for settings, Room for relational data with a tested migration, scoped storage for files, Keystore-backed encrypted storage for the token — each choice documented with the access-pattern argument. Deliverable: the app plus the choice log — the ladder, climbed deliberately.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: persistence guidance is platform-shaped and version-sensitive — DataStore vs SharedPreferences is a migration story, not a debate, and this course confers no certificate. State the API levels your answers assume.

cards.front: SharedPreferences vs DataStore?
cards.back: SharedPreferences: synchronous-ish XML, no type safety, main-thread reads risk ANRs. DataStore (Preferences/Proto): coroutine/Flow-based, async, transactional, typed schemas. New code uses DataStore; SharedPreferences is legacy you migrate.

cards.front: Room in an interview answer?
cards.back: SQLite with compile-time safety: @Entity tables, @Dao interfaces (queries checked at build time), migrations for schema changes (never destructive in prod), all behind a Repository. The trap: database work off the main thread.

cards.front: What’s SQLite’s role under Room?
cards.back: Room is a compile-time-safe layer over SQLite: the same relational engine, with Room generating the boilerplate and validating queries at build time. The interview line: ‘Room doesn’t replace SQLite — it civilizes it.’

cards.front: How do you handle files and secrets on Android?
cards.back: Scoped storage: app-specific directories need no permissions; shared media via MediaStore; no more broad external-storage access. Secrets: EncryptedSharedPreferences/DataStore backed by the Android Keystore — never plaintext.

cards.front: How do you choose the persistence store in a design question?
cards.back: By access pattern: preferences → UserDefaults/DataStore; structured relational → Room/Core Data; documents/JSON → files; secrets → Keychain/Keystore; large blobs → files with DB metadata. The interview line: ‘I choose from the access pattern, then justify the tradeoff.’

quiz.q: The choosing rule’s core is:
choices: Access pattern first — queries, relationships, and size decide the store
quiz.explain: Storage choice follows how data is read, written, and related — not habit.

quiz.q: The Android Keystore’s job is:
choices: Hardware-backed key storage so encryption keys never sit in app memory or files
quiz.explain: Keys that never leave secure hardware can’t be extracted from a stolen database file.

quiz.q: Knowing raw SQLite still matters with Room because:
choices: Migrations, complex queries, and debugging all bottom out at SQL
quiz.explain: The abstraction leaks at the interesting parts; SQL fluency is the foundation.

quiz.q: Room validates your SQL:
choices: At compile time — bad queries fail the build
quiz.explain: Annotation processing checks queries during compilation — a whole class of runtime crashes disappears.

modules.title: App Architecture
modules.summary: Welcome to App Architecture — module 5 of the Android path. I'm your instructor, and this is architecture the Google-recommended way: layers, DI, and offline-first — discussed as tradeoffs so the design round sounds senior. We cover MVVM with ViewModel and Flow, the repository pattern, Hilt DI, single-activity with Navigation, offline-first design, and testing layers. By the end, you will design the seams first — because the code follows the seams.
objectives: Understand and apply: MVVM with ViewModel and Flow
Understand and apply: repository pattern
Understand and apply: dependency injection: Hilt
Understand and apply: single-activity with Navigation
Understand and apply: offline-first design

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **MVVM on Android** — UI observes ViewModel StateFlow; ViewModel calls the repository; unidirectional data flow — events up, state down.
- **Repository pattern** — 'The only class that knows where data lives': mediating network and Room, the seam the tests target.
- **Hilt** — Constructor injection with generated components: testable (swap fakes), lifecycle-aware scoping — 'the class declares needs, Hilt supplies them.'
- **Single-activity + Navigation** — One Activity, many destinations: shared ViewModel scoping, consistent back-stack, deep-link routing in one graph — 'the Activity is the stage; destinations are the scenes.'
- **Navigation graph** — Declarative destinations, arguments, and back-stack behavior in one place — navigation as data.
- **Offline-first** — Local database as source of truth; UI reads local, writes queue for sync; conflict-resolution policy stated — 'what happens when the sync conflicts?'
- **Sync strategy** — WorkManager for deferred sync; the repository mediating network ↔ cache; UI states for stale/offline.
- **Testing layers** — Unit (JUnit + fakes, fast) → Espresso (critical journeys, slow, few) → screenshot (visual regressions) — 'logic in units, devices for what only devices prove.'
- **Seams-first design** — Architecture as the shape of the boundaries — implementations follow; seams are where testability lives.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Structure one feature as UI → ViewModel (StateFlow) → Repository → (network + Room): draw the seams, then implement — state what each layer owns.
2. Add Hilt: constructor-inject the repository, scope it, swap a fake in tests — show the test that DI made possible.
3. Convert the feature to offline-first: Room as source of truth, WorkManager sync, conflict policy written down — then test airplane-mode behavior.
4. Define the Navigation graph for three destinations with arguments and deep links: verify the back stack behaves — state the graph's job in one sentence.
5. Write the testing pyramid for the feature: view-model units with fakes, one Espresso journey, the screenshot case — state what each layer proves.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Architecture brief + build. The offline-first feature, complete: layered MVVM with Hilt, repository mediating network and Room, Navigation graph, sync with conflict policy, and the three-layer test plan — plus the one-page architecture brief (pattern choice, forces, the conditional that would change it). Deliverable: the feature and the brief — seams designed first.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: 'Google-recommended' is a snapshot — recommendations evolve (and teams deviate), and this course confers no certificate. State the guidance version you follow; interviewers reward awareness of the drift, not recitation of a snapshot.

cards.front: How do you structure MVVM on Android?
cards.back: UI (Compose/Views) observes ViewModel state (StateFlow); ViewModel calls a Repository; Repository mediates data sources (network, Room). Unidirectional data flow: events up, state down. The interview line: ‘the Repository is the only class that knows where data lives.’

cards.front: MVC vs MVVM on iOS — the honest comparison?
cards.back: MVC in UIKit decays into Massive View Controller; MVVM extracts state and logic into testable view models with the view as a binding layer. Coordinators own navigation so view controllers stop knowing about each other.

cards.front: Why single-activity with Navigation?
cards.back: One Activity hosting many destinations (fragments/compose screens): shared ViewModel scoping, consistent back-stack handling, transitions, and deep-link routing in one graph. The interview line: ‘the Activity is the stage; destinations are the scenes.’

cards.front: What does offline-first design require?
cards.back: Local database as source of truth (Room), repository mediating network ↔ cache, sync strategy (WorkManager for deferred sync), conflict-resolution policy, and UI states for stale/offline. The interview probe: ‘what happens when the sync conflicts?’

cards.front: How do you discuss Android testing layers?
cards.back: Unit (JUnit + fakes for ViewModels/Repository logic — fast), Espresso (UI flows on device — slow, use sparingly), screenshot tests (visual regressions). The interview line: ‘I test logic in units and reserve instrumentation for what only the device can prove.’

quiz.q: Espresso tests belong at the top of the pyramid because they are:
choices: Slow and device-bound — few, targeted, for critical user journeys
quiz.explain: Instrumentation cost means each Espresso test must earn its place; logic lives in fast units.

quiz.q: In offline-first, the local database is:
choices: The source of truth the UI reads; the network syncs to it
quiz.explain: UI never waits on network: reads hit local data, writes queue for sync.

quiz.q: The Navigation component’s graph gives you:
choices: Declarative destinations, arguments, and back-stack behavior in one place
quiz.explain: Navigation-as-data: the graph documents and enforces the app’s flow.

quiz.q: MVVM’s testability win comes from:
choices: View models holding logic independent of UIKit — unit-testable without a UI
quiz.explain: Logic decoupled from UIViewController can be tested as plain objects.

modules.title: Guided Android App Build
modules.summary: Welcome to the Guided Android App Build — module 6 of the Android path. I'm your instructor, and this is a complete offline-first app — network, Room, Compose — built to be walked through as the centerpiece of the Android loop. We build a list-detail app with offline cache: the spec, networking with Retrofit and coroutines, a Room-backed repository, Compose UI with ViewModels, and unit tests for the repository. notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **List-detail with offline cache** — The canonical Android interview app: every layer exercised — network, cache, UI — with offline as the design constraint.

cards.front: How do you attack a ‘list-detail with cache’ app spec?
cards.back: Layers: networking (async, cancellable) → repository (network + local cache, single source of truth) → view models (state) → UI. The interview line: ‘the repository is the only class that knows where data lives.’

cards.front: How do you structure Compose UI with ViewModels + repository tests?

cards.front: How do you turn a guided build into an interview narrative?

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'App spec: list-detail with offline cache'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?

quiz.q: A build narrative should lead with:
choices: The problem, constraints, and key decisions with alternatives
quiz.explain: Decisions are what get probed; leading with them controls the conversation.

quiz.q: Repository tests use fakes (not mocks) for data sources because:
choices: Fakes provide working in-memory behavior — testing state transitions, not call counts

quiz.q: Centralizing auth in an interceptor beats per-call headers because:
choices: Token refresh and injection happen once — every call inherits it correctly
quiz.explain: Cross-cutting concerns in one place: no call site can forget the token.

quiz.q: The repository’s job in the list-detail spec is:
choices: Mediating network and cache — one data API for the view models
quiz.explain: View models stay source-agnostic; caching policy lives in one seam.

modules.title: C and Memory Models
modules.summary: Welcome to C and Memory Models — the opening module of the Embedded Software Engineering Interview Prep path. I'm your instructor, and this is C at the metal: memory layout, volatile, and the undefined behaviors embedded interviews use as shibboleths. We cover pointers, arrays, and decay; stack vs heap vs static; volatile and why it matters; alignment, padding, and packing; the undefined-behavior greatest hits; and reading C under time. By the end, you will be able to state your worst-case RAM usage at compile time — and mean it.
objectives: Understand and apply: pointers, arrays, and decay
Understand and apply: stack vs heap vs static
Understand and apply: volatile and why it matters
Understand and apply: alignment, padding, packing
Understand and apply: undefined behavior greatest hits

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Array-pointer decay** — Arrays decay to pointers to their first element in most expressions — sizeof stops working across function boundaries; 'inside the function it's a pointer; always pass the length.'
- **Stack** — Automatic, fast, tiny — overflow is the classic crash; the first suspect in a HardFault.
- **Heap (embedded)** — Often banned: fragmentation and nondeterminism have no place in RTOS firmware's hot path.
- **Static allocation** — Fixed at link time, deterministic — the embedded default; 'my RAM usage is a number in the map file, not a hope.'
- **volatile** — The value can change outside program flow (hardware registers, ISR-shared flags): no register caching, no elided reads — required for MMIO and ISR flags, NOT a substitute for atomics or barriers.
- **Alignment and padding** — CPUs want multi-byte types at aligned addresses — the compiler inserts padding; structs have the size the alignment dictates, not the sum of members.
- **Packed structs** — __attribute__((packed)) removes padding for wire/disk formats — at the cost of slower or faulting unaligned access; 'I pack for the protocol, not by default.'
- **Undefined behavior** — The compiler's license to assume: signed overflow, null dereference, use-after-free, data races — 'works in debug' proves nothing; sanitizers prove the negative.
- **Strict aliasing** — The optimizer's assumption about pointer types — violated casually, punished mysteriously; the UB interviewers probe when they're serious.
- **Reading C fast** — Datasheets, HALs, and legacy drivers are C — you'll read ten times more than you write; reading speed is the bottleneck.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Predict the sizeof and member offsets of three structs by hand (with padding), then verify with a program — state the alignment rule each time.
2. Write the decay demo: pass an array to a function, observe sizeof's answer inside, fix it by passing the length explicitly.
3. Write a polling loop over a fake status register with and without volatile: compile optimized, observe the elided reads — the volatile lesson, earned.
4. Pack a struct for a wire format, then measure the unaligned-access cost on your target (or read the architecture manual's warning) — state when packing is justified.
5. Compile a signed-overflow example at -O2 with and without -fwrapv: observe the optimizer's assumption — then write the UB-free version.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Memory-model portfolio. A single C file (host-compiled) demonstrating: the padding/offset predictions with verification, the decay fix, the volatile polling loop, a packed wire-format struct with the justification comment, and one UB example with its safe rewrite — each with the interview-style explanation. Deliverable: the file plus explanations — C at the metal, demonstrated.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: host-compiled C exercises teach the language model, not the target — real MCUs add errata, toolchains, and debuggers, and this course confers no certificate. State what's host-proven vs target-proven; interviewers respect the distinction.

cards.front: What’s array-pointer decay, and why do interviewers probe it?
cards.back: Arrays decay to pointers to their first element in most expressions — sizeof stops working across function boundaries. The interview line: ‘inside the function it’s a pointer; always pass the length explicitly.’

cards.front: Stack vs heap vs static in embedded?
cards.back: Stack: automatic, fast, tiny — overflow is the classic crash. Heap: often banned (fragmentation, nondeterminism) in RTOS firmware. Static: fixed at link time, deterministic — the embedded default. The interview line: ‘I can tell you my worst-case RAM usage at compile time.’

cards.front: What does ‘volatile’ actually do, and when is it required?
cards.back: It tells the compiler the value can change outside program flow (hardware registers, ISR-shared flags) — so no caching in registers, no reordering/eliding reads. Required for memory-mapped registers and ISR-shared flags; it is NOT a substitute for atomics or barriers.

cards.front: Why do structs have padding, and when do you pack them?
cards.back: Alignment: CPUs require (or prefer) multi-byte types at aligned addresses — the compiler inserts padding. Packing (__attribute__((packed))) removes it for wire/disk formats, at the cost of slower or faulting unaligned access. The interview line: ‘I pack for the protocol, not by default.’

cards.front: How do you discuss undefined behavior in a C interview?
cards.back: As the compiler’s license to assume: signed overflow, null dereference, use-after-free, data races — ‘anything can happen’ includes ‘works until the optimizer upgrades.’ The interview line: ‘I write so UB can’t happen; sanitizers prove it.’

quiz.q: Fluency in reading C matters for embedded interviews because:
choices: Datasheets, HALs, and legacy drivers are C — you inherit them before you rewrite them
quiz.explain: You’ll read ten times more C than you write; reading speed is the bottleneck.

quiz.q: Signed integer overflow in C is:
choices: Undefined behavior — the optimizer may assume it never happens
quiz.explain: Compilers exploit the UB assumption for optimization; ‘works in debug’ proves nothing.

quiz.q: A packed struct is required when:
choices: The memory layout must match an exact wire/disk format with no padding
quiz.explain: Protocols define byte-exact layouts; compiler padding would corrupt the format.

quiz.q: A status register polled in a loop must be volatile because:
choices: The compiler would otherwise optimize the repeated read away, never seeing hardware changes
quiz.explain: Without volatile, the compiler may read once and reuse the cached value forever.

modules.title: RTOS Concepts
modules.summary: Welcome to RTOS Concepts — module 2 of the Embedded path. I'm your instructor, and this is real-time thinking: scheduling, determinism, and why there is no malloc in the hot path — the conceptual core of embedded loops. We cover tasks, priorities, and scheduling; preemption and context switches; tickless idle and power; static allocation; and a tour of FreeRTOS primitives with Zephyr at a glance. By the end, you will budget context switches like any other cost.
objectives: Understand and apply: tasks, priorities, scheduling
Understand and apply: preemption and context switches
Understand and apply: tickless idle and power
Understand and apply: memory: static allocation, no heap
Understand and apply: freeRTOS primitives tour

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Priority-based preemptive scheduling** — The highest-priority ready task runs; preemption on events/ticks; deterministic context switches — an RTOS optimizes for deadline guarantees, not throughput.
- **Preemption cost** — Register save/restore, stack switch, cache/TLB disturbance — microseconds that compound at high tick rates; 'context switches are the RTOS's tax.'
- **Tickless idle** — Program the next wakeup (timer or interrupt) and sleep deeply until then — no periodic wakeups burning power; 'every avoided wakeup is battery life.'
- **Static allocation** — Fixed-size pools and arrays sized at compile time; object pools for variable lifetimes — bounded worst-case behavior, fragmentation-free.
- **FreeRTOS primitives** — Tasks, queues, semaphores, mutexes — the vocabulary most embedded interviews assume; the small footprint with the huge ecosystem.
- **Zephyr** — The modern RTOS: device-tree-driven, broader protocol/security stack — 'FreeRTOS for the tiny MCU, Zephyr when the product needs the stack.'
- **Device tree** — Hardware description as data files, not #ifdefs — the same firmware builds for many boards; board differences become data.
- **Determinism** — Bounded worst-case timing — the property that separates real-time from fast; measured in guarantees, not averages.
- **No malloc in the hot path** — Dynamic allocation's nondeterminism (fragmentation, unbounded time) disqualifies it where deadlines live.
- **GPOS vs RTOS** — Time-slicing fairness (throughput) vs priority preemption (deadlines) — the fundamental scheduling fork.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Design a three-task system on paper: priorities, periods, shared resources — then walk a preemption scenario and name the context-switch points.
2. Budget the tick: at 1 kHz with a 2 µs switch cost, compute the tax — then redesign tickless and state the power saving qualitatively.
3. Replace a malloc-based design with object pools: size the pools at compile time, show the worst-case RAM in the (hypothetical) map file.
4. Write the FreeRTOS-primitive choice for five IPC needs (signal, mutual exclusion, resource counting, data handoff, ISR-to-task): name the primitive and the rule per choice.
5. Compare FreeRTOS vs Zephyr for two products (a sensor node, a connected gateway): the footprint/stack tradeoff — verdict with the flip condition.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: RTOS design brief. For a sensor node: task set with priorities and periods, the scheduling analysis (what preempts what, the switch budget), the IPC map (primitive per need), the static-allocation plan with worst-case RAM, and the tickless-idle power story. Deliverable: the brief — real-time thinking, written down.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: paper RTOS design is not firmware — real targets add interrupt latencies, errata, and measurement, and this course confers no certificate. The interview tests the conceptual core; the lab proves the rest. State which is which.

cards.front: How do you explain RTOS scheduling?
cards.back: Priority-based preemptive: the highest-priority ready task runs, preemption on events/ticks, deterministic context switches. Contrast with GPOS time-slicing fairness — an RTOS optimizes for deadline guarantees, not throughput.

cards.front: What’s the cost of preemption and context switches?
cards.back: Saving/restoring registers, stack switch, cache/TLB disturbance — microseconds that add up at high tick rates. The interview line: ‘context switches are the RTOS’s tax; I budget them like any other cost.’

cards.front: What’s tickless idle, and why does power care?
cards.back: Instead of waking on every OS tick, the RTOS programs the next wakeup (timer or interrupt) and sleeps deeply until then — no periodic wakeups burning power. The interview line: ‘every avoided wakeup is battery life.’

cards.front: How do you do ‘static allocation, no heap’ in practice?
cards.back: Fixed-size pools and arrays sized at compile time, object pools for variable lifetimes, and link-time verification of worst-case RAM. The interview line: ‘my RAM usage is a number in the map file, not a hope.’

cards.front: FreeRTOS vs Zephyr — how do you position them?
cards.back: FreeRTOS: the ubiquitous small RTOS — tasks, queues, semaphores, minimal footprint, huge ecosystem. Zephyr: modern, device-tree-driven, broader protocol/security stack, Linux-foundation backed. The interview line: ‘FreeRTOS for the tiny MCU, Zephyr when the product needs the stack.’

quiz.q: Zephyr’s device-tree-driven configuration means:
choices: Hardware description lives in data files, not #ifdefs — portable across boards
quiz.explain: Board differences become data, not code branches — the same firmware builds for many targets.

quiz.q: Object pools replace malloc in RTOS firmware because:
choices: Fixed-size, deterministic, fragmentation-free — bounded worst-case behavior
quiz.explain: Pools give dynamic lifetimes with static guarantees: the embedded compromise.

quiz.q: Tickless idle saves power by:
choices: Eliminating periodic tick wakeups — sleeping until the next real event
quiz.explain: Deep sleep between events beats waking a thousand times a second to do nothing.

quiz.q: High tick rates hurt because:
choices: Each tick can force context-switch overhead — the tax compounds with frequency
quiz.explain: Tickless designs exist precisely to avoid paying this tax when there’s no work.

modules.title: Drivers and Peripherals
modules.summary: Welcome to Drivers and Peripherals — module 3 of the Embedded path. I'm your instructor, and this is hardware literacy: the peripheral set every embedded interview assumes, DMA, and the datasheet-reading skill that proves you can learn any chip. We cover GPIO, timers, and counters; UART, SPI, I2C (the big three buses); DMA; interrupts versus polling; and clock trees with baud rates. By the end, you will verify clocks before blaming the peripheral.
objectives: Understand and apply: GPIO, timers, counters
Understand and apply: UART, SPI, I2C: the big three buses
Understand and apply: DMA: moving data without the CPU
Understand and apply: interrupts vs polling
Understand and apply: clock trees and baud rates

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **GPIO** — Digital in/out; modes (push-pull/open-drain); edge-triggered interrupts — the simplest peripheral and the bring-up starting point.
- **Timers** — Counters with prescalers: PWM output, input capture for measurement, periodic interrupts — 'the most underused peripheral.'
- **UART** — Async point-to-point, no clock line (baud agreement) — simplest debug channel; the bring-up lifeline.
- **SPI** — Fast, full-duplex, 4 wires, one master — displays, flash; speed at the cost of pins.
- **I2C** — 2-wire multi-drop with addressing — sensors, EEPROM; wire-count frugality at the cost of speed.
- **DMA** — Peripheral → memory transfers in hardware while the CPU sleeps or computes — configure source/dest/increment, handle transfer-complete, watch cache coherency.
- **Interrupts vs polling** — Interrupts: event-driven, power-efficient, concurrency complexity. Polling: simple, deterministic, wasteful — 'poll when timing is tight and simple; interrupt when events are sparse and power matters.'
- **Clock trees** — Source (HSE/HSI/PLL) → dividers/multipliers → bus clocks → peripheral clocks — baud rates, timer periods, and power all derive from here.
- **Baud-rate math** — Divisors computed from the peripheral clock — wrong clock tree, wrong divisor, garbage on the UART.
- **Datasheet reading** — Register map and functional description first — registers define what's configurable; everything else is context.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. For one timer, compute the prescaler/period for a 1 kHz PWM from the bus clock: show the clock-tree path and the arithmetic — the baud-rate-math muscle, trained.
2. Choose the bus for three peripherals (a display, a temperature sensor, a debug console): UART/SPI/I2C with the speed/wires/device-count argument per choice.
3. Design a DMA transfer for sensor acquisition: source, destination, increment settings, the transfer-complete ISR, and the cache-coherency check — on paper, completely.
4. Decide interrupts vs polling for three events (a 10 kHz sample clock, a rare button press, a UART RX stream): the timing/power/simplicity argument per event.
5. Read one unfamiliar peripheral's datasheet section (register map + functional description) and write the five-line bring-up sequence — the learn-any-chip drill.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Peripheral bring-up portfolio. For one bus peripheral (your choice): the datasheet reading notes, the clock-tree derivation, the init sequence as commented pseudocode or real code, the DMA or interrupt design, and the choosing-rule write-up (why this bus, why this trigger mode). Deliverable: the portfolio — hardware literacy, demonstrated.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: paper bring-up is not bring-up — real chips have errata, silicon bugs, and scope-measured reality, and this course confers no certificate. The interview tests whether you can read the map; the bench tests whether you can walk the territory.

cards.front: GPIO and timers — the interview basics?
cards.back: GPIO: digital in/out, modes (push-pull/open-drain), interrupts on edges. Timers: counters with prescalers — PWM output, input capture for measurement, periodic interrupts. The interview line: ‘timers are the most underused peripheral; PWM and capture solve half of embedded.’

cards.front: UART vs SPI vs I2C — the choosing rule?
cards.back: UART: async point-to-point, no clock line (baud agreement), simplest debug. SPI: fast, full-duplex, 4 wires, one master — displays, flash. I2C: 2-wire multi-drop with addressing — sensors, EEPROM. Choose by speed, wire count, and device count.

cards.front: What does DMA buy you?
cards.back: Moving data without the CPU: peripheral → memory transfers run in hardware while the CPU sleeps or computes. The interview details: configure source/dest/increment, handle the transfer-complete interrupt, and watch cache coherency on MCUs with data cache.

cards.front: Interrupts vs polling — how do you choose?
cards.back: Interrupts: event-driven, power-efficient, fast response — but add concurrency complexity. Polling: simple, deterministic timing, wastes cycles/power. The interview line: ‘poll when timing is tight and simple; interrupt when events are sparse and power matters.’

cards.front: Why do interviewers ask about clock trees?
cards.back: Because baud rates, timer periods, and power all derive from the clock configuration: source (HSE/HSI/PLL) → dividers/multipliers → bus clocks → peripheral clocks. Wrong clock tree = wrong baud rate = garbage on the UART. The interview line: ‘I verify clocks before I blame the peripheral.’

quiz.q: When bringing up a new peripheral, you read first:
choices: The register map and functional description for that peripheral
quiz.explain: Registers define what you can configure; everything else is context around them.

quiz.q: A UART baud-rate mismatch is usually caused by:
choices: Wrong peripheral clock in the clock tree — the divisor math used the wrong input frequency
quiz.explain: Baud divisors derive from the peripheral clock; misconfigured clocks scale every timing value.

quiz.q: Polling wastes power because:
choices: The CPU spins checking a flag instead of sleeping until the event
quiz.explain: A polling loop burns active cycles; an interrupt lets the core sleep between events.

quiz.q: DMA’s primary benefit is:
choices: Data moves without CPU involvement — the core is free for other work
quiz.explain: The DMA controller is a separate engine; the CPU only sets up and gets interrupted on completion.

modules.title: Concurrency and Interrupts
modules.summary: Welcome to Concurrency and Interrupts — module 4 of the Embedded path. I'm your instructor, and this is concurrency where the stakes are hardware: ISRs, priority inversion, and the synchronization patterns that keep real-time systems correct. We cover ISR discipline, critical sections, mutexes versus semaphores in an RTOS, priority inversion with inheritance, register-level races, and lock-free ring buffers. By the end, your critical sections will be measured in instructions.
objectives: Understand and apply: iSRs: short, no blocking
Understand and apply: critical sections and disabling interrupts
Understand and apply: mutexes vs semaphores in an RTOS
Understand and apply: priority inversion and inheritance
Understand and apply: race conditions at the register level

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **ISR discipline** — Short, no blocking, no heap, minimal work — set a flag or push to a queue; the task does the heavy lifting.
- **Critical sections** — Interrupt masking around shared access — 'measured in instructions, not functions'; the tool for ISR-task sharing.
- **Mutex (RTOS)** — Ownership + priority inheritance — for mutual exclusion; the RTOS knows who holds it.
- **Semaphore (RTOS)** — Counting, no ownership — for signaling and resource pools; 'never use a semaphore where I need ownership semantics.'
- **Priority inversion** — Low-priority holder + medium-priority preempter = high-priority task waits unboundedly — the classic Mars Pathfinder story.
- **Priority inheritance** — Holder temporarily inherits the blocked high-priority task's level — the inversion fix, built into RTOS mutexes.
- **Register-level races** — Read-modify-write with an ISR between the read and the write — fixed by atomic set/clear registers, critical sections, or lock-free handoff.
- **Lock-free ring buffer** — Single-producer/single-consumer: head owned by consumer, tail by producer — disjoint writes need no mutual exclusion.
- **Interrupt priorities vs RTOS** — Know which priorities the kernel masks — the configuration interviewers probe when they're serious.
- **Deferred interrupt work** — The pattern: ISR signals, task processes — keeping ISRs short and the real work schedulable.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write the ISR rules as a checklist, then audit a sample ISR against it: find the blocking call, the heap use, the overlong work — fix all three.
2. Demonstrate priority inversion on paper: three tasks, one mutex, the unbounded wait — then apply priority inheritance and show the bound restored.
3. Design the sharing for one ISR-task handoff twice: critical-section version and ring-buffer version — state when each wins.
4. Choose mutex vs semaphore for five scenarios: defend each with the ownership rule — 'ownership semantics' as the deciding test.
5. Write the deferred-work pattern for one peripheral: ISR pushes to queue, task drains — with the queue-depth and overflow policy stated.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Concurrency-correctness brief. For one subsystem (e.g., sensor acquisition): the ISR design with the discipline checklist, the sharing map (what's shared, the protection per item), the inversion analysis with the inheritance answer, and the deferred-work flow. Deliverable: the brief — real-time correctness, argued.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: paper concurrency analysis is necessary but not sufficient — real systems need measurement (worst-case execution times, actual latencies), and this course confers no certificate. The interview tests the patterns; the lab proves the bounds.

cards.front: What are the ISR rules you’d state in an interview?
cards.back: Short, no blocking, no heap, minimal work — set a flag or push to a queue and let a task do the heavy lifting. Protect shared data (critical sections), and know your interrupt priorities vs the RTOS kernel’s.

cards.front: How do you protect a critical section on a microcontroller?
cards.back: Briefly disable interrupts (or raise to a priority mask) around the shared access — shortest possible region. For task-task sharing, RTOS mutexes; for ISR-task sharing, interrupt masking is the tool. The interview line: ‘critical sections are measured in instructions, not functions.’

cards.front: Mutex vs semaphore in an RTOS?
cards.back: Mutex: ownership + priority inheritance — for mutual exclusion. Semaphore: counting, no ownership — for signaling and resource pools. The interview line: ‘I never use a semaphore where I need ownership semantics.’

cards.front: Explain priority inversion and its fix.
cards.back: A low-priority task holds a mutex a high-priority task needs; a medium-priority task preempts the low one — the high task waits unboundedly. Fix: priority inheritance (holder temporarily inherits the waiter’s priority), the classic Mars Pathfinder story.

cards.front: What does a race condition look like at the register level?
cards.back: Read-modify-write on a shared peripheral register: ISR fires between the read and the write, clobbering the ISR’s change. Fixes: atomic set/clear registers (hardware), critical sections, or the lock-free ring buffer for data handoff.

quiz.q: A single-producer/single-consumer ring buffer avoids locks because:
choices: Producer and consumer each own one index — no shared mutable state to race on
quiz.explain: Head owned by consumer, tail by producer: disjoint writes need no mutual exclusion.

quiz.q: Read-modify-write races happen because:
choices: The operation isn’t atomic — an interrupt between read and write loses the interrupt’s update
quiz.explain: Two writers interleaved across a non-atomic sequence: the last write wins and one update vanishes.

quiz.q: Priority inheritance fixes inversion by:
choices: Temporarily boosting the lock holder to the blocked high-priority task’s level
quiz.explain: The holder can’t be preempted by medium-priority tasks anymore, so it releases the lock promptly.

quiz.q: A mutex’s ownership (vs a binary semaphore) enables:
choices: Priority inheritance and unlock-by-owner checks — the RTOS knows who holds it
quiz.explain: Ownership is what lets the kernel boost the holder’s priority and catch misuse.

modules.title: Debugging Hardware and Software
modules.summary: Welcome to Debugging Hardware and Software — module 5 of the Embedded path. I'm your instructor, and this is debugging as a demonstrable skill: from HardFault registers to logic-analyzer traces — plus the war story every embedded behavioral round wants. We cover JTAG/SWD, logic analyzers versus oscilloscopes, printf via semihosting and UART, HardFault diagnosis on Cortex-M, Valgrind for host-side code, and the debugging war story. By the end, you will read a fault like a lab report.
objectives: Understand and apply: JTAG/SWD: halt, step, watch
Understand and apply: logic analyzers and oscilloscopes
Understand and apply: printf over semihosting and UART
Understand and apply: hardFault diagnosis on Cortex-M
Understand and apply: valgrind for host-side code

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **JTAG/SWD** — Halt, step, breakpoints, watchpoints, memory/register inspection — 'printf tells you what happened; the debugger shows you the state when it happened.' SWD is the 2-wire modern standard.
- **Logic analyzer** — Digital protocol decoding: UART/SPI/I2C transactions, timing across channels — 'decodes the conversation.'
- **Oscilloscope** — Analog reality: signal integrity, noise, voltage levels — 'checks the physics.'
- **Semihosting** — Debugger-shuttled I/O for early bring-up before UART works — halts the target per call; 'for bring-up, not for the field.'
- **UART printf** — The field logging channel — cheap, always available, the production debug port.
- **HardFault diagnosis** — Stacked PC/LR plus CFSR/HFSR: the faulting location and cause class (bus fault, usage fault, precise vs imprecise) — diagnosis starts in registers, not guesswork.
- **Valgrind/memcheck** — Host-side memory debugging: leaks, invalid reads/writes, use-after-free — 'I prove memory correctness on the host where the tools are rich.'
- **War story structure** — Stakes fast, hypotheses tested (not a heroic montage), wrong turns included, lesson + what changed — method and honesty score.
- **Watchpoints** — Break on data access, not just code location — the tool for 'who corrupted this variable.'
- **Reproduce under the debugger** — The discipline: fault → reproduce → watchpoint → root cause — no guessing, no 'it works now.'

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Walk a HardFault diagnosis on paper: given stacked registers and CFSR bits, identify the cause class and the faulting instruction — the lab-report reading drill.
2. Compare the debug channels for one bug: what JTAG shows that printf can't, what the analyzer decodes that the scope can't — pick the right tool per symptom.
3. Write the semihosting-vs-UART decision for two phases (bring-up, field): the cost that disqualifies semihosting at real-time rates.
4. Run Valgrind memcheck on a sample C program with a planted leak and overrun: read the report, fix both, re-run clean — the host-side proof habit.
5. Draft your war story: stakes, hypotheses tested, the wrong turns (included), the lesson, what changed afterward — two minutes spoken, honest throughout.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Debug portfolio. Three artifacts: a written HardFault diagnosis walkthrough (registers → cause → fix), a tool-choice matrix (symptom → tool → why) for the debug channels, and your two-minute war story recorded — plus the Valgrind-clean report for a sample program. Deliverable: the portfolio — debugging as a demonstrable skill.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: war stories are judged on honesty — embellishment is detectable and disqualifying, and this course confers no certificate. The wrong turns are part of the story; a debugging history with no dead ends isn't credible.

cards.front: What do JTAG/SWD give you that printf doesn’t?
cards.back: Halt, step, breakpoints, watchpoints, memory/register inspection — full control of the core. SWD is the 2-wire modern standard. The interview line: ‘printf tells you what happened; the debugger shows you the state when it happened.’

cards.front: Logic analyzer vs oscilloscope — when each?
cards.back: Logic analyzer: digital protocol decoding (UART/SPI/I2C transactions, timing relationships across channels). Oscilloscope: analog reality (signal integrity, noise, actual voltage levels). The interview line: ‘the analyzer decodes the conversation; the scope checks the physics.’

cards.front: What’s semihosting, and when do you use it?
cards.back: The debugger shuttles I/O (printf, file access) to the host — invaluable for early bring-up before UART works. The costs: it halts the target per call and vanishes without the debugger. The interview line: ‘semihosting for bring-up, UART printf for the field.’

cards.front: How do you diagnose a HardFault on Cortex-M?
cards.back: Read the stacked registers (the faulting PC/LR tell you where), check CFSR/HFSR for the cause class (bus fault, usage fault, precise vs imprecise), then reproduce under the debugger with a watchpoint. The war-story version of this answer is behavioral gold.

cards.front: What’s Valgrind for in an embedded interview?
cards.back: Host-side memory debugging: memcheck finds leaks, invalid reads/writes, and use-after-free in the code you test on Linux before it ships to the target. The interview line: ‘I prove memory correctness on the host where the tools are rich.’

quiz.q: A war story’s wrong turns should be:
choices: Included — they show honest debugging method and make the lesson credible
quiz.explain: Real debugging includes dead ends; hiding them makes the story — and you — less believable.

quiz.q: Valgrind’s memcheck catches:
choices: Invalid memory accesses and leaks — at the cost of much slower execution
quiz.explain: Instrumented execution tracks every allocation: overruns and leaks become precise reports.

quiz.q: The first thing you read in a Cortex-M HardFault is:
choices: The stacked PC/LR and fault status registers (CFSR/HFSR) to locate cause and site
quiz.explain: Hardware records the fault class and the stacked context — the diagnosis starts there, not in guesswork.

quiz.q: Semihosting printf’s main cost is:
choices: Each call halts the target for debugger round-trips — unusable at real-time rates
quiz.explain: It’s a debug-channel convenience, not a runtime logging strategy.

modules.title: Embedded Capstone
modules.summary: Welcome to the Embedded Capstone — module 6 of the Embedded path. I'm your instructor, and this is a real firmware build: RTOS tasks, a driver, a power budget — documented and demoed; the artifact that ends 'do you do embedded?' debates. We spec a sensor node with an RTOS, write the driver layer for one bus peripheral, design tasks and IPC, budget power with sleep modes, and build a host-side test harness. By the end, you will demo working hardware with honest numbers.
objectives: Demonstrate end to end: spec: a sensor node with an RTOS
Demonstrate end to end: driver layer for one bus peripheral
Demonstrate end to end: task design and IPC
Demonstrate end to end: power budget and sleep modes
Demonstrate end to end: host-side test harness

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Sensor-node spec** — Sampling rates and power budget first — the spec drives the architecture, not the reverse.
- **Driver layer** — One bus peripheral, properly abstracted: init, transfer, error handling — the hardware seam.
- **Task design and IPC** — Task per concern (sample, process, transmit) with queue handoff — decoupled timing domains, each meeting its deadline.
- **Power budget** — Milliamps × duty cycle: the math that makes 'low power' a claim with evidence — 'the power budget is the architecture.'
- **Sleep modes** — Tickless idle and peripheral shutdown between work — every avoided wakeup as battery life.
- **Host-side test harness** — Logic compiled for the host behind hardware interfaces; unit-tested with Valgrind, sanitizers, coverage — 'prove logic on the host, integrate on the target.'
- **Demo and writeup** — Working hardware plus honest numbers: spec, architecture, power math, test evidence, what you'd change.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write the sensor-node spec: sensors, sampling rates, latency needs, the power budget target — one page, signed off before code.
2. Build the driver layer for one bus peripheral: init, polled transfer, then interrupt/DMA — the hardware seam, tested on host where possible.
3. Design the tasks and IPC: sample/process/transmit with queue handoff, priorities assigned, the inversion check — on paper first.
4. Compute the power budget: active current × duty cycle + sleep current × sleep time — state the battery-life number and the assumption behind each term.
5. Build the host-side harness: hardware behind interfaces, logic unit-tested with sanitizers — then write the demo script and the honest-numbers writeup.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: The embedded capstone. The sensor node: spec, driver layer, RTOS task design with IPC, power budget with sleep modes, host-side test harness — documented and demoed (hardware or faithful simulation, stated honestly). Deliverable: the firmware, the writeup with power math and test evidence, and the demo — the artifact that ends the debate.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: a capstone is one system, honestly built — it doesn't prove breadth across targets or production hardening, and this course confers no certificate. State what's simulated vs real hardware; honest numbers beat impressive claims.

cards.front: How do you design an RTOS sensor node (capstone-style)?
cards.back: Spec the sampling rates and power budget first → driver layer per peripheral (one bus each) → tasks per concern (sample, process, transmit) with queue/IPC handoff → sleep modes between work. The interview line: ‘the power budget is the architecture.’

cards.front: What’s tickless idle, and why does power care?
cards.back: Instead of waking on every OS tick, the RTOS programs the next wakeup (timer or interrupt) and sleeps deeply until then — no periodic wakeups burning power. The interview line: ‘every avoided wakeup is battery life.’

cards.front: What’s a host-side test harness for firmware?
cards.back: Compile the logic for the host (x86) with the hardware behind interfaces, then unit-test with the rich host tooling (Valgrind, sanitizers, coverage). The interview line: ‘I prove logic on the host and integrate on the target.’

cards.front: How do you demo and write up an embedded capstone?
cards.back: Demo: the thing working (sensor → processing → output) with the power/task story narrated. Writeup: spec, architecture, power budget math, test evidence, what you’d change. The interview line: ‘working hardware plus honest numbers.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Spec: a sensor node with an RTOS'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: The power-budget math belongs in the writeup because:
choices: Embedded claims need numbers — battery life is the spec that matters
quiz.explain: ‘Low power’ is a claim; milliamps × duty cycle is evidence.

quiz.q: Host-side testing’s biggest win is:
choices: Rich tooling (sanitizers, Valgrind, coverage) that doesn’t exist on the MCU
quiz.explain: Bugs found under ASan on the host never become HardFault mysteries on the target.

quiz.q: Tickless idle saves power by:
choices: Eliminating periodic tick wakeups — sleeping until the next real event
quiz.explain: Deep sleep between events beats waking a thousand times a second to do nothing.

quiz.q: Task-per-concern with queue IPC is the right shape because:
choices: Sampling, processing, and transmitting have different timing needs — isolation plus clean handoff
quiz.explain: Decoupled timing domains communicate through queues; each meets its own deadline.

modules.title: Embedded Mock Circuit
modules.summary: Welcome to the Embedded Mock Circuit — the final module of the Embedded path. I'm your instructor, and these are embedded-flavored mocks: C under time, RTOS design, live hardware-debugging scenarios — plus the war story — debriefed into the last reps. By the end, your leaks will be found while fixes are cheap.
objectives: Apply in professional practice: timed C deep-dives
Apply in professional practice: RTOS whiteboard rounds
Apply in professional practice: hardware debugging scenarios
Apply in professional practice: behavioral: the war story
Apply in professional practice: debrief and triage

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Timed C deep-dives** — Layered answers: 30-second correct, mechanism, edge case — 'the classic bug here is…' before they ask; UB questions answered with the optimizer's perspective.
- **RTOS whiteboard rounds** — Tasks, priorities, IPC, the inversion question — drawn and defended, not recited.
- **Hardware debugging scenarios** — 'The sensor reads garbage' — the hypothesis-driven debug walkthrough, aloud, with the tool choice per step.
- **War story (behavioral)** — Stakes, hypotheses, wrong turns, lesson — method and honesty as the scoring rubric.
- **Debrief and triage** — Within the hour: leaks, holds, biggest leak by frequency × weight, 48-hour redrill.
- **Taper plan** — No new material, redrill from the log, timed mocks, rest.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Run a timed C deep-dive mock (30 min): pointers, volatile, UB — layered answers with the optimizer's perspective.
2. Run an RTOS whiteboard mock: design the task set live, defend the IPC choices, answer the inversion probe.
3. Run a hardware-debugging scenario mock: 'garbage on the UART' — hypothesize aloud (clocks first), pick tools per step, land the root cause.
4. Tell the war story once, recorded: two minutes, stakes-hypotheses-wrong turns-lesson — review for credibility gaps.
5. Debrief all four within the hour: template, ranked leaks, 48-hour redrills — then the taper.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Embedded mock portfolio. The four-mock circuit over two weeks — C deep dive, RTOS whiteboard, debugging scenario, war story — each debriefed with the template. Close with the taper schedule. Deliverable: four debriefs and the taper — the last reps, converted.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: mocks can't reproduce the bench — real debugging has smells, heat, and intermittent faults, and this course confers no certificate. What the circuit trains is the hypothesis-driven narration; the lab provides the rest.

cards.front: How do you handle timed language deep-dives?
cards.back: Answer in layers: the 30-second correct answer, then the mechanism, then the edge case — and say ‘the classic bug here is…’ before they ask. The interview line: ‘I answer the question, then the question behind the question.’

cards.front: How do you handle framework whiteboard rounds?
cards.back: Narrate the architecture as you draw: components, lifecycles, data flow — then zoom into the probed area. The interview line: ‘I draw the system first so we both know where the deep dive lives.’

cards.front: How do you tell a debugging war story?
cards.back: Set the stakes fast (what was down, who was affected), narrate the investigation as hypotheses tested (not a heroic montage), name the wrong turns honestly, and land the lesson + what changed afterward. War stories score on method and honesty.

cards.front: How do you debrief and triage after a mock?
cards.back: Within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), rank leaks by frequency × interview weight, and redrill the top one within 48 hours. The interview line: ‘the mock is the test; the debrief is the studying.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: Weak-spot triage should prioritize leaks by:
choices: Frequency × interview weight — what costs the most points most often
quiz.explain: Expected value: fix what loses you the most points most often.

quiz.q: A war story’s wrong turns should be:
choices: Included — they show honest debugging method and make the lesson credible
quiz.explain: Real debugging includes dead ends; hiding them makes the story — and you — less believable.

quiz.q: Drawing the system before the deep dive is strong because:
choices: It establishes shared context — the probe lands somewhere meaningful
quiz.explain: Context first, depth second: the diagram makes the deep dive legible.

modules.title: Test Strategy and the Pyramid
modules.summary: Welcome to Test Strategy and the Pyramid — the opening module of the Software Testing & QA Interview Prep path. I'm your instructor, and this is strategy before tools: the pyramid, risk-based planning, and the layering judgment QA interviews probe before any framework question. We cover the test pyramid, what belongs at each layer, test doubles (mocks, stubs, fakes), risk-based planning, shift-left with CI gating, and arguing strategy aloud. By the end, you will allocate test budget where failure hurts most — and say why.
objectives: Understand and apply: the test pyramid: unit, integration, e2e
Understand and apply: what belongs at each layer
Understand and apply: test doubles: mocks, stubs, fakes
Understand and apply: risk-based test planning
Understand and apply: shift-left and CI gating

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Test pyramid** — Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests, few e2e at the top — the economics: e2e is slow, flaky, expensive; push coverage down, justify every e2e.
- **Unit layer** — Pure logic and algorithms — provable in milliseconds; where validation logic belongs.
- **Integration layer** — Component interactions: DB, API contracts — what only the seams can prove.
- **E2E layer** — Critical user journeys only — the most expensive proof, spent sparingly.
- **Mocks vs stubs vs fakes** — Dummy: placeholder. Stub: canned responses. Fake: working simplified implementation. Mock: verifies interactions — fakes/stubs for state, mocks sparingly for contracts.
- **Risk-based planning** — Test effort follows failure probability × impact — not uniform coverage; 'strategy is resource allocation under uncertainty, argued out loud.'
- **Shift-left** — Testing earlier: CI gates, pre-merge checks — defects found when they're cheapest; the cost-of-defect curve flattened.
- **CI gating** — Required checks as mechanical quality gates — no merge without green; enforced, not cultural.
- **Escape rate** — Bugs reaching production — the headline quality metric; 'I optimize for escaped defects, not test count.'
- **Arguing strategy** — From risk: what breaks × what hurts — then the pyramid allocation with the economics stated.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Draw the pyramid for an app you know: place ten real test cases at their layers — then find the two e2e tests that should be units and move them.
2. Write the risk matrix for one feature: probability × impact per risk — allocate the pyramid from the matrix, not from habit.
3. Classify five test doubles in a sample suite (mock/stub/fake/dummy): find the over-mocked test and rewrite it with a fake — state what the rewrite bought.
4. Design the shift-left gates for one repo: pre-merge checks, required CI checks, the defect-cost argument for each gate.
5. Argue a strategy aloud in three minutes: risks first, pyramid allocation, the economics — the interview shape of this skill.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Strategy brief. For a product you choose: the risk matrix, the pyramid allocation with the per-layer test list, the test-double policy, and the shift-left gate design — each argued from risk and economics. Deliverable: the brief — strategy before tools, written down.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: strategy is argued from risk, and risk estimates are judgments — two good testers can disagree honestly, and this course confers no certificate. The interview tests the reasoning; production tests the estimates. State your assumptions.

cards.front: Draw the test pyramid in words.
cards.back: Many fast unit tests at the base, fewer integration tests in the middle, few end-to-end tests at the top. The economics: e2e is slow, flaky, and expensive — push coverage down the pyramid, and justify every e2e test’s existence.

cards.front: What belongs at each test layer?
cards.back: Unit: pure logic and algorithms. Integration: component interactions (DB, API contracts). E2E: critical user journeys only. The interview line: ‘each layer tests what only that layer can prove.’

cards.front: Mocks vs stubs vs fakes?
cards.back: Dummy: placeholder. Stub: canned responses. Fake: working simplified implementation (in-memory DB). Mock: verifies interactions (was this called?). Use fakes/stubs for state, mocks sparingly for interaction contracts.

cards.front: What do risk-based planning and shift-left mean in practice?
cards.back: Risk-based: test effort follows failure probability × impact — not uniform coverage. Shift-left: move testing earlier (CI gates, pre-merge checks) so defects are found when they’re cheapest. The interview line: ‘I spend test budget where failure hurts most.’

cards.front: How do you argue test strategy in an interview?
cards.back: From risk: what’s most likely to break × what hurts most — then the pyramid allocation that covers it, with the economics stated. The interview line: ‘strategy is resource allocation under uncertainty, argued out loud.’

quiz.q: Leading with risk (not coverage %) is strong because:
choices: It shows you allocate testing where failure actually hurts — engineering judgment
quiz.explain: 100% coverage of the wrong things is worse than 60% of the right things.

quiz.q: Shift-left reduces cost because:
choices: Defects found earlier are dramatically cheaper to fix than escaped ones
quiz.explain: The cost-of-defect curve rises steeply with lateness; early gates flatten it.

quiz.q: A mock differs from a stub in that it:
choices: Verifies interactions (calls made), while a stub just returns canned data
quiz.explain: Stubs provide state; mocks assert behavior — over-mocking couples tests to implementation.

quiz.q: An E2E test for input validation is usually wrong because:
choices: Validation logic is provable in milliseconds at the unit layer — E2E is the most expensive way to check it
quiz.explain: Push each check to the cheapest layer that can prove it.

modules.title: Automation Frameworks
modules.summary: Welcome to Automation Frameworks — module 2 of the QA path. I'm your instructor, and this is the framework landscape at selection depth: WebDriver versus Playwright versus Cypress, POM discipline, and how to justify the choice. We cover Selenium WebDriver's architecture, Playwright's auto-waiting model, the Page Object Model, Cypress's tradeoffs, and Appium basics for mobile. By the end, your framework answers will be criteria-first — engineering, not advocacy.
objectives: Understand and apply: selenium WebDriver architecture
Understand and apply: playwright's auto-waiting model
Understand and apply: page Object Model
Understand and apply: cypress's tradeoffs
Understand and apply: mobile: Appium basics

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **WebDriver architecture** — Language bindings → WebDriver protocol (HTTP/JSON wire) → browser driver → real browser — cross-browser and cross-language, with explicit waits as the price.
- **Playwright's auto-waiting** — Actions wait for actionability — no sleep/flaky waits; multiple engines, network interception, parallelism built in.
- **Page Object Model** — One class per page encapsulating selectors and actions — 'selectors live in exactly one file per screen.'
- **Cypress tradeoffs** — In-browser: superb debugging (time travel, real DOM) — but same-origin/tab limits; 'trades browser-architecture limits for the best debugging experience.'
- **Appium** — WebDriver-protocol mobile automation: one API over iOS (XCUITest) and Android (UiAutomator2) — cross-platform coverage at the cost of speed.
- **Criteria-first selection** — Criteria before candidate tools — 'criteria-first prevents rationalizing a pre-chosen favorite.'
- **Flakiness sources** — Timing, order-dependence, environment — classified before fixed; 'a flaky test is either fixed or quarantined, never tolerated.'
- **Explicit vs auto waits** — The framework comparison that matters most in practice: who owns the waiting determines who owns the flakiness.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write the selection criteria for a hypothetical team (browsers, languages, CI, debugging needs) — then score WebDriver, Playwright, and Cypress against them; state the winner and the runner-up's case.
2. Build a three-page POM for a demo app: selectors encapsulated, tests reading as user intent — then change one selector and show the single-file fix.
3. Take one flaky test: classify the flakiness (timing/order/environment), apply the proper wait or isolation fix — state the classification before the fix.
4. Compare an explicit-wait script with an auto-waiting equivalent: run both under load, count the flakes — the empirical comparison.
5. Write the Appium-vs-native decision for one mobile feature: the coverage/speed tradeoff argued — verdict with the flip condition.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Framework selection brief. For a team you define: the criteria, the scored comparison (WebDriver/Playwright/Cypress + Appium for mobile), the POM structure sketch, and the flakiness policy (classify → fix-or-quarantine). Deliverable: the brief — selection as engineering.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: framework advice decays — the landscape moves yearly and team context dominates, and this course confers no certificate. Date your recommendation; 'as of 2026' is part of the answer.

cards.front: How do you explain Selenium WebDriver’s architecture?
cards.back: Language bindings → WebDriver protocol (HTTP/JSON wire) → browser driver → real browser. That layering is why it’s cross-browser and cross-language — and why it needs explicit waits: the protocol has no built-in actionability checks.

cards.front: Why does Playwright win framework comparisons lately?
cards.back: Auto-waiting (actions wait for actionability — no sleep/flaky waits), multiple browser engines, network interception, parallel execution, and first-class async. The interview comparison: Selenium WebDriver’s explicit waits vs Playwright’s built-in resilience.

cards.front: What’s the Page Object Model buying you?
cards.back: One class per page encapsulating selectors and actions: tests read as user intent (‘loginAs(user)’), and UI changes touch one place. The interview line: ‘selectors live in exactly one file per screen.’

cards.front: What are Cypress’s tradeoffs?
cards.back: Runs in-browser: great debugging (time travel, real DOM access), automatic waiting — but same-run origin limits (iframes/multi-domain need workarounds) and no multi-tab. The interview line: ‘Cypress trades browser-architecture limits for the best debugging experience.’

cards.front: Appium basics — how do you position it?
cards.back: WebDriver-protocol mobile automation: one API driving iOS (XCUITest) and Android (UiAutomator2) — cross-platform scripts at the cost of speed and flakiness vs native frameworks. The interview line: ‘Appium for cross-platform coverage; native frameworks where depth matters.’

quiz.q: Selection criteria must come before candidate tools because:
choices: Criteria-first prevents rationalizing a pre-chosen favorite
quiz.explain: Tools-first selection is advocacy; criteria-first is engineering.

quiz.q: Appium’s core value proposition is:
choices: One WebDriver-style API automating both iOS and Android
quiz.explain: Cross-platform mobile tests through a unified protocol — trading some speed for coverage breadth.

quiz.q: Cypress’s architectural tradeoff is:
choices: In-browser execution gives superb debugging but same-origin/tab limitations
quiz.explain: Running inside the browser enables time-travel debugging; the cost is the browser’s own sandbox limits.

quiz.q: The Page Object Model’s main benefit is:
choices: Encapsulating page structure so UI changes don’t rewrite every test
quiz.explain: A selector change updates one page object instead of dozens of tests.

modules.title: API and Contract Testing
modules.summary: Welcome to API and Contract Testing — module 3 of the QA path. I'm your instructor, and this is APIs as the test surface: contract thinking, schema validation, and consumer-driven contracts — the backend-adjacent depth modern QA roles require. We cover HTTP semantics for testers, status codes and error contracts, schema validation, consumer-driven contracts (Pact-style), and mocking dependencies. By the end, you will test the contract, not just the responses.
objectives: Understand and apply: HTTP semantics for testers
Understand and apply: status codes and error contracts
Understand and apply: schema validation
Understand and apply: consumer-driven contracts (Pact-style)
Understand and apply: mocking dependencies

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **HTTP safety/idempotency** — GET safe, PUT idempotent, POST neither — the semantics testers assert, not just the status codes.
- **Status-code classes** — 2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx with exact meanings — 429 as the explicit throttle signal ('back off, respect Retry-After').
- **Error contracts** — Can clients program against the errors? Stable codes, messages, request IDs — the contract's unhappy half.
- **Schema validation** — Shape, types, required fields — the response's promise, mechanically checked.
- **Consumer-driven contracts** — Each consumer's expectations as verifiable pacts — provider changes that break specific consumers, caught before deploy.
- **Mocking dependencies** — Isolating the system under test from unstable or unavailable collaborators — with the fidelity caveat stated.
- **Performance-adjacent API checks** — Response-time budgets per endpoint in CI, payload sizes, N+1 detection — the perf questions QA owns.
- **Reading a load-test report** — Percentiles not averages, error rate vs load steps, saturation signals, the bottleneck's location — 'I read the tail, then find what's saturated.'
- **Senior answer structure** — Definition, mechanism, fit-and-tradeoff — then stop; structure separating senior answers from recitation.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write the HTTP-semantics checklist for one API: method safety/idempotency per endpoint, the exact status codes asserted, the headers checked — then run it against a real API.
2. Add schema validation to three API tests: shape, types, required fields — break the schema deliberately and watch the test catch it.
3. Write one consumer-driven contract (Pact-style): the consumer's expectations as a pact — then change the provider and watch the pact fail before deploy.
4. Set a response-time budget for two endpoints in CI: the threshold, the percentile measured, the gate that fails the build — the performance-adjacent check, live.
5. Read one load-test report (sample or generated): percentiles per step, error rates, the saturation signal — write the three-line verdict.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Contract-testing portfolio. For one API: the HTTP-semantics test suite, schema validation on key endpoints, one consumer-driven pact with the break-it demonstration, and the CI response-time budgets — plus a load-test report reading with the verdict. Deliverable: the suite plus the report reading — the contract, tested.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: contract tests verify the agreement, not the behavior behind it — a green pact with a broken provider is a false comfort, and this course confers no certificate. State what each test layer proves; no layer proves everything.

cards.front: What HTTP semantics must a tester know cold?
cards.back: Methods’ safety/idempotency (GET safe, PUT idempotent, POST neither), status-code classes (2xx/3xx/4xx/5xx) and their exact meanings, headers (auth, content negotiation, caching). Testers who speak HTTP write better API tests and better bug reports.

cards.front: What do you check in API/contract testing?
cards.back: Status codes and error contracts (can clients program against them?), schema validation (shape, types, required fields), auth boundaries, idempotency of retries, and consumer-driven contracts (Pact) so provider changes don’t break consumers silently.

cards.front: OperationQueue vs GCD?
cards.back: OperationQueue: higher-level — dependencies between operations, cancellation, priorities, max concurrency. GCD: lighter, C-level queues. The interview line: ‘dependencies and cancellation buy the Operation abstraction; otherwise GCD.’
