cards.front: What are performance-adjacent API checks, and how do you read a load-test report?
cards.back: Adjacent checks: response-time budgets per endpoint in CI, payload sizes, N+1 detection. Reading a report: percentiles (not averages), error rate vs load steps, saturation signals, and the bottleneck’s location. The interview line: ‘I read the tail, then find what’s saturated.’

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'HTTP semantics for testers'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: A load-test report’s most important numbers are:
choices: Percentile latencies and error rates per load step — the tail under stress
quiz.explain: Averages hide the user experience; percentiles per step reveal where it breaks.

quiz.q: Operation dependencies give you:
choices: Declarative ordering (‘B after A’) without manual synchronization
quiz.explain: The queue topologically sorts the graph; you declare relationships, not locks.

quiz.q: Consumer-driven contract testing (Pact-style) catches:
choices: Provider changes that break specific consumers — before deploy
quiz.explain: Each consumer’s expectations become verifiable contracts the provider must satisfy.

quiz.q: A 429 status code tells the client to:
choices: Back off — rate limited; respect Retry-After
quiz.explain: 429 is the server’s explicit throttle signal; hammering through it escalates the block.

modules.title: Performance Testing
modules.summary: Welcome to Performance Testing — module 4 of the QA path. I'm your instructor, and this is performance testing literacy: the test types, the percentiles that matter, and scripting a basic load test in k6 — enough to own the topic in QA loops. We cover load, stress, spike, and soak; throughput with p95/p99; k6 scripting basics; JMeter thread groups; and reading a load-test report. By the end, 'performance claims without before/after numbers are stories' will be your line too.
objectives: Understand and apply: load, stress, spike, soak
Understand and apply: throughput and latency percentiles (p95/p99)
Understand and apply: k6 scripting basics
Understand and apply: jMeter thread groups
Understand and apply: reading a load-test report

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Load test** — Expected traffic: measure latency/throughput under the load you actually expect.
- **Stress test** — Beyond capacity: find the breaking point — where it breaks and how it breaks.
- **Spike test** — Sudden surges: test autoscaling and burst absorption — the thundering-herd rehearsal.
- **Soak test** — Sustained load over hours: find the leaks — memory, connections, the slow degradations.
- **p95/p99** — The tail: 'a 100ms average with a 5s p99 means 1% of users suffer' — SLOs are written on percentiles because experience lives in the tail.
- **Throughput** — Requests per second sustained — with the latency measured alongside; throughput without latency is half the story.
- **k6 scripting** — JS-scripted load tests with thresholds as gates: stages, VUs, assertions — code-reviewed load tests in the pipeline.
- **k6 thresholds** — Pass/fail assertions on metrics — 'the test proves the SLO or it fails.'
- **JMeter thread groups** — The classic model: threads, ramp-up, loops — GUI-driven, mature, broad protocol support.
- **Report reading** — Percentiles per load step, error rates, saturation signals, bottleneck location — 'read the tail, find what's saturated.'

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Script a k6 load test for a demo endpoint: stages (ramp, sustain), thresholds on p95 and error rate — run it and read the tail.
2. Run the same endpoint to stress: raise VUs past capacity, find the breaking point — write the 'where and how it breaks' note.
3. Spike it: 10× surge for 60 seconds — observe the autoscaling (or the queueing); write the absorption verdict.
4. Compare k6 vs JMeter for one team scenario: the scripted-vs-GUI tradeoff argued — verdict with the team-context reason.
5. Write the before/after for one optimization: baseline percentiles, the fix, re-measured percentiles — the numbers that prove it.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: Load-test portfolio. For one endpoint: the k6 script with thresholds, the four test-type runs (load/stress/spike/soak) with reports, the report readings with verdicts, and one before/after optimization with the numbers. Deliverable: the portfolio — performance testing literacy, evidenced.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: load-test numbers are environment-shaped — test hardware, network, and data realism change everything, and this course confers no certificate. State the environment with the numbers; a percentile without context is a story, not evidence.

cards.front: Load vs stress vs spike vs soak?
cards.back: Load: expected traffic, measure latency/throughput. Stress: beyond capacity, find the breaking point. Spike: sudden surges, test autoscaling. Soak: sustained load over hours, find leaks. Report percentiles (p95/p99), not averages — averages hide the tail.

cards.front: Why do performance interviews insist on p95/p99?
cards.back: Averages hide the tail: a 100ms average with a 5s p99 means 1% of users suffer. SLOs are written on percentiles because user experience lives in the tail. Always report the distribution, never just the mean.

cards.front: k6 vs JMeter — how do you compare them?
cards.back: k6: JS-scripted, developer-friendly, great for CI-integrated load tests with thresholds as gates. JMeter: GUI-driven, mature, huge protocol support, heavier. The interview line: ‘k6 for code-reviewed load tests in the pipeline; JMeter where the team already lives in it.’

cards.front: What are performance-adjacent API checks, and how do you read a load-test report?
cards.back: Adjacent checks: response-time budgets per endpoint in CI, payload sizes, N+1 detection. Reading a report: percentiles (not averages), error rate vs load steps, saturation signals, and the bottleneck’s location. The interview line: ‘I read the tail, then find what’s saturated.’

cards.front: How do you discuss performance in an interview?
cards.back: With numbers and method: the budget, the measurement (percentiles), the bottleneck found, the fix, the re-measurement. The interview line: ‘performance claims without before/after numbers are stories.’

quiz.q: Before/after numbers matter because:
choices: They prove the fix worked and quantify the win — otherwise it’s anecdote
quiz.explain: Optimization without measurement is indistinguishable from guessing.

quiz.q: A load-test report’s most important numbers are:
choices: Percentile latencies and error rates per load step — the tail under stress
quiz.explain: Averages hide the user experience; percentiles per step reveal where it breaks.

quiz.q: k6’s thresholds turn a load test into:
choices: A gate: breaching p95/error-rate assertions fails the run
quiz.explain: Thresholds are pass/fail assertions on metrics — the test proves the SLO or it fails.

quiz.q: p99 latency of 2s means:
choices: 99% of requests were faster than 2s — 1% were slower
quiz.explain: Percentiles describe the distribution’s tail: p99 is the near-worst case users feel.

modules.title: Test Planning and Reporting
modules.summary: Welcome to Test Planning and Reporting — module 5 of the QA path. I'm your instructor, and this is the craft QA interviews respect most: plans, traceability, defect discipline, and metrics that measure quality — not just activity. We cover test plans that get read, traceability from requirements to cases, defect lifecycle and severity, metrics (escape rate, flakiness), and exploratory testing charters. By the end, you will present conclusions, not queries.
objectives: Understand and apply: test plans that get read
Understand and apply: traceability: requirements to cases
Understand and apply: defect lifecycle and severity
Understand and apply: metrics: escape rate, flakiness
Understand and apply: exploratory testing charters

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Test plan that gets read** — Scope and risk focus, traceability, entry/exit criteria, environment needs — 'a plan is argued choices, not a form.'
- **Traceability** — Requirements → cases: every requirement tested, every test justified — the coverage argument that survives audit.
- **Defect lifecycle** — New → triaged → in progress → fixed → verified → closed (reopened on regression) — the discipline of the queue.
- **Severity vs priority** — Severity = impact on users; priority = fix order (business decision) — different axes, conflated at your peril.
- **Escape rate** — Bugs found in production that testing missed — the headline quality metric.
- **Flakiness rate** — Unreliable tests erode trust — measured, quarantined, fixed-or-deleted; never tolerated.
- **Exploratory charters** — Time-boxed missions with a goal, session notes, debriefs — skilled investigation, not random clicking; repeatable and reportable.
- **BLUF reporting** — Bottom line up front: recommendation first, the one chart that proves it, caveats briefly, the decision needed — 'executives decide.'
- **Entry/exit criteria** — The gates: when testing starts, when it's done — decided in the plan, not in the moment.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Write a one-page test plan for a feature you know: scope in/out with reasons, risk focus, entry/exit criteria — then cut every sentence that isn't a decision.
2. Build the traceability matrix for five requirements: requirement → cases → status — find the untested requirement and the unjustified test.
3. Run a defect triage on five sample bugs: assign severity AND priority separately — defend one case where they differ (severe but low priority, or trivial but urgent).
4. Compute escape rate and flakiness rate for a sample suite: write the two numbers, then the action each number demands.
5. Write one exploratory charter (45-minute mission), execute it on a demo app, debrief in writing — the charter → notes → debrief loop, complete.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: QA craft portfolio. For one release: the one-page test plan, the traceability matrix, the triaged defect log with severity/priority separated, the quality metrics (escape rate, flakiness) with the actions they demand, and one executed exploratory charter with debrief — plus the BLUF stakeholder summary. Deliverable: the portfolio — the craft, evidenced.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: metrics measure the past — escape rate tells you where quality was, not where it will be, and this course confers no certificate. Report metrics with their limits stated; a metric without caveats is a vanity number.

cards.front: What makes a test plan that gets read?
cards.back: Scope and risk focus (what’s in/out and why), traceability (requirements → cases), entry/exit criteria, and environment needs — one page of decisions, not a template dump. The interview line: ‘a plan is a set of argued choices, not a form.’

cards.front: How do you discuss defect lifecycle and severity?
cards.back: Lifecycle: new → triaged → in progress → fixed → verified → closed (reopened if it regresses). Severity (impact) vs priority (fix order) are different axes — a cosmetic bug on the checkout button can be high priority. The interview line: ‘severity is impact; priority is scheduling.’

cards.front: What QA metrics actually matter?
cards.back: Escape rate (bugs reaching production — the headline), flakiness rate (unreliable tests erode trust), MTTR on failures, and coverage as a secondary signal. The interview line: ‘I optimize for escaped defects, not test count.’

cards.front: How do you make exploratory testing rigorous?
cards.back: Charters: time-boxed missions with a goal (‘explore checkout with invalid inputs for 45 minutes’), session notes, and debriefs. It’s skilled investigation, not random clicking — the charter makes it repeatable and reportable.

cards.front: How do you present to non-technical stakeholders?
cards.back: Lead with the recommendation, then the one chart that proves it; plain language, no jargon; name caveats briefly and honestly; end with the decision you need. The interview line: ‘I present conclusions, not queries.’

quiz.q: Leading with the recommendation works because:
choices: Executives decide — the supporting evidence follows the decision they need to make
quiz.explain: BLUF (bottom line up front): busy stakeholders need the ask before the analysis.

quiz.q: An exploratory testing charter provides:
choices: A time-boxed mission and focus — making exploration deliberate and reportable
quiz.explain: Charters bound the session with purpose; notes and debriefs turn findings into artifacts.

quiz.q: Defect escape rate measures:
choices: Bugs found in production that testing missed — the headline quality metric
quiz.explain: It answers the only question stakeholders care about: did quality gates work?

quiz.q: Severity vs priority differ in that:
choices: Severity = impact on users; priority = order of fixing (business decision)
Severity is decided by testers only
quiz.explain: A severe bug in a deprecated feature can be low priority; a trivial bug blocking launch is high priority.

modules.title: Guided Automation Build
modules.summary: Welcome to the Guided Automation Build — module 6 of the QA path. I'm your instructor, and this is a real automation suite: UI, API, CI, reports — built to be demoed; the artifact that converts QA interviews from Q&A into show-and-tell. We scaffold a framework with Playwright, write page objects for a demo app, add API contract tests, wire a CI pipeline with reporting, and practice flaky-test triage. By the end, you will demo the suite, not describe it.
objectives: Build and demonstrate: framework scaffold with Playwright
Build and demonstrate: page objects for a demo app
Build and demonstrate: API contract tests
Build and demonstrate: CI pipeline with reporting
Build and demonstrate: flaky-test triage

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Framework scaffold** — The runnable skeleton: config, fixtures, reporters — the foundation every later test inherits.
- **Page objects** — Selectors in exactly one file per screen; tests reading as user intent ('loginAs(user)') — the maintainability pattern.
- **API contract tests** — Status, schema, error contracts in the same suite — the backend-adjacent depth, automated.
- **CI pipeline** — Triggers, parallel jobs, artifacts, secrets via the platform (never in YAML), branch protection requiring the checks — 'the pipeline is the definition of done.'
- **Reporting** — The suite's output as evidence: pass/fail, flakiness history, the report stakeholders actually open.
- **Flaky-test triage** — Quarantine first, then classify (timing/order/environment/real bug) — 'fixed or quarantined, never tolerated'; quarantine preserves signal with a dated fix-or-delete decision.
- **Branch protection** — Required checks as mechanical gates — quality enforced, not cultural.
- **Build narrative** — Problem → constraints → decisions → result → 'what I'd do with more time' — the delivery vehicle for the demo.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Scaffold the Playwright framework: config, one fixture, the reporter — run the empty suite green before writing any test.
2. Build page objects for three screens of a demo app: write one test per screen reading as user intent — then change a selector and show the single-file fix.
3. Add API contract tests for two endpoints: status, schema, error contract — the backend-adjacent layer, in the same run.
4. Wire the CI pipeline: push/PR triggers, parallel jobs, artifact upload, the required-check gate — break the build deliberately and watch the gate hold.
5. Plant one flaky test: quarantine it, classify it, fix it properly — document the triage as the interview answer.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: The automation suite. The complete build: Playwright scaffold, page objects for a demo app, API contract tests, CI pipeline with reporting and branch protection — plus the flaky-test triage log and the build narrative. Deliverable: the suite, the pipeline, the narrative — the demo that converts interviews.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: a demo suite proves you can build the shape — production suites add the long tail (data, environments, maintenance burden), and this course confers no certificate. Present the suite as what it is: the pattern, executed well, sized honestly.

cards.front: Why does Playwright win framework comparisons lately?
cards.back: Auto-waiting (actions wait for actionability — no sleep/flaky waits), multiple browser engines, network interception, parallel execution, and first-class async. The interview comparison: Selenium WebDriver’s explicit waits vs Playwright’s built-in resilience.

cards.front: What’s the Page Object Model buying you?
cards.back: One class per page encapsulating selectors and actions: tests read as user intent (‘loginAs(user)’), and UI changes touch one place. The interview line: ‘selectors live in exactly one file per screen.’

cards.front: What goes in an API contract / OpenAPI sketch?
cards.back: Endpoints, methods, request/response schemas, status codes, error model, auth, rate limits, and versioning — enough that a client team could build against it. The interview line: ‘the contract is the interface; code is the implementation.’

cards.front: How do you structure a GitHub Actions CI pipeline?
cards.back: Triggers on push/PR, jobs for lint/test/build/scan in parallel where possible, artifacts uploaded once, secrets via GitHub Secrets (never in YAML), and branch protection requiring the checks. The interview line: ‘the pipeline is the definition of done.’

cards.front: How do you triage flaky tests?
cards.back: Quarantine first (don’t let flakes erode trust), then classify: timing (add proper waits), order-dependence (isolate state), environment (pin it), or real bug (the flake was signal). The interview line: ‘a flaky test is either fixed or quarantined — never tolerated.’

quiz.q: A build narrative should lead with:
choices: The problem, constraints, and key decisions with alternatives
quiz.explain: Decisions are what get probed; leading with them controls the conversation.

quiz.q: Quarantining flakes (instead of deleting) is right because:
choices: It preserves the signal while protecting trust — with a dated fix-or-delete decision
quiz.explain: Ignored flakes teach the team to ignore red builds; quarantine keeps the build honest.

quiz.q: Branch protection requiring CI checks ensures:
choices: No code merges without passing the pipeline — the gate is enforced, not cultural
quiz.explain: Required checks make quality gates mechanical rather than relying on everyone remembering.

quiz.q: Writing the contract before the implementation is strong because:
choices: It forces interface decisions early, when they’re cheap — and enables parallel client/server work
quiz.explain: Contract-first surfaces disagreements before code cements them.

modules.title: QA Mock Circuit
modules.summary: Welcome to the QA Mock Circuit — the final module of the QA path. I'm your instructor, and these are QA-flavored mocks: scenario design, framework grilling, and plan whiteboards — debriefed into the final study plan. By the end, you will whiteboard the reasoning, not just the answer.
objectives: Apply in professional practice: timed testing-scenario rounds
Apply in professional practice: framework deep-dives
Apply in professional practice: test-plan whiteboard
Apply in professional practice: behavioral ledger
Apply in professional practice: debrief and triage

notes.title: Concepts
notes.body:
- **Testing-scenario rounds** — Restate the goal, enumerate risks, allocate the pyramid, name tools per layer with reasons — 'I whiteboard the reasoning.'
- **Framework deep-dives** — Criteria first, then the pick — selection as engineering under follow-up pressure.
- **Test-plan whiteboard** — Scope, risks, traceability, entry/exit — the plan as argued choices, drawn live.
- **Behavioral ledger** — Story bank, stories-told-where, feedback, stumping questions — every round fresh.
- **Debrief and triage** — Within the hour: leaks, holds, biggest leak by frequency × weight, 48-hour redrill.
- **Taper plan** — No new material, redrill from the log, timed mocks, rest.
- **Anchoring** — Restating the scenario's goal first — 'a brilliant plan for the wrong problem' is the classic whiteboard failure.

notes.title: Hands-on procedure
notes.body:
Work this module the way the interview tests it — hands on, timed, and narrated aloud. Follow the sequence below in order; each step builds the next.

1. Run a timed scenario mock: 'test this feature' — goal restated, risks enumerated, pyramid allocated, tools named with reasons — 30 minutes.
2. Run a framework deep-dive mock: defend your framework pick against 'why not X?' — criteria first, every time.
3. Run a test-plan whiteboard mock: draw the plan live — scope, traceability, entry/exit — then defend the cuts.
4. Run one behavioral round from the ledger: two-minute STAR answers, no repeats.
5. Debrief all four within the hour: template, ranked leaks, 48-hour redrills, ledger update — then the taper.

notes.title: Project brief
notes.body: QA mock portfolio. The four-mock circuit over two weeks — scenario design, framework deep dive, plan whiteboard, behavioral — each debriefed with the template and the ledger updated. Close with the taper schedule. Deliverable: four debriefs, the ledger, the taper — reasoning, whiteboarded.

notes.title: Honesty note
notes.body: Honest scope: mocks simulate the format, not the stakes — and this course confers no certificate. QA loops vary by company (automation-heavy vs strategy-heavy); the circuit trains the format, and company research covers the rest.

cards.front: How do you handle QA whiteboard rounds (scenarios, test plans, frameworks)?
cards.back: Structure first: restate the goal, enumerate risks, allocate the pyramid, name the tools per layer with reasons. For frameworks: criteria, then the pick. The interview line: ‘I whiteboard the reasoning, not just the answer.’

cards.front: What’s a behavioral ledger?
cards.back: Your running record: story bank entries, which stories you’ve told where, feedback received, and follow-up questions that stumped you. It stops you from repeating the same story and turns each behavioral round into training data.

cards.front: How do you debrief and triage after a mock?
cards.back: Within an hour, write what leaked (fumbled complexity? silent coding? weak STAR?), rank leaks by frequency × interview weight, and redrill the top one within 48 hours. The interview line: ‘the mock is the test; the debrief is the studying.’

cards.front: What’s the final two-week taper?
cards.back: Stop learning new topics; redrill weak patterns from your debrief log, run full timed mocks, fix sleep, and rehearse your story bank aloud. The taper converts knowledge into performance — cramming new material now only adds noise.

cards.front: The interviewer asks you to go deep on 'Timed testing-scenario rounds'. What answer structure makes you sound senior?
cards.back: Three beats: (1) one-sentence definition, (2) how it works mechanically, (3) when it fits and its key tradeoff — then stop and invite the follow-up. Structure is what separates a senior answer from a recitation.

quiz.q: The taper period’s rule is:
choices: No new material — redrill weak spots, mock timed, rest
quiz.explain: Performance comes from consolidation and recovery, not last-minute breadth.

quiz.q: Weak-spot triage should prioritize leaks by:
choices: Frequency × interview weight — what costs the most points most often
quiz.explain: Expected value: fix what loses you the most points most often.

quiz.q: A behavioral ledger prevents:
choices: Repeating the same story across rounds and losing track of feedback
quiz.explain: Loops have multiple behavioral touchpoints; the ledger keeps each one fresh and improving.

quiz.q: Restating the scenario’s goal first is strong because:
choices: It proves you solve the asked problem — whiteboard answers drift without anchoring
quiz.explain: Anchoring prevents the classic failure: a brilliant plan for the wrong problem.

scriptLabs.title: Sliding window: maximum sum of k
scriptLabs.brief: Implement the classic fixed-size sliding window in Python — the pattern interviewers expect you to recognize in under a minute. O(n) time, O(1) extra space.
scriptLabs.starter:
def max_sum_k(arr, k):

    window_sum = sum(arr[:k])
    best = window_sum

scriptLabs.solution:
import time

class TokenBucket:
    def __init__(self, capacity, refill_per_second):
        self.capacity = capacity
        self.refill_per_second = refill_per_second
        self.tokens = capacity
        self.last = time.monotonic()

    def allow(self):
        now = time.monotonic()
        elapsed = now - self.last
        self.last = now
        self.tokens = min(self.capacity,
                          self.tokens + elapsed * self.refill_per_second)
        if self.tokens >= 1:
            self.tokens -= 1
            return True
        return False

scriptLabs.title: One-page design doc: URL shortener
scriptLabs.brief: Write the one-page design doc you’d produce in a 45-minute system-design round: requirements, API, data model, and scaling — with the decisions an interviewer probes.
scriptLabs.starter:
# URL shortener — design doc

## Requirements
<!-- functional + non-functional: what must it do, at what scale? -->

## API
<!-- endpoints, methods, status codes -->

## Data model
<!-- what’s stored, keyed how? -->

## Scaling
<!-- what breaks first, and the fix -->
scriptLabs.hint: Walk the standard arc: requirements → estimation → API → data model → scaling → failure modes. Name the ID strategy and the hot-URL problem.
scriptLabs.solution:
# URL shortener — design doc

## Requirements
- Shorten long URLs; redirect short → long with HTTP 301.
- Scale: 100M new URLs/month (~40 writes/s avg, ~400 peak), 10:1 read:write ratio.
- Availability over strong consistency: a slightly stale redirect is fine.

## API
- POST /shorten {url} → 201 {id}; GET /{id} → 301 Location: url.
- Rate-limit POST per API key (token bucket).

## Data model
- Key-value: id → url (+ created_at, owner). IDs: base62(counter) — unique by
  construction, no collision checks. Counter via a dedicated range allocator.
- Cache: hot URLs in Redis (a small fraction of ids serve most redirects);
  cache-aside with TTL; on miss, read the store and repopulate.

## Scaling
- Stateless app tier behind a load balancer; shard the KV store by hash(id).
- Redirects served from edge cache/CDN where possible.
- Failure modes: counter allocator down → pre-allocated ranges per host;
  cache cold → DB absorbs with connection pooling and read replicas.

scriptLabs.title: Top 3 earners per department (SQL)
scriptLabs.brief: The canonical top-N-per-group query: rank employees within each department with a window function, then filter. A SQL-screen staple.
scriptLabs.starter:
-- Return the top 3 highest-paid employees in each department.
-- Columns: dept_name, emp_name, salary
-- Tables: employees(emp_id, emp_name, dept_id, salary),
--         departments(dept_id, dept_name)
SELECT
scriptLabs.hint: Rank inside each partition first in a CTE, then filter on the rank in the outer query — window functions can’t go in WHERE.
scriptLabs.solution:
WITH ranked AS (
  SELECT d.dept_name, e.emp_name, e.salary,
         ROW_NUMBER() OVER (PARTITION BY e.dept_id ORDER BY e.salary DESC) AS rn
  FROM employees e
  JOIN departments d ON d.dept_id = e.dept_id
)
SELECT dept_name, emp_name, salary
FROM ranked
WHERE rn <= 3
ORDER BY dept_name, salary DESC;

scenarios.title: System-design round: URL shortener
scenarios.context: You have 45 minutes. The interviewer says: ‘Design a URL shortener like bit.ly.’

steps.prompt: The interviewer asks for requirements. What’s your strongest opening?

options.text: Jump straight to the database schema — the tables are obvious
options.why: Drawing the schema before scoping risks designing the wrong system; interviewers fail candidates who skip requirements.

options.text: Ask clarifying questions, then state functional and non-functional requirements out loud
options.why: Requirements bound every downstream decision (estimation, API, data model). Scoping first is the expected opening.

options.text: Start drawing boxes and arrows for the architecture
options.why: Boxes without requirements are decoration — you can’t size or choose components for an unscored problem.

options.text: Estimate users and QPS first, then circle back to requirements
options.why: Estimation needs the requirements’ scale numbers; doing it first means inventing the inputs.

steps.prompt: Estimation: 100M new URLs/month, 10:1 read:write. What do you do?

options.text: Compute rough storage, bandwidth, and QPS with stated assumptions, driving toward design decisions
options.why: Order-of-magnitude math with narrated assumptions is what’s graded — and it must feed decisions (shard? cache? CDN?).

options.text: Skip estimation — it’s just arithmetic
options.why: Skipping it signals you don’t size systems; interviewers read it as a missing engineering habit.

options.text: Compute everything to six decimal places for precision
options.why: False precision wastes time and misses the point: estimation is about orders of magnitude, not arithmetic.

options.text: Ask the interviewer to do the estimation for you
options.why: Estimation is your job in the round; outsourcing it forfeits the signal.

steps.prompt: API design: which is the strongest choice?

options.text: POST /shorten to create, GET /{id} returning 301 to redirect
options.why: RESTful semantics: POST creates (201), GET with a 301 redirect is cacheable and correct for redirection.

options.text: GET /shorten?url=... to create short URLs
options.why: GET must be safe and idempotent — using it for creation breaks caching, logging, and retry semantics.

options.text: One POST endpoint that both creates and redirects based on a flag
options.why: Overloading one endpoint conflates two resources and two semantics; it’s un-RESTful and hard to cache.

options.text: WebSocket stream for shortening and redirecting
options.why: Full-duplex streaming for a request/response problem adds machinery with zero benefit.

steps.prompt: Scaling writes: which tradeoff do you name out loud?

options.text: ‘We’ll just use a bigger database machine’
options.why: Vertical scaling has a hard ceiling and a single point of failure — it’s not a scaling strategy.

options.text: Shard the key-value store by hash of the ID, cache hot URLs, and name the consistency tradeoff (eventual is fine for redirects)
options.why: Names the scaling mechanism, the hot-key mitigation, and the explicit consistency choice — the complete senior answer.

options.text: Put everything in one Redis and hope
options.why: Hope isn’t capacity planning; a single store is a single point of failure at this scale.

options.text: Shard by creation timestamp
options.why: Time-based sharding hotspots the newest shard — hash sharding spreads load evenly.

scenarios.title: Coding round: stuck on DP
scenarios.context: ‘Find the maximum sum of non-adjacent elements.’ Ten minutes in, your tabulation has an off-by-one and the example fails.

steps.prompt: You’re stuck 10 minutes in. Strongest move?

options.text: State the brute-force recursion aloud with its complexity, then fix the recurrence from the definition
options.why: Shows honest reasoning, banks a correct fallback, and re-deriving from the state definition is how DP bugs actually get fixed.

options.text: Sit silently until the fix comes to you
options.why: Silent debugging is unscoreable — the interviewer can’t grade thought they can’t see.

options.text: Ask the interviewer for the recurrence
options.why: Asking for the core insight forfeits the problem’s main signal; ask for a nudge only after showing your attempt.

options.text: Switch to a different approach entirely without diagnosing
options.why: Abandoning a nearly-right solution wastes the invested reasoning; diagnose first.

steps.prompt: You spot it: the state transition is right but the base cases are wrong. What do you say?

options.text: ‘The recurrence is dp[i] = max(dp[i-1], dp[i-2] + nums[i]); my bases for i=0,1 were wrong — fixing them now’
options.why: Names the recurrence, localizes the bug precisely, and narrates the fix — the complete recovery.

options.text: Quietly rewrite the whole thing from scratch
options.why: Rewriting without diagnosis risks reintroducing the same bug and hides your debugging method.

options.text: ‘This is basically the Fibonacci pattern’ and move on
options.why: Pattern-naming without fixing leaves failing code on the board — the tests still fail.

options.text: Blame the example as a trick case
options.why: The example is the specification; dismissing it signals you don’t test against reality.

steps.prompt: Time’s almost up and one case still fails. What closes strongest?

options.text: Walk through the failing case aloud, name the exact fix you’d apply, and state the final complexity
options.why: A diagnosed near-miss with a named fix and complexity analysis scores far better than silence or hand-waving.

options.text: Say ‘it’s basically done’ and hope they don’t notice
options.why: Interviewers always notice; claiming done on failing code destroys credibility.

options.text: Delete the failing test case
options.why: Deleting evidence of the bug is the opposite of engineering — and instantly visible.

options.text: Apologize repeatedly for running out of time
options.why: Apologies don’t score; a crisp diagnosis of the remaining gap does.

scenarios.title: Behavioral: ‘Tell me about a conflict’
scenarios.context: The behavioral round. The interviewer asks about a disagreement with a teammate.

steps.prompt: How do you open the answer?

options.text: Two sentences of situation, then your task — STAR structure, tight
options.why: STAR’s S+T set context fast; the bulk of the time belongs to your actions.

options.text: Five minutes of backstory so they ‘really understand’
options.why: Long setups burn the clock; interviewers score actions and results, not prologues.

options.text: Jump straight to the result — the ending is what matters
options.why: Results without context aren’t evidence; the situation makes the result meaningful.

options.text: Start with how frustrated you felt
options.why: Feelings-first framing centers emotion over professional behavior — the story should show judgment.

steps.prompt: Mid-story you realize you’re running long. What do you do?

options.text: Land the Action and Result in the next 30 seconds — compress, don’t trail off
options.why: Pacing discipline: the A and R carry the score, so protect them even when compressing.

options.text: Speed up and cram in every remaining detail
options.why: Rushed detail is unintelligible; a compressed landing beats a frantic data dump.

options.text: Ask ‘should I keep going?’
options.why: Outsourcing pacing to the interviewer signals you can’t manage your own time.

options.text: Skip to ‘and it all worked out’
options.why: Skipping the Action deletes the evidence — the part being scored.

steps.prompt: Follow-up: ‘What would you do differently?’ Strongest answer?

options.text: Name one specific thing you’d change and what it would have changed
options.why: Shows reflection and growth with a concrete counterfactual — exactly what the question probes.

options.text: ‘Nothing — it worked out’
options.why: Claims of perfection signal zero self-awareness; every real story has a lesson.

options.text: Explain why it was really the teammate’s fault
options.why: Blame in the reflection turn fails the ownership test outright.

options.text: Give a generic ‘I’d communicate better’
options.why: Vague lessons aren’t lessons; specificity is what makes reflection credible.

choices: all rejects on the first rejection; allSettled waits for every outcome
mockTasks.explain: all short-circuits on first failure; allSettled reports each promise’s fulfilled/rejected status.

choices: Pages revalidate in the background on an interval — fresh without rebuilds
mockTasks.explain: Stale-while-revalidate at the page level: serve cached, regenerate on schedule.

mockTasks.q: let is the right scope function when you want to:
choices: Transform a (possibly null) value and return the result
mockTasks.explain: let’s lambda returns its last expression — the transform-and-return shape.

mockTasks.q: A packed struct is required when:
choices: The memory layout must match an exact wire/disk format with no padding
mockTasks.explain: Protocols define byte-exact layouts; compiler padding would corrupt the format.

mockTasks.q: A mock differs from a stub in that it:
choices: Verifies interactions (calls made), while a stub just returns canned data
mockTasks.explain: Stubs provide state; mocks assert behavior — over-mocking couples tests to implementation.

mockTasks.q: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. The amortized cost per append is:
mockTasks.explain: The O(n) copy cost of a resize is spread over the ~n/2 appends since the last resize: O(1) each.

mockTasks.q: Cursor pagination avoids the ‘missing rows’ problem of offset because:
choices: It pages relative to a stable key instead of a shifting row number
mockTasks.explain: New inserts shift offsets; a keyset cursor anchors to the last seen key, immune to shifts.

mockTasks.q: Promise.then callbacks run before setTimeout(0) callbacks because:
mockTasks.explain: The spec processes the entire microtask queue after each macrotask — promises always win the race.

mockTasks.q: A BFF mainly solves:
choices: Over/under-fetching by shaping responses per client
mockTasks.explain: Each client gets an aggregation layer tuned to its screens instead of N chatty service calls.

mockTasks.q: Protocol extensions with default implementations enable:
choices: Shared behavior across conforming types without a base class
mockTasks.explain: Mixins via extensions: types gain behavior by conforming, no inheritance chain required.

mockTasks.q: @MainActor on a class guarantees:
choices: Its methods run on the main thread — safe for UI work
mockTasks.explain: The compiler enforces the hop: UI-touching code can’t accidentally run elsewhere.

mockTasks.q: StateFlow suits UI state because:
choices: It always holds the latest value and replays it to new collectors
mockTasks.explain: New collectors (e.g. after rotation) immediately get current state — no missed updates.

mockTasks.q: Priority inheritance fixes inversion by:
choices: Temporarily boosting the lock holder to the blocked high-priority task’s level
mockTasks.explain: The holder can’t be preempted by medium-priority tasks anymore, so it releases the lock promptly.

mockTasks.q: p99 latency of 2s means:
choices: 99% of requests were faster than 2s — 1% were slower
mockTasks.explain: Percentiles describe the distribution’s tail: p99 is the near-worst case users feel.

mockTasks.q: The most robust way to handle duplicate deliveries is:
choices: Idempotent consumers, so reprocessing is safe
mockTasks.explain: Duplicates are inevitable in distributed systems; idempotency makes them harmless.

mockTasks.q: The 0/1 knapsack decision at each item is:
choices: Take it or skip it, respecting remaining capacity
mockTasks.explain: The 0/1 constraint forces a binary choice per item: dp[i][w] = max(skip, take).

mockTasks.q: useCallback’s purpose is:
choices: Preserving function identity across renders so memoized children don’t re-render
mockTasks.explain: A new function identity each render defeats memo on children; useCallback stabilizes it.

mockTasks.q: PKCE exists to protect:
choices: Public clients (mobile/SPA) that can’t keep a secret — the code exchange is bound to the challenger
mockTasks.explain: Without a client secret, PKCE’s code_verifier/code_challenge pair prevents authorization-code interception.

answerBank.q: Walk me through how you’d analyze the time complexity of your solution.
answerBank.a: I state the Big-O bound, which case it describes, and the dominant operation — e.g. ‘O(n log n) time worst case from the sort, O(n) space for the output array.’ Then I sanity-check it against the constraints: does n log n fit n = 10⁵? Saying it out loud while pointing at the code turns the analysis into gradable evidence.

answerBank.q: How do you approach a system design question?
answerBank.a: Requirements first (functional + non-functional, asked out loud), then back-of-envelope estimation with stated assumptions, then API and data model, then the happy-path architecture, then scaling bottlenecks and failure modes. I think aloud and treat the interviewer as a collaborator — and I close by naming the tradeoffs I’d revisit with more time.

answerBank.q: Two pointers vs sliding window — when is each the right call?
answerBank.a: Two pointers for pair-finding on ordered data (sorted two-sum, container with most water) or fast/slow traversal (cycle detection). Sliding window for contiguous subarrays under a constraint (max sum of k, longest substring without repeats) — expand right, shrink left while the constraint is violated. Both are O(n) time, O(1) space; the signal words are ‘pair’ vs ‘contiguous.’

answerBank.q: How would you design a rate limiter?
answerBank.a: Requirements: per-user/IP limits and burst policy. Algorithm: token bucket if bursts are allowed, leaky bucket for smoothed output — I’d state the choice and why. Distributed state in Redis with a Lua script for atomic check-and-decrement, and RateLimit-* headers so clients can program against it.

answerBank.q: Tell me about a conflict with a teammate.
answerBank.a: STAR, two minutes: brief situation and my task, then the bulk on my actions — what I did, why, and how I handled their perspective — then the measurable result and one specific thing I’d do differently. I own my part of the conflict; blame never appears in my version.

answerBank.q: REST vs GraphQL — how do you choose?
answerBank.a: REST for resource-oriented CRUD with cacheable endpoints; GraphQL when clients need varied, nested data and over/under-fetching hurts (mobile, aggregations). I always name GraphQL’s costs: harder caching, query-complexity limits, and N+1 resolvers needing batching. The choice follows the clients’ data needs, not hype.

answerBank.q: Your solution works but is O(n²). How do you optimize it in the round?
answerBank.a: I name the bottleneck operation out loud, then reach for the standard unlocks: a hash map to turn lookups O(1), sorting to enable two pointers or binary search, or recognizing the DP substructure. I state the new complexity and verify it against the constraints before rewriting — optimizing the wrong bottleneck wastes the round.

answerBank.q: Walk me through how you debug a tough production bug.
answerBank.a: State the stakes fast, then narrate hypotheses tested — not a heroic montage. Name the tools per step (logs for what happened, traces for where, debugger/watchpoints for state), include the wrong turns honestly, and land the lesson plus what changed afterward. War stories score on method and honesty.

answerBank.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with a technical decision.
answerBank.a: Use STAR: the situation in two sentences, your responsibility, what YOU did (raised the concern with the tradeoff analysis, proposed the alternative with its costs), and the measurable result plus the lesson. Interviewers score evidence of behavior — make your decisions explicit, and show you can disagree and commit.
